News.title: British Airways jet seconds from disaster over London after pilot blunder in one of ‘most serious near misses in years’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MID-AIR SCARE British Airways jet seconds from disaster over London after pilot blunder in one of ‘most serious near misses in years’

A BRITISH Airways jet was “seconds from disaster” after stalling when a pilot blundered above London at around 4,000ft, it has been revealed.

Sources said the first officer’s error required a physical intervention by the captain as the Airbus A320 was on its approach to Heathrow.

They called it: “The most serious ‘near miss’ in the UK in years”.

The drama on Flight BA919 from Dusseldorf took place above Canary Wharf on July 6.





The Sun understands that one of the aircraft’s air data systems had failed on it.

It is said the jet suffered a stall and the captain had to step in to overide the first officer’s initial input to try and remedy the problem.

A source said: “To recover from this position is difficult, especially so low to the ground.

“It is unheard of for a captain to physically intervene in the cockpit.”

Senior figures acknowledged there was almost a “hull loss” — the aviation term for when an aircraft is destroyed or seriously damaged.

The captain is now understood to be grounded on “stress leave”.

The incident has been listed as “Loss of Control In-flight” and branded as “Pilot Induced”.

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch has launched a probe into the “serious incident”.



BA said it was assisting the investigation and the Civil Aviation Authority said it could not comment on an ongoing review.

News.title: Fears herd of elephants have been poisoned as 15 die after mystery illness that paralysed babies & mums before death
News.content:
ELEPHANT TRAGEDY Fears herd of elephants have been poisoned as 15 die after mystery illness that paralysed babies & mums before death

THERE are fears a mystery poison has wiped out 15 elephants after a deadly illness left mums and babies paralysed before they suddenly died.

The shocking die-off has sparked an urgent investigation in southern Kenya near Amboseli National Park.



Ten of the 15 elephants suffered the same terrifying symptom – partial paralysis that left them unable to stand before they died within a day or two.

The other five carcasses were too badly decomposed or had been scavenged, leaving experts unable to establish what killed them.



Only one of the dead elephants was a bull, with most of the victims females and calves.

The elephants died between June 24 and July 24, with all the carcasses discovered outside the park on community land around 10 to 20 miles from its boundaries.

KWS head of communication Duncan Wanyama said the bodies were found at different locations between around 15km and 30km from the park’s boundaries.

The Kenya Wildlife Service said there is currently no evidence pointing to a single cause.

But preliminary tests on tissue samples at a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a “potential toxic substance”.

A separate analysis by a government laboratory came back negative for the toxins tested.



Further tests are now under way as experts race to uncover what caused the devastating deaths.

KWS said: “Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source,”

The authority said there was no risk to humans.

Experts are examining the carcasses and tissue samples have been sent to laboratories to establish whether disease, poisoning or another factor is to blame.



The alarming deaths have triggered fears of a repeat of previous elephant poisonings linked to poaching and human-wildlife conflict in Kenya.

The scale of the catastrophe is particularly chilling because it is the worst elephant die-off recorded in the Amboseli ecosystem for decades.

Officials said the deaths are the first mass elephant mortalities on this scale recorded in the region for decades, after successful efforts to crack down on poaching.

The victims included elephants of different ages and sexes, suggesting the deaths were not confined to one family or demographic.



Amboseli and its surrounding ecosystem straddles the border with Tanzania and is one of Africa’s most famous wildlife landscapes.

The region is home to more than 2,000 elephants, according to figures from the Amboseli Trust for Elephants in 2025.

The spectacular park is famed for its vast savannahs and breathtaking views of Mount Kilimanjaro across the border in Tanzania.

It is also home to some of Africa’s last “super tuskers” – giant bulls whose enormous tusks weigh more than 45kg (100lb).

One of the most famous, Craig, died in January aged 54 after fathering numerous calves.



KWS said there are plans to preserve Craig’s remains for public display.

The latest mystery echoes a devastating elephant die-off in Botswana’s Okavango Delta in 2020.

More than 350 elephants died in the shocking outbreak, which was later linked to toxic cyanobacterial blooms in waterholes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Scientists said warming temperatures and changing rainfall patterns had helped create the conditions for the deadly blooms.

Now Kenyan wildlife experts are desperately trying to establish whether the Amboseli deaths have a similarly sinister environmental cause.

News.title: New £20k reward in bid to solve chilling ‘murder’ mystery of boy, 8, who vanished during Charles and Diana’s wedding
News.content:
'COUNTLESS QUESTIONS' New £20k reward in bid to solve chilling ‘murder’ mystery of boy, 8, who vanished during Charles and Diana’s wedding

COPS have launched a fresh appeal to solve the chilling murder of an eight-year-old boy who vanished on the day of Prince Charles and Princess Diana’s wedding.

A £20,000 Crimestoppers reward is still being offered for information that could finally crack the 45-year mystery of what happened to schoolboy Vishal Mehrotra.



Vishal disappeared from Upper Richmond Road in Putney, South West London, on July 29, 1981, as millions celebrated the royal wedding.

Seven months later his body was found 50 miles away in a wooded area at Alder Copse near Rogate, West Sussex, in February 1982.



No one has ever been charged over his murder.

Today, on the 45th anniversary of his disappearance, detectives renewed their plea for anyone with information to come forward.

A Sussex Police spokesman said: “Detectives investigating the murder of eight-year-old Vishal Mehrotra have launched a fresh appeal for information on the 45th anniversary of his disappearance.

“Vishal was reported missing on July 29 1981 having disappeared from Upper Richmond Road, Putney, London, on the day of the then Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer’s wedding.



“Metropolitan Police carried out a thorough missing persons inquiry over several months until Vishal’s remains were found in Alder Copse, a wooded area near the village of Rogate, on February 21 1982.

“It then became a murder investigation, led by Sussex Police, working closely with the Met.

“Despite extensive inquiries and multiple investigative reviews taking place since that time, the case remains unsolved.”

Detective Chief Inspector Mark Cullimore, the senior investigating officer, said Vishal’s family spent decades searching for answers.

He said: “We know Vishal’s murder caused deep shock and heartbreak to his family and that they have spent every day since his disappearance determined to find answers as to what happened to him and who was responsible.



“Over the years, our investigation has fully examined numerous lines of inquiry – including those raised in documentaries and podcasts – to try and identify any suspects.

“We have thoroughly explored any new investigative techniques or forensic opportunities that have arisen since 1981 through advancements in technology, and we have conducted two comprehensive reviews to identify any other viable inquiries that should be completed.

“Unfortunately, there remains no evidence to show who was responsible for Vishal’s tragic death.



“We are asking anyone with any information relating to Vishal’s disappearance and murder to please get in touch with us – no matter how small or insignificant you think a piece of information might be, it could be key in helping us get justice for Vishal and provide the answers his family so desperately need and deserve.”

Vishal’s younger sister, Mamta Mehrotra, said the pain of losing her brother had never faded.

She said: “I was only a little girl when my brother Vishal disappeared, but the impact of losing him has stayed with me every day of my life.

“For many people, this case is something they may have seen in the news, a documentary, or a podcast.

“For us, Vishal was not a headline. He was a son, a brother, a child with his whole life ahead of him. He was loved, and he is still loved.



“More than four decades have passed, yet we still do not know what happened to him. We still do not know who took him from us or why.”

The £20,000 Crimestoppers reward remains available for information leading detectives to the person responsible for Vishal’s murder.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Officers urged anyone who remembers seeing Vishal on the day he disappeared, or who has any information about his death, to come forward.

They say even the smallest detail could prove vital.

News.title: Phone of Brit woman, 38, found dead in Athens suitcase was ‘being used by mystery person after she lost her life’
News.content:
A MYSTERY person was chillingly using the phone of a dead Brit woman in the days after she lost her life, according to Greek media.

The victim, named locally as Elisabeth Ross, was found stuffed in a suitcase in an abandoned building, sparking a major Interpol probe.



Elisabeth, 38, is believed to have flown from Edinburgh to the Greek capital on June 26 and was staying at friend’s house.

She was last heard from on July 15, three days before a homeless man allegedly discovered her body.



Forensic tests suggested that she died a number of days before she was found.

Elisabeth’s mobile phone has now become a key focus of the case, with sources from the “Greek FBI” telling local media that it remained active after she died.



A mystery user was reportedly sending messages, potentially intended to create the impression that she was alive.

But once the case made headlines, the phone was said to be eerily switched off.



Do you know more about this tragedy? Please contact joseph.mannion@the-sun.co.uk or Whatsapp 07840651456

Cops are now keenly awaiting the results of toxicology tests to determine the circumstances of Elisabeth’s death.

Attempts are being made to track her final movements by analysing CCTV footage and identifying witnesses who saw her last.



Her body was found at 7 Evelpidon Street in the neighbourhood of Kypseli on July 18, shortly after 1pm.

There were no visible wounds on the body or any clear signs of a struggle, police confirmed.

But cops suspect she was “lured” to the location by a “homeless person” who “left her in the state she was found,” an official told The Times.

A homeless man who reportedly first found the victim inside the building which had been deserted for at least two years.

He entered a room inside and found the suitcase on the ground.



Police rushed to the scene but initially couldn’t identify the woman as she reportedly had no identification on her.

They announced she was aged around 30, approximately 5ft 4in with reddish hair tied in a bun and wearing black shorts and a T-shirt.

Her shorts had French university insignia on them which led investigators to believe she wasn’t a local Greek resident, local media reports.

One Greek officer told The Sun: “To find a foreign national dead in a suitcase here in the heart of Athens is a first.

“In the history of Greek British relations, it is unprecedented.”



The mysterious nature of her death sparked an instant probe by Greek officials who called on Interpol and US investigators to help.

Police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou previously told Skai TV authorities were treating the incident “as a criminal act, given how the body was found”.

Local hotels are also being searched to try and locate the victim’s final movements.

Interpol typically get involved in such cases when a national police force requests international cooperation for cross-border crimes.

The British embassy in Greece and the woman’s father have reportedly been informed of her death.



An autopsy is expected to be carried out in the coming days to determine how she died.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.

“Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An FDCO spokesperson told The Sun: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time.

“We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

DOG HORROR Three people rushed to hospital after ‘XL-bully dog attack’ at home – as armed cops swoop on residential street

THREE people have been rushed to hospital after they were injured in a dog attack.

Police and an air ambulance rushed to the scene Hall i’ Th’ Wood, Bolton at around 3.30pm today.

Three people are in hospital following reports of a dog bite at an address in Barrie Way.



Witnesses reported that an “XL-bully type” dog was seized as police dog units and armed officers attended the scene.



It is understood that armed police went into a house with a dog handler.

The animal was then removed and placed in an animal transport van.

Greater Manchester Police said enquiries are ongoing and no arrests have been made.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Officers were called just before 3.30pm on Wednesday 29 July 2026 to a report of a dog bite at an address on Barrie Way in Bolton.

“Emergency services attended and three people have been taken by ambulance to hospital.



“One dog has been seized. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing.”

News.title: When will the July heatwave end? Met Office forecast
News.content:
THE UK’s latest heatwave is reaching its peak, bringing high temperatures and official weather alerts across the country.

With temperatures set to climb as high as 35C in the South East, many people are looking ahead to when cooler conditions may return.



What is the Met Office’s definition of a heatwave?

According to the Met Office, a heatwave is declared when a location records at least three consecutive days with daily maximum temperatures meeting or exceeding a specific threshold.

These thresholds vary by UK county to reflect local climate conditions:



25C for Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales, and parts of northern/western England

for Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales, and parts of northern/western England 26C to 27C across central and southern counties

across central and southern counties 28C for Greater London

Late July has met these criteria across large parts of England and Wales, confirming that the UK is officially experiencing its fourth heatwave of Summer 2026.

Provisional Met Office data shows July has run 3C above average nationwide, putting it on track to rank among the top three or four warmest Julys on record.



The current spell peaks on Wednesday (July 29) with temperatures reaching up to 35C in the South East.

In response, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued an amber heat-health alert covering London, the South East, East Midlands, and East of England from Tuesday until Thursday.

How long will the heatwave last?

Relief from the heat is on the horizon as the current spell breaks heading into August, yielding to more changeable weather before high pressure returns later in the month.

According to the official Met Office long-range weather breakdown, the start of August will bring a noticeable shift in weather conditions.



Sunday, August 2 – Tuesday, August 11

“Mostly dry away from the north and northwest initially, where scattered showers are expected.

“There is a chance that some other western parts could see some rain by the end of the weekend.

“Temperatures ranging from around average in the North West to warm in the South East, perhaps becoming very warm in the South East through the weekend.

“It will probably become more changeable thereafter, with potential for an area of low pressure to move close to or across the UK early in August.

“This could bring spells of heavy rain and perhaps some strong winds for some areas.



“It may become more settled again towards the end of the first week of August.”

Wednesday, August 12 – Wednesday, August 26

“Dry and settled conditions will probably dominate much of this period with high pressure patterns tending to affect the UK.

“This may be interrupted at times by Atlantic frontal systems, especially in the north, or thunderstorms in the south.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“However, overall rainfall amounts will likely be below normal.

“Temperatures will probably be above normal and some spells of hot weather and heatwaves are possible, especially in the south.”

News.title: Dozens fall ill with ‘severe’ food poisoning at sold-out festival after ‘eating at Yorkshire Pudding stall’
News.content:
PUD PERIL Dozens fall ill with ‘severe’ food poisoning at sold-out festival after ‘eating at Yorkshire Pudding stall’

DOZENS of revellers at a sold-out festival were struck down with severe food poisoning after reportedly eating from a Yorkshire Pudding stall.

Environmental health officials are investigating after being told about a spike in food poisoning cases at Truck Festival in Steventon, Oxfordshire.



One festival-goer claimed unwell revellers “mobbed” the toilets as the outbreak unfolded at Hill Farm last weekend.

It quickly emerged that most of those who reported upset stomachs had bought food from The Yorky food stall.



Around 30,000 people attended the four-day bash, which cost £320 a ticket and featured stars such as the Maccabees, The Wombats and Two Door Cinema Club.

Dubbed the “UK’s most warped village fete”, the event has been running since 1998 and is known for its wacky entertainment.



But it was revellers’ stomachs that were left feeling unusual after the event.

The festival’s website previously featured a picture of the stand, although this has now seemingly been removed.



A screenshot taken before the image disappeared shows the eatery being promoted as “traditional Yorkshire roast wraps with trimmings”.

It offered British roast pork, premium pork sausage, roast chicken and a “Giant Yorkshire Pudding with creamy mash potato”.

Steakhouse chips, stuffing, gravy and mushy peas were also on the menu.

The outbreak was reportedly so severe one woman had to be taken to John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford for further tests, with doctors told her she had suspected food poisoning, the Daily Mail reports.

Revellers have since complained online about the outbreak.



One person wrote on the Truck Festival Facebook group: “Shall we discuss the elephant in the room – who else got food poisoning from a f***ing Yorkshire Pudding?

“Having the trots with those toilets is NOT for the faint of heart.”

A second reveller replied: “Yup, only just recovered. Luckily I was staying off site, how on earth people managed who camped.

“Definitely needs to be reported. Yorky need to review their practice. And Truck need to review who they invite to sell to their punters.”

The customer complained to Truck Festival and later received an apology email which read: “I can tell you that on Sunday morning we were made aware of similar reports via our medics.



“Our health and safety team was able to quickly identify the suspected source as a third-party vendor which was removed from operation within 90 minutes of the first report.

“During the day we also completed and passed on a report to the local Environmental Health Officer, who we are assisting in carrying out further investigations.”

One disgruntled festival-goer said they complained to staff at the stall about how the chicken in their £17 meal was not cooked properly. It was not clear if she ate the food or ended up unwell.

Another told the Daily Mail: “It soon became clear that a lot of people were ill. A couple camping next to us were in the medical tent all day on Sunday.

“I saw a lot of people repeatedly rushing to the toilets which were mobbed. The medical tent was handing out Imodium left, right and centre.”



The reveller added that the stall was immediately shut down when the issue became clear – but only after people had been eating from it for all of Saturday.

Some of those affected are now considering legal action, the report said.

The Yorky is believed to be operated by the Cardiff-based firm Event Mobile Catering.

The company services the biggest festivals in the country, including Glastonbury, Boomtown, Download and Creamfields.

It also serves up grub at iconic national sport venues like Silverstone and the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.



A spokesman for Truck Festival told the Daily Mail: “On Sunday morning, our on-site medical team received reports from a number of attendees with similar symptoms.

“Our Health and Safety team launched an immediate investigation and identified a third-party food vendor as the suspected source. That vendor was removed from operation within 90 minutes of the first report.

“We reported our findings to the local Environmental Health Officer the same day and are supporting their ongoing investigation into the cause.

“We share the disappointment and frustration of those whose weekend was affected.”

Vale of White Horse District Council confirmed the festival had informed it of a number of revellers reporting food poisoning symptoms.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The council is now investigating alongside the food stall, the UK Health Security Agency and the trader’s local registering authority Cardiff City Council.

The Sun has approached The Yorky’s operating company, Event Mobile Catering, for comment.

News.title: Mother & husband arrested after he finds 5 dead babies in boxes at home following ‘row with her about what was in them’
News.content:
BABY TRAGEDY Mother & husband arrested after he finds 5 dead babies in boxes at home following ‘row with her about what was in them’

A MOTHER and husband have been arrested after he found five dead babies in boxes at home following a row with her about what was in them.

The macabre remains were found at the couple’s apartment in Orange, south-east France, on Monday.



The 32-year-old mother had reportedly given birth to a healthy baby around the same time before being taken to hospital with “abdominal pain”.

She was discharged before being arrested two days later on Wednesday.



Her partner was also taken into custody.

The shocking case is now being treated as one of France’s most serious alleged infanticide investigations.

Following the grim discovery, an investigation has been into the murder of a minor under 15.

The grim discovery came after the husband argued with his wife about cardboard boxes inside their home.

The couple cannot be named for legal reasons.

An investigating source said: “The woman was complaining about abdominal pain when they argued, the day after she gave birth on Sunday.



“The husband stayed behind when she was taken to hospital, and looked inside the cardboard boxes they had been arguing over – that’s when he found the five dead babies.

“All the foetuses were decomposing, and had a been around for quite a while.”

The five sets of remains were reportedly found inside the same plastic bag.

A source close to the investigation told Le Parisien that the horrified husband took the bag to the hospital, which then alerted police.

The woman had reportedly suffered three failed pregnancies before giving birth to the latest baby.



She is also understood to suffer from the psychological disorder pregnancy denial.

The Public Prosecution Service has contacted child welfare services over the couple’s two other children.

The pair have a boy and girl aged eight and 12, as well as the newborn baby.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Prosecutors also want the juvenile court to decide the fate of the little boy born on Monday evening.

The newborn was reportedly healthy after being delivered at home on Sunday, according to a source cited by La Provence.

News.title: Dementia UK demands urgent social care reform amid Andy Burnham's passionate pledge
News.content:
Dementia UK demands urgent social care reform amid Andy Burnham's passionate pledge

EXCLUSIVE: Affected families have waited far too long for a social care support with many now at crisis point, Dementia UK warns, as the charity tells leaders to get around the table

View 3 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets residents and staff members as he visits a care home (Image: Getty Images)

Dementia UK has demanded the the Prime Minister to make the difficult decisions to tackle the crisis-hit social care sector head-on now.

‌



Andy Burnham today invited opposition leaders for urgent talks to give people the dignity and support they deserve by finally getting a grip of the creaking system. He says the government has reached a fair pay agreement to come in for the 2028/29 financial year - but says he wants a bigger reform to lift the drained social care workforce.

‌



Dementia UK say they are encouraged by the launch of the Big Conversation but say the changes need to come and soon. They say urgent social care reform is required now after the new PM accused politicians of a 'shameful' response to the issue with families at risk of being plunged into debt and poverty

‌



View 3 Images He vowed to sort out social care as he delivered a speech in north London (Image: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PA Wire)

Dad with dementia makes deathbed confession that 'shocks' entire family READ MORE :

'There's an urgent need for reform'

Speaking to the Mirror, James White, Head of Campaigns at Dementia UK, said: "Families affected by dementia have waited far too long for a social care system that works for them. Every day, Dementia UK hears from people navigating a fragmented system, often without specialist support, pushing them to crisis point. Bringing forward the Commission’s timetable is a positive step in recognising the urgent need for reform.

“A national conversation on this scale is an important opportunity to hear directly from people who use social care and the families who support them. People affected by dementia must be at its heart, and their experiences must meaningfully shape the Casey Commission’s recommendations and the Government's response.

‌



"Baroness Casey has already recognised the need for better support for people affected by dementia. The Government must now turn that recognition into practical reform. The real test will be whether families can access co-ordinated, specialist support from diagnosis through to the end of life.”

The comments come as TV favourite and former Mirror columnist Fiona Phillips' husband said Mr Burnham's proposals for social care offered hope as the Labour leader received early backing from one of the country's most high-profile campaigners on the issue.

Martin Frizell, 67, began caring for Fiona at home when she was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s in 2022 after months of brain fog and anxiety symptoms.

‌



Since then, he has repeatedly urged the government to do more for carers, highlighting his own struggles with mental health and the sense of "guilt" that comes with balancing work and full-time care. Fiona first revealed her diagnosis to the Mirror in July 2023 after living with the condition for 18 months.

View 3 Images Fiona Phillips' husband has praised the proposals for social care

Burnham's bid to help his dad and ' millions like him'

The Prime Minsiter, whose father also has Alzheimer’s, promised to reform social care to help "my dad and the millions like him" faced with the unfairness of the current system.

‌



His first steps include accelerating Baroness Louise Casey’s review of social care so it will report next year, drawing up reforms to improve the "strength and the capability" of the workforce, and holding cross-party talks with the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to find a consensus on the issue.

Age UK also welcomed Mr Burnham's speech today as the PM outlined his plans to fix social care. Caroline Abrahams, the charity's director, said: “The Prime Minister made clear today that he is totally committed to fundamental social care reform and that can only be a good thing for older people.

"These are exciting times and we look forward to hearing a lot more after the summer break, if not before.”“It’s right that the Prime Minister has asked Louise Casey to accelerate her independent commission so it reports in a year’s time and we hope the Big Conversation she launched today will help to draw out what the public want to see from social care, as well as thinking through the funding options.

Article continues below

"We won’t all necessarily have to pay more as individuals for a better system of social care but it’s likely we’ll have to pay differently: at present older people often face big bills when they are in crisis- for example after a fall. It would be much better if we followed the example of many other developed nations & paid in to a big pot in advance or after our deaths, so when we need care it’s there for us, however much or little money we actually have.”

News.title: France wildfires live: 42C heatwave threatens nuclear plant after shock arrests
News.content:
A scorching heatwave threatens to force the closure of the Golfech nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after operations at the site resumed following a 17-day shutdown

A scorching heatwave threatens to worsen wildfires and force the closure of a nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after it came back online.

The Golfech nuclear power plant was shut down for 17 days after temperatures in the River Garonne, from which the plant draws water to cool its reactors, approached the regulatory limit of 28C. But France's latest heatwave - which will see temperatures in the region soar to 42C today - could force state-owned electricity company EDF to shut the plant down again.

Meanwhile, astonishing arrests have been made as firefighters continue to battle wildfires that have ravaged 42,000 hectares of south-west France and spread into parts of the Bordeaux metropolitan area. More than 220,000 people in the Gironde region have been evacuated over the past week in what has been France's largest peacetime evacuation.

But while many have sought refuge in evacuation centres, a handful of people have instead found themselves in police custody. A man was arrested after allegedly "posing" as a psychologist offering paid counselling sessions to those affected by the fires, French police told Sky News.

Two men were arrested several days ago on suspicion of "stealing food and supplies" intended for those affected by the wildfires, the broadcaster reported. Officers have been standing outside evacuation centres and fire-ravaged areas to keep people safe and ensure restricted zones are protected.

Although the regional prefecture said the wildfires remain "stabilised", with "several flare-ups" brought under control overnight, officials warned weather conditions remain "unfavourable" today.

News.title: Furious Donald Trump issues Iran a chilling threat with foul-mouthed outburst
News.content:
Furious Donald Trump issues Iran a chilling threat with foul-mouthed outburst

US President Donald Trump, who met Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, swore in a rant about attacking Iran after Tehran again targeted a US base in Jordan

View 4 Images Donald Trump has made an angry outburst (Image: AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

US President Donald Trump has let out a foul-mouthed outburst threatening to "beat the f***ing sh** out of Iran" after attacks on US bases throughout the Middle East.

‌



Responding angrily to the latest missile firings by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) he declared: “We're going to beat the f***ing sh** out of them. We’ll be hitting them hard. They’re going to get a beating."

‌



Tehran’s elite IRGC claimed they had targeted a US base in Jordan with ballistic missiles but the US the weapons were all shot down. The assault happened shortly after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with the US President in Washington on Tuesday. On Wednesday US Centcom said the attack originated from Iran, but all missiles were intercepted.

‌



Gary Lineker shows FIFA disgust in four-word response to Gianni Infantino bombshell READ MORE :

View 4 Images US-Saudi strikes hit Iraqi pro-Iranian militia hard (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

It said: “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in an attempted surprise attack on U.S. forces based in the Middle East.” In a separate flare-up a joint US-Saudi attack launched waves of airstrikes across seven provinces of Iraq in an effort to hit pro-Iranian militia.

‌



Around 20 fighters were killed and 32 were wounded in the attack as the Iran war looks set to continue to expand across the region. The US military confirmed that the attack was in response to dozens of attacks by pro-Iranian fighters in Iraq in recent days.

In a statement Centcom said the US and Saudi forces struck “multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites” in eastern Iraq on Tuesday, retaliating against more than 30 drone attacks in the past three days by “Iran-aligned terrorists.”

View 4 Images US leader Donald Trump and Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu are pictured during their meeting (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



All of those killed in the joint US-Sadui attack were thought to have been in the Iraqi Popular Mobilisation Forces, which was formed in 2014. Many of its main forces that belong to the Shia faction trace their origins to the insurgency against the UK and US forces. They went on to battle the Sunni Islamic State terror group in Iraq and have been mobilised by Tehran to act on its behalf against the US.

And according to Gaza health officials two Palestinians have been killed and 29 others injured in Gaza over the past 24 hours. One of the fatalities was a new death, while the other succumbed to earlier wounds. Additional victims remain trapped under debris or lie dead on roads with Palestinian Civil Defence crews unable to reach them, the ministry said in a statement.

View 4 Images Mourners carry coffins after Iraqi pro-Tehran PMF fighters killed (Image: AP Photo/Hadi Mizban)

Article continues below

Since the so-called Gaza “ceasefire”, the Health Ministry has recorded 1,209 deaths and 3,943 injuries, alongside 803 bodies retrieved from the rubble. The toll since the outbreak of the war in October 2023 now stands at 73,335 killed and 174,052 wounded. The latest wars across the Middle East were sparked by the 2022 October 7 attacks by Hamas on Israel. As Israeli retaliatory attacks got underway on Gaza, Hezbollah in neighbouring Lebanon attacked and this drew Iran into the conflict.

News.title: Armed police swarm street after three injured in suspected 'XL-bully' rampage
News.content:
Armed police swarm street after three injured in suspected 'XL-bully' rampage

Armed police and other emergency services rushed to a property in Barrie Way, Bolton, following reports of a dog attack with three people rushed to hospital

View 2 Images A witness claimed the dog appeared to be an "XL-bully type" (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

Three people have been rushed to hospital following a suspected by an "XL-bully type dog".

‌



Police said they were called just before 3:30pm today to reports of a dog bite at an address in Barrie Way, Bolton.

‌



An air ambulance landed at Hall i' Th' Wood, a manor house in Bolton now used as a museum, with paramedics attending the scene alongside police dog units and armed officers.

‌



View 2 Images The incident took place at a property in Barrie Way

Free apples in Tesco for next few weeks for certain customers at 800 stores READ MORE :

The force confirmed that three people were taken to hospital by ambulance and that a dog had been seized, reported by witnesses to be an "XL-bully type".

Armed police were seen going into the house, alongside a dog handler who removed the animal from the house and placed it in an animal transport van.

‌



GMP said that enquiries were ongoing with no arrests made, reported the Manchester Evening News.

In a full statement a spokesperson said: "Officers were called just before 3.30pm on Wednesday 29 July 2026 to a report of a dog bite at an address on Barrie Way in Bolton.

"Emergency services attended and three people have been taken by ambulance to hospital. One dog has been seized. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

‌



The Government moved to ban XL bullies in 2024 with then Prime Minister Rishi Sunak saying they posed a “danger to our communities” following a spate of attacks by them. Statistics show that incidents involving dogs have risen by more than a third over the previous five years - and more than a third involved the now banned dog.

Unregistered pets can be seized and owners fined and prosecuted. February 1, 2024, was the deadline for owners to register the banned dogs with around 40,000 put down on the list before that date.

Other banned breeds in the UK include the Pit Bull Terrier, Japanese Tosa, Dogo Argentino and Fila Brasileiro.

Article continues below

And the government announced last month it will introduce new safety measures for banned dog breeds. In an update shared in Parliament on June 9, it was said that the new measures will protect children from dangerous dogs at home and will strengthen safeguards around banned breeds, including XL Bully types.

From November 1, 2026, owners must not leave a child under the age of 12 in close proximity to a banned breed dog in a domestic setting or other private settings without adult supervision. This will be a condition of the Certificate of Exemption, which allows owners to legally keep a banned breed.

News.title: 'Flash drought' declared in half of England as heatwaves result in driest July on record
News.content:
'Flash drought' declared in half of England as heatwaves result in driest July on record

Multiple UK regions have officially been declared in drought as farmers warn crop damage could trigger higher supermarket prices and even shortages of baking potatoes

View 5 Images Almost half of the UK is in drought (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Almost half of England has officially been plunged into drought after a succession of sweltering heatwaves has resulted in the driest July on record.

‌



The Environment Agency has declared drought across seven regions spawning central, eastern and southern England, warning the country is now using water faster than nature can replace it.

‌



Farmers say the prolonged dry spell is already damaging crops, forcing supermarkets to push up prices - and could even lead to shortages of some vegetables, including baking potatoes.

‌



The areas now officially in drought are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the entirety of London, the Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex, which covers Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and Gloucestershire.

View 5 Images A view of a very dry Primrose Hill, London (Image: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

England has received just 7% of its average July rainfall, while southern England has seen only 1% of what would normally be expected.

‌



The Environment Agency said the combination of a dry spring, a hot summer and repeated heatwaves has triggered a "flash" drought, despite reservoirs and groundwater being replenished by a wet winter.

The announcement comes as parts of the UK endure a fourth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures climbing into the 30s.

Three earlier wildfires have already fuelled wildfires, damaged rivers and wildlife, hit agriculture and prompted hosepipe bans affecting millions of people.

‌



Many farmers say the impact is already severe. Paul Francis, of Long Farms in Suffolk, said the lack of rainfall had significantly reduced yields of rapeseed, potatoes, onions and carrots, with vegetables also expected to be smaller than usual.

"You feel helpless," he said. "England is usually good for enough rain for crops and we work hard to grow them but the weather can spoil it."

View 5 Images Some UK areas have experienced a fourth heatwave (Image: ANDY RAIN/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



He warned there could be shortages of baking potatoes and onions this year, adding that supermarkets should increase prices to better support farmers facing mounting losses.

National Farmers Union deputy president Paul Tomkins said: "Farmers and growers have always had to contend with the weather, but what they are experiencing now is climate change in action.

"Across every sector and every part of the country, farmers and growers are seeing first-hand the impact of dry weather and drought, with more extreme conditions making it harder, riskier and more costly to produce the nation's food."

‌



The NFU is urging ministers to make it easier for farmers to build reservoirs and store water by simplifying planning rules and introducing more flexible water abstraction licences.

Water minister Emma Hardy said: "Our climate is changing, droughts are becoming increasingly common, and we need to be prepared for this new normal.

"We're delivering long-term change in the water industry and driving record investments in infrastructure, including nine new reservoirs.

‌



View 5 Images Low water levels at Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex (Image: Tony Kershaw / SWNS)

"We expect water companies to follow their drought plans, to go further and faster to reduce leaks, and to ensure supplies are not disrupted even in the driest of weather."

Robert Palmer, deputy director of climate and campaign organisation Uplift, said: "For weeks we've watched wildfires destroy homes, crops and wildlife. Half the country is now suffering from drought. Climate breakdown is no longer a threat in the future – it's here now.

‌



"Yet politicians are still considering new oil and gas drilling – the very thing driving the climate crisis. Rather than listening to the fossil fuel lobby and Donald Trump, our leaders must follow the science, which shows that the world already has far more oil and gas than can ever be safely burned.

"Every new oil and gas field approved, particularly on the scale of the Rosebank oil field, will lead to more harm – more severe drought, worsening wildfires, more floods.

View 5 Images Forecasters say there won't be significant rain in the coming days (Image: Tony Kershaw / SWNS)

‌



"Governments need to act now, not just on how we adapt to these frightening changes, but to stop them from getting worse. That means standing up to the oil and gas firms and saying no to new drilling and Rosebank."

Forecasters say little meaningful rain is expected before next week, and even then only small amounts are forecast.

Met Office meteorologist Liam Eslick said the high-pressure system dominating the UK's weather is likely to persist into August and the first half of September, reports the Independent.

Article continues below

"We want a good soaking, a good long period of rain to come, but in the forecast at the moment, especially over the next few days, there's not actually a lot going on for England," he said.

"The only time we may see a little bit more in the way of extensive rain is possibly on Sunday evening into Monday. There may be some heavier bursts, but it's not going to be long-lived. It's not going to provide anything substantial for England."

News.title: 'Fixing social care is personal for Andy Burnham - and a second chance on unfinished business'
News.content:
Andy Burnham’s speech on social care was deeply personal.

Ditching his notes, he spoke for 30 minutes about his desire to fix the broken system that is causing misery for families, carers and the NHS.

His voice broke at the end, when he said he would face up to the challenge for millions of people, including his dad Roy who has Alzheimer’s.

Burnham, who is close to his parents, has spoken about his heartbreak that his father doesn’t know that he has become the Prime Minister.

‌



His speech was fuelled by the frustration and anger of engaging with the system - but high praise for those working in it.

He said carers should be the “best paid in society not the worst”, and overseas workers should know they are appreciated.

The praise for foreign born workers who care for his dad is significant.

Assisted dying debate should only come after hospice and care changes, says Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 2 Images 'Prime Ministers don’t always speak this frankly. But this is Burnham’s style - politics is personal' (Image: Kirsty Wigglesworth/Pool AP via)

‌



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has come under fire for immigration reforms that would make it harder for people to settle in Britain, including care workers. His comments suggest there may be some wiggle room to help carers.

Prime Ministers don’t always speak this frankly. But this is Burnham’s style - politics is personal.

It’s also unfinished business for Burnham. As Health Secretary under Gordon Brown, he called for a national care service in 2009.

He tried to build cross-party consensus but the Tories branded the idea of taxing people's estates after they died as a "death tax". Labour was booted out of power the following year.

‌



Since then, nothing has changed. Successive PMs tried and failed to reform social care. Theresa May was forced to drop plans to get people to pay more - dubbed a "dementia tax". Boris Johnson claimed he had an "oven ready" plan and then kicked it down the road.

Keir Starmer made a start, commissioning Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Louise Casey to look at it and promising cross-party talks - but little progress was made.

Now Burnham has a second chance.

He says he's willing to stake his political capital on it. He'll need to. It will take enormous energy and political skill to get it right.

‌



Already, Reform is accusing him of bringing in a "death tax" and the right-wing papers are screaming about tax rises.

But social care cannot be ignored any longer. Our society is ageing and some 2million people in England have unmet care needs. The NHS desperately needs to be able to discharge patients safely into the community.

If Burnham wants to build a lasting legacy as a PM, he must fix this mess.

News.title: Prince Harry could face paying millions out of own pocket after failed legal action
News.content:
Prince Harry could face paying millions out of own pocket after failed legal action

Prince Harry was among seven household names who sued the publisher of the Daily Mail accusing it of unlawful information gathering but a High Court judge dismissed the claims

View 4 Images Prince Harry at the High Court in London earlier this year (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Prince Harry could have to pay millions of pounds from his own pocket to cover the costs of his failed legal action against the publisher of the Daily Mail.

‌



A group of seven household names, including the Duke of Sussex, Sir Elton John and Baroness Doreen Lawrence, sued Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL), accusing it of unlawful information gathering. ANL strongly denied the claims. Earlier this month, following an 11-week High Court trial in London, the claims were dismissed in their entirety in a 436-page judgment.

‌



Today, the case returned to the court for a hearing over costs where it was heard that there was a shortfall between the insurance cover and ANL’s costs, which are more than £34million.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry lost his legal case against the publisher of the Daily Mail (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

At the hearing, lawyers for ANL said the group of household names, which also include Sadie Frost, Elizabeth Hurley, David Furnish and former MP Sir Simon Hughes, should pay its costs on an indemnity rather than a standard basis, which would be more favourable to ANL in terms of the amount they can recover.

Antony White KC, for the publisher, said the legal claims were brought for a “collateral purpose” of trying to pressure the Government into introducing the second stage of the Leveson Inquiry, describing it as “a campaign rather than ordinary and reasonable litigation”.

‌



The barrister said that the cases “were launched in a blaze of publicity knowing that these were likely to attract significant attention on the world stage” with a press release in October 2022.

Discussing the high-profile figures, Mr White said: “They knew that this was an all-out attack on Associated. They were at pains to emphasise that there were others who could join the bandwagon.”

Mr White also said he was “sad” to say that Baroness Lawrence was “recruited as the national treasure”, adding: “That is a matter of regret for my client, but it is not to be shrunk from.”

‌



The barrister later criticised the breadth of the allegations and how they “shifted”.He said that the claimants cast a “strikingly wide” net for their claim “in the hope of catching some fish”. He said that the court should “step back and ask itself why the net was cast so wide”.

View 4 Images Among the high profile claimants was Baroness Doreen Lawrence (Image: PA)

Mr White added that “the answer surely is that these proceedings were brought as a vanguard, or first wave” of cases ahead of a “banquet of litigation”. Nicholas Bacon KC, for the group of claimants, said that Mr Justice Nicklin should not award ANL their costs on the stricter, indemnity basis.

‌



The barrister said in written submissions that it could be “very significant” if the group of seven had to pay ANL’s costs on this stricter basis and could lead to them being without enough insurance cover.

He said that on the standard basis, a judge will need a good reason to award more costs than were set out in court-approved budgets, but this does not apply when costs are awarded on an indemnity basis.

Mr Bacon said that ANL’s incurred costs as of earlier this month were nearly £34.5 million, which “exceed its approved budget” by more than £18.6 million.

‌



He continued: “The above figures reflect an astonishingly high legal spend by Associated and an entirely cavalier approach to the principle of proportionality and the overriding objective, which seeks to ensure that parties are on an equal footing.”

The barrister added that the group of seven household names have obtained insurance cover of a combined £16.2 million. Mr Bacon said: “At that level of cover, the claimants would reasonably expect to be insured for the total of Associated’s incurred costs and approved estimated costs.

View 4 Images Sir Elton John was among the claimants (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“If the claimants were required to pay Associated’s costs on the indemnity basis, however, the current level of cover would be insufficient to meet their total costs exposure, possibly to the tune of many millions of pounds.” The barrister later said that the group had “conducted themselves honestly and in good faith”.

He continued: “In particular, the court largely accepted the claimants’ evidence, commended their straightforward answers and declined to find that any of them were in any way dishonest.”

Mr Bacon said that it was “always inevitable” that the cases would attract publicity and that it was “unrealistic to expect that the claimants themselves would remain wholly silent”.

‌



He added: “The court did not find in its judgment that the claimants did not genuinely believe they had been the victims of unlawful information gathering or that the allegations they pursued in their claims, as reflected in the press release of October 2022, were made disingenuously.”

Mr Bacon said that the cases “were neither speculative nor weak” and had merit, with the breadth of the allegations “carefully monitored and crafted” by the judge through case management decisions.

Article continues below

He also said: “It must follow from the outcome of the court’s decisions on the evidence, which went against the claimants, that they should pay Associated’s costs of the claims. It would, however, be unjust to make an order that they do so on the indemnity basis.”

The hearing before Mr Justice Nicklin is expected to conclude today or tomorrow, with a decision due in writing at a later date.

News.title: Six 'dine-and-dashers' spark police manhunt after unpaid £600 seafood bill
News.content:
Six 'dine-and-dashers' spark police manhunt after unpaid £600 seafood bill

Police are investigating six diners at The Oyster Shack in Bigbury, Devon, who allegedly dashed off in a black Range Rover without paying a bill of nearly £600

View Image The diners allegedly left The Oyster Shack without paying (Image: theoystershack/Instagram)

A group of six diners tucked into their meals at a seafood restaurant before allegedly slipping away without settling a bill of almost £600.

‌



Police are investigating the customers of The Oyster Shack in Bigbury, Devon, who are claimed to have dashed off in a black Range Rover last Saturday and the restaurant has heard nothing from them since.

‌



There was a party of three men and three women who ordered four lobsters and a fruits de mer seafood platter before heading out one by one without settling their bill, said the restaurant.

‌



Free apples in Tesco for next few weeks for certain customers at 800 stores READ MORE :

The group accumulated a tab of almost £600 before fleeing and since then The Oyster Shack says it has made repeated attempts to reach the diners on the contact number provided at the time of booking, according to Devon Live.

And the restaurant's owner stated in an update on Wednesday that the group has yet to make contact and they have left the matter now with the police.

Kieron Vanstone, owner of The Oyster Shack, said: "We've given them a deadline for response but they're still dodging our calls. We have left the matter with the police."

‌



While also on Facebook the restaurant stated: " For a small independent restaurant like ours, this isn’t just a financial loss, it’s incredibly upsetting for our staff, who worked hard to provide a warm welcome, only to have their trust abused.

"We’re sharing this not to shame anyone, but to warn other restaurants, pubs and local businesses to stay vigilant if they encounter a similar group."

While the restaurant's CCTV system was unfortunately out of action at the time, a fellow diner managed to note down the registration plate of the black Range Rover the group is believed to have departed in, and all available information has since been handed over to the authorities.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for Devon and Cornwall Police confirmed that they were looking into the incident and they have appealed for anyone with information to get in touch.

The statement read: "Police are aware of an incident where a number of customers left The Oyster Shack, Bigbury, without paying their bill on Saturday 25 July.

"Enquiries into this matter are ongoing. Anyone with any information that may assist investigating officers is asked to call police on 101 or visit our website quoting 50260196491".

News.title: More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares
News.content:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covers much of central, eastern and southern England, and is a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.

It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.

North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.

Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.

News.title: Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
News.content:
In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms.

"I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"

For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".

But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.

The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.

Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.

He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.

The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".

Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.

The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".

News.title: Moment police officers set foot in 'horror scene' funeral home
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing

Boxes of tissues sit on a coffee table in a front room at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors. There are opulent chairs, upholstered in pale yellow; a black and white print of a trawler that nods to Hull's fishing heritage.

It feels like an attempt to put customers at ease, painting the picture of a caring, community-led business.

But on the other side of a partition wall - an area Legacy's director Robert Bush ordered an employee to keep hidden from others in the industry - is a labyrinth of dimly-lit corridors.

A police officer shines her torch into messy side rooms, strewn with rubbish and in total disorder.

"It's strange, innit?" she remarks.

News.title: Saudi Arabia's dilemma as it tries to stay out of US-Iran war
News.content:
Saudi Arabia is facing a difficult dilemma. Ever since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February, the Saudis have largely tried to stay out of it.

But now, after being attacked from three sides, the Saudis have had enough. This week, they carried out joint strikes with the US on Iranian proxy militias in Iraq who they believe have been launching drones at the Kingdom.

For Saudi Arabia the dilemma now is whether to keep on hitting back as a deterrent, or whether to try to de-escalate the situation, perhaps by paying off some of their adversaries.

So who is attacking who and why?

First, a bit of context. There are broadly two sides in the conflict that has been consuming the Gulf and other parts of the Middle East for five months now.

On one side there is Iran and its Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). Allied to them are the Houthis in Yemen, a tribal group who took over much of the country in 2014.

Also backed by Iran are the Popular Mobilisation Forces in Iraq, the paramilitary group that has allegedly carried out 30 drone strikes on Saudi Arabia and has now been attacked in return.

Then there is Hezbollah in Lebanon, still a potent force but one that is currently lying low.

News.title: Police to take no further action against Polanski over guillotine re-post
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has said it will be taking no further action after Green Party leader Zack Polanski re-posted a photo of a man wearing a T-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

In a statement, the force said it did not believe sharing the picture constituted an offence.

However, it added that the wearing of the T-shirt should be recorded as a crime and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset Police, who cover Bristol where the photo was taken.

Polanski previously told the BBC he had made an "inadvertent mistake" by re-posting the image.

In response to the Met's decision, a Reform UK spokesman said: "Once again we see that we are living in two tier Britain."

Reform UK reported Polanski to the police on Monday after he shared the Instagram post.

The Green Party of England and Wales leader had shared the photo, which he said was the fifth image in a series of 20, having accepted a request to collaborate with the Instagram account of a photographer at an event.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Polanski said: "If I'd done it deliberately I'd be apologising but because this was a mistake I think the important thing is that I point out this was a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence, and also crucially I make a commitment to be better on social media."

Announcing the decision to take no further action, a Met Police spokesperson said: "We absolutely understand the reaction to this image being shared online, particularly in the context of increasing threats towards politicians.

"We take the safety and security of those in public life, including politicians, very seriously.

"Where we identify threats we take appropriate action and where there is evidence of offences we will investigate.

"While there will be people who will argue that those who shared the image in this Instagram post should be subject to criminal action, our review has concluded that on this occasion, the threshold is not met."

News.title: Some tech shares are plunging - what does that mean for the AI revolution?
News.content:
The euphoria for this technology has boosted the value of some world's biggest companies even as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on the building blocks of the technology.

But over the last few weeks, the value of some of the companies that make those building blocks has plummeted - prompting some to question whether what some have dubbed "the AI bubble" is about to burst.

Some of the sharpest falls have been in Asia, with shares in Korean chip makers such as SK Hynix and Samsung down 46% and 35% respectively over the last month as investors worry the recent boom in demand for the chips that power AI is unsustainable.

Yet these shares still are up threefold and fivefold respectively over the last year, leading many to conclude that some caution and profit taking after such massive gains was inevitable â and indeed healthy.

The South Korean stock market is notoriously volatile, but concerns have spilled over into the big US companies.

Shares in Google and Tesla plunged briefly before recovering last week after both firms pledged to spend billions more on AI in the months and years to come despite so far it losing them money.

And with other big names such as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon reporting their latest financial results this week, investors have the opportunity to scrutinise just how much these companies are now betting on AI.

"There is still a healthy degree of scepticism about the ability of these investments to generate a commensurate level of return," Russ Mould, an investment director at AJ Bell, said.

But according to leading tech investor Eileen Burbidge despite the concerns there's not yet a serious reckoning.

"The AI bubble hasn't burst but it's letting out air," she told the BBC.

News.title: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina
News.content:
Fifa has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over their behaviour after their World Cup final loss to Spain and throughout the tournament.

Last week, the world governing body appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at the New York New Jersey Stadium, with multiple Argentina players and backroom staff involved in altercations with Spain players following their 1-0 loss in July.

On the recommendation of the prosecutor, Fifa will investigate Argentina players Nahuel Molina (two counts) and Leandro Paredes (three counts), and Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala (one count) for alleged assault under article 14 of Fifa's disciplinary code.

Molina may also face disciplinary action for one count of alleged unsporting behaviour under article 14.

Team-mate Thiago Almada and Spain midfielder Gavi are also accused of the same breach.

Under Fifa's disciplinary code, players and officials face at least a one-match suspension for unsportsmanlike conduct and at least three matches for assault.

News.title: Peppa Pig owners win copyright battle against 'impostor' Wolfoo
News.content:
In a ruling this week, the judge said "all videos featuring Wolfoo" must be taken down before 16:00 BST on Monday.

Hasbro and Peppa Pig's creators Astley Baker Davies Ltd originally took court action in London in 2022.

They claimed SConnect had attempted "to deceive the young Wolfoo viewership, most aged between two and five, into believing that Wolfoo is the same character as Peppa Pig" or connected to Peppa, the judge wrote.

The companies initially complained about Wolfoo's appearance and artwork, but focused their legal case on the audio because they believed it would be easier to prove that sound clips were directly copied.

The evidence of "copying of the audio clips is compelling", the judge decided.

"That copying was extensive, seemingly endemic at least so far as the English language Wolfoo videos are concerned."

SConnect denied the copyright infringement claim but accepted that some Wolfoo videos made before mid-2020 included audio from Peppa Pig because an independent third-party contractor had used the clips without the company's knowledge.

SConnect said all infringing videos were removed, and that Wolfoo animations made after mid-2020 used only voices and sounds that were created in-house.

However, the judge said the fact the sounds were supplied by a third party was "irrelevant"; that while many infringing videos were removed, some were simply moved to other channels; and that the claim that all new sounds were recorded in-house "can be disproved".

BBC News has asked SConnect for comment.

The judge said clips from Peppa Pig were found in all 92 English-language Wolfoo videos that were examined, and about 75% of the foreign-language videos.

News.title: Serial killer given whole life orders for murders of two men as police investigate four more deaths
News.content:
Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said.

He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.

News.title: Libel claim against Matt Hancock thrown out
News.content:
In April last year at the High Court, Mrs Justice Collins Rice said she believed there were "compelling reasons for further investigation at trial" and refused Hancock's attempt to have the claim thrown out.

Earlier this year, Hancock appealed against that decision and Lord Justice Warby, sitting with Lady Justice King and Lady Justice Whipple at the Court of Appeal, said in a judgment on Wednesday that Mrs Justice Collins Rice had "erred in law".

"The Holocaust was a deliberate genocidal campaign to eradicate an entire people for motives of ethnic or religious prejudice. The Covid vaccine rollout was not," the judge said.

"On the undisputed facts it was, at least in part, a benevolent public health programme with the aim of saving lives."

He added that Bridgen's post "did not suggest that the vaccine rollout was worse than the Holocaust, but it did expressly suggest some form of comparability" and that it suggested the vaccines were a "crime against humanity".

Hancock was granted a summary judgment â a legal step which ends the claim in his favour without a trial.

Afterwards he said it was a case that "should never have been brought" and that "people must be free to state their own opinions without fear of libel action".

"I was right to call out what I clearly saw were anti-vax and antisemitic conspiracy theories, and this judgment reaffirms that right," he added.

Posting on X after the judgment, Bridgen said the three judges at the hearing in May were "clearly thinking about declaring me the winner".

He added: "Yet nine weeks later that same panel produced a unanimous written judgment in which they found against me on every single point, thus handing the victory to Mr Hancock without a trial, and labelling one of my arguments 'egregious', a point not put to my legal team at the oral hearing.

"It is hard to understand why the written judgment does not reflect what took place at the oral hearing."

Bridgen said he would be seeking advice to see if he could take the case to the Supreme Court.
