Newcastle denied any falling out between Hall and Howe following media reports which highlighted the player's frustrations.

However, leading up to the World Cup, the youngster was granted limited minutes towards the conclusion of the campaign.

It is understood he feels the lack of game time was a factor that contributing to his omission from the Three Lions squad that travelled stateside.

Newcastle eventually finished a disappointing 12th in the Premier League, having achieved a fifth-placed finish to secure Champions League qualification the previous year.

3 Shaw has played nearly every minute under Carrick Credit: Getty

Levelling up

Presenter Angelina Kelly added: "If I was Lewis Hall I would feel disrespected that you’ve lost your place to Dan Burn. That cost him his place at the World Cup, essentially because of what Eddie Howe decided to do at Newcastle.

"So, I would be absolutely fuming if I was him, and I would be looking at Newcastle and thinking, ‘you don’t value me, so I’m going to go somewhere that will.’

"I think Man United would value him because, we have to be honest about our full-backs, we’ve been struggling.

"Are Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw of the calibre we need to challenge for a Premier League title? No."

Newcastle have not sold a player to United since Andy Cole completed a then-British record £7million move in January 1995.

Hall scored twice at Old Trafford during the 2023/24 campaign in what was a 3-0 victory for Newcastle in the Carabao Cup and again in a 3-2 defeat at the end of that season.

Sports.title: Brazilian footballer slapped with unusual punishment for breaking opponent’s leg
Sports.content:
A Brazilian footballer been banned for up to six months after being handed an unusual punishment for breaking another player’s leg.

Internacional defender Victor Gabriel was shown a straight red card for a sickening challenge on Cruzeiro winger Gabriel Pec last week.

5 Gabriel has been handed a serious punishment for his studs-up red card challenge Credit: ge

Pec, who was making his debut for Cruzeiro after joining from LA Galaxy, was left with a fractured left tibia after the studs-up tackle.

And while Gabriel was immediately given his marching orders on the pitch, he has now been dealt an even harsher sanction.

Eye for an eye

Brazil’s Superior Court of Sports Justice - the country’s highest independent body for discipline - has dished out a never-before-seen punishment.

Gabriel has now been suspended until Pec returns to training following his recovery from the leg break.

With such injuries having no clear timeline for recovery, the ban has been capped at a maximum of six months.

Brazil’s Superior Court of Sports Justice said: “The offender may remain suspended until the injured party is able to return to training, respecting a maximum period of 180 days.”

While Gabriel is now staring at a lengthy spell out of action, he can still launch an appeal on the decision.

The 25-year-old told the court that his horror challenge was 'a completely unfortunate incident'.

Gabriel had only been on the pitch for 14 minutes when he flew into Pec as he looked to stop a Cruzeiro counter attack.

The referee initially played the advantage before pulling play back to send off the Internacional man, while Pec was stretchered off after blood could be seen pouring from his leg.

5 Gabriel sent Pec flying into the air with his horror challenge Credit: ge

5 Gabriel put his head in his hands after being given his marching orders Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

At his hearing, Gabriel told the court: "I apologised to him [Pec] and offered my help.

"I asked him ‌to forgive me for not having had any ill intent, and all I could do at that moment was pray for him.

"Since that night, it's been incredibly difficult for me. My whole life I've prepared for moments of happiness, and instead, it's been sleepless nights."

Punishments for a red card vary according to country, with Premier League and EFL players getting a one-match ban, which can be extended to three for serious foul play or violent conduct.

UEFA and FIFA also both ban players for one match but can add extra sanctions, such as a fine, for an especially serious offence.

US player Folarin Balogun was fined $40,000 (£30,000) for 'serious foul play' during the World Cup, but controversially saw his one-game ban suspended after President Donald Trump's intervention with FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

5 Gabriel had been making his 16th league appearance of the season, which ended in dismissal Credit: Getty

Road to recovery

As both players prepare for a lengthy spell away from the pitch, Pec has since undergone successful surgery following the career-threatening tackle.

In a statement shared on Instagram, the seven-cap Brazil Under-23s star wrote: “The surgery was successfully completed.

“To the honour and glory of God. Without Him, none of this would have been possible.

“I thank and praise the Lord for the lives of the doctors – Sergio, Rodrigo and Gustavo.

“I also want to thank all the supporters, family members, friends and staff. Thank you for so many messages of love and affection.

“In the midst of this challenge, I have chosen to keep my eyes fixed on Christ.

5 Pec joined Cruzeiro earlier in July after two years at MLS side LA Galaxy

“He is my strength, my refuge, my fortress, where I find peace and joy. And I have been learning to find contentment even in the midst of trials.

“I am doing my best to recover as well as possible and as quickly as I can so I can continue doing what I love. My dreams and goals remain intact.”

After both players' saw their involvement end with the horror tackle, Pec's Cruzeiro teammates went on to claim a 2-1 win in the Brazilian top-flight clash with Internacional.

Sports.title: Saudi boxing chief Turki Alalshikh on verge of breaking into English football with EFL club
Sports.content:
Saudi boxing chief Turki Alalshikh on verge of breaking into English football with EFL club

Saudi boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh is on the verge of breaking into English football with Derby County.

According to reports, the independent football regulator is set to make a decision on Alalshikh's investment into the Championship club next week.

3 Alalshikh has transformed boxing since his involvement in the sport Credit: Getty

The Daily Telegraph's John Percy states that the EFL have completed all the necessary background checks on the Saudi Arabian businessman.

And sources suggest that the Rams are confident that the major investment will be approved after the interest first emerged in May.

Derby have been out of the Premier League since 2008 when they recorded the worst season in Premier League history.

They managed to accumulate just 11 points and have been into League One since then as well.

But Alalshikh is prepared to invest heavily and try to return the Rams to England's top flight.

This wouldn't be the first time that Alalshikh has involved himself in football, though.

He has owned Spanish club Almeria and Egyptian side Pyramids FC in the past but has been looking to invest in EFL clubs.

Alalshikh's wealth

The latest reports suggest that Alalshikh is worth $2.8billion, and he has accumulated that wealth from various means.

He is the chairman of the Saudi GEA and is heavily involved in boxing.

Alalshikh is one of the leading figureheads in Riyadh Season, which has transformed boxing and put on some of the biggest fights in history.

3 Alalshikh doesn't lack ambition or money Credit: Getty

He is widely seen as the mastermind behind the 'Battle of Britain' between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

A new boxing venture between he and Dana White and Frank Warren known as Zuffa Boxing has been brought into existence with big plans.

Alalashikh is also a close advisor to the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia, Mohammed bin Salman.

Advice

talkSPORT's Simon Jordan revealed last year that he advised Alalshikh on which English club to buy.

So, his interest in English football has been around for over a year now.

He actually told the Saudi supremo to buy Sheffield Wednesday.

3 Derby could be set for a very bright future Credit: Shutterstock

Speaking about that conversation in 2025, Jordan said: “If I was buying a football club and I was really motivated and had your kind of dough, I would buy Sheffield Wednesday."

Expanding on that, Jordan said: “I told him that. We’ll see what they do; they are captains of their own ship, aren’t they?

“Be careful what you wish for. We’ve already got enough foreign investment in our football clubs, but if this is the direction of travel, that’s the way I’d go.

"It’s a big football club.

“There’s a reason why Hillsborough got used up to a point, for FA Cup semi-finals.

“But I’ve been to that club, I’ve watched it, I’ve seen the fan base. I know the Saudis can look across the city at Sheffield United and think their mate who owns that football club hasn’t had the greatest of times over there, but I think it’s a powerhouse."

“You buy a powerhouse like Sheffield Wednesday that’s in Yorkshire, not just Sheffield, that could be garnered and pushed forward, no disrespect to [current owner, Dejphon] Chansiri, but somehow or another he’s managed to steal defeat from the jaws of victory."

In the end, Alalshikh chose not to take Jordan's advice but his interest in English football never went away.

He is now one step away from adding Derby to a growing portfolio of sporting acquisitions.

Sports.title: John Stones better than Virgil van Dijk as he’s ranked against Premier League and England greats
Sports.content:
John Stones better than Virgil van Dijk as he’s ranked against Premier League and England greats

John Stones is England's greatest defender since Bobby Moore, according to talkSPORT's Rory Jennings.

The former Manchester City centre-back has also been hailed as better than Virgil van Dijk ahead of his move to Serie A.



5 Stones has been hailed as England's best defender since World Cup-winning captain Moore Credit: Getty

Stones is a free agent having left City at the end of last season, bringing a trophy-laden decade at the club to an end.

The 32-year-old is set to join reigning Italian champions Inter Milan on a two-year deal.

His imminent arrival comes despite interest from the likes of Chelsea and Arsenal this summer.



Prior to Stones completing the switch, Jennings and Ade Oladipo debated his legacy live on Drive.

England's 'greatest' defender

Before the comparisons to Van Dijk, Jennings labelled the former Everton man as England's best defender for 60 years.



He exclaimed: "Greatest (England) defender since Bobby Moore. Of course he is.

"He’s England’s greatest defender. If you look at what he’s done."

Stones has won 94 caps for the Three Lions since making his debut aged 20 in 2014, scoring three goals.



Meanwhile, this summer's World Cup represented his sixth major international tournament.

Turning his attention to Stones' City achievements, Jennings pinpointed the 2018/19 Premier League title race.

5 Jennings believes Stones has a greater Premier League legacy than Van Dijk Credit: talkSPORT

Pep Guardiola's side were crowned champions as they finished one point clear of Liverpool, who lost just once all season.



The Reds' only defeat came away to City in January 2019, with Stones making a crucial goal-line clearance during the 2-1 victory.

Highlighting the importance of Stones' intervention, Jennings said: "Liverpool would have won the league that season. Liverpool lost one game that entire season. They lost one game.

"And the reason that they lost one game that entire season and didn’t win the league, the year that Man City won the league, was because John Stones produced a season-defining clearance off the line.

"So when people talk about great moments when teams have won the league, you want to talk about what Arsenal did at Anfield in 1989.



"You want to talk about what (Sergio) Aguero did against Queens Park Rangers. People should talk about what John Stones did. 1.12cm to clear that ball off the line, it won City the league.

5 Van Dijk has won more individual accolades during his Premier League career but has just two Premier League titles to his name Credit: Getty

"So when you say there hasn’t been the moment, there’s the moment."

Stones' Premier League legacy

The debate quickly turned to Stones' standing amongst the Premier League's best defenders, namely Van Dijk.

Asked if he had ever been the best centre-back in the league, Jennings replied: "I would argue that John Stones, being at the heart of a Manchester City defence.



"A Manchester City team that retained a league title for four years in a row, won a treble, allowed Pep Guardiola to almost redefine the way that teams play football.

"What Pep Guardiola did, and he chose John Stones to do, was win a treble. The way they won that treble was because of what happened to John Stones."

However, Oladipo hit back with his own argument for Van Dijk, who has been a near ever-present for Liverpool since 2018.

5



He explained: "Virgil van Dijk, apart from the injury season, has played 50 plus games every single season he’s been at Liverpool.

"In fact, he’s played every minute of every Premier League game, barring the injury hit season, since he’s been at Liverpool."

Jennings continued to back Stones, though, who won six Premier League titles and the treble during ten years at City.

Having joined the club from Everton in 2016, he made a total of 295 appearances across all competitions.



He responded by stating: "He’s been there for the entirety of Pep Guardiola. So Pep Guardiola, when they were spending all of that money, when they had all of those riches, when they were winning all of that silverware, he was an ever-present.

"They never felt like they needed to move him on. They never ever felt like they needed to improve upon him."

Jennings continued: "It would always be Stones and (Vincent) Kompany. Then it became Stones and (Ruben) Dias. Then it became Stones and (Aymeric) Laporte.

"It was always Stones plus one if Stones was fit, always. The way that he played for Man City, the amount of trophies that he won. He’s won as many league titles as Rio Ferdinand."



Van Dijk 'best in the world'

Oladipo hit back by referencing Van Dijk's status within world football, having finished second behind Lionel Messi for the Ballon d'Or in 2019.

He recalled: "I think he’s a fantastic defender, but you’re talking about Virgil van Dijk, who at one stage in his career was considered the best defender in the world.

"He was the favourite for the Ballon d’Or, people say he was robbed of the Ballon d’Or. So this is not even a defender discussion. He was considered the best player.

"John Stones has never been considered the best defender, let alone the best player."



5 Oladipo hailed Van Dijk's standing in the global game as well as lauding Stones' ability Credit: talkSPORT

For Jennings, though, Stones' legacy is also boosted by his off-field behaviour.

He concluded: "I say this as a compliment to John Stones, but he’s not at all newsworthy. He’s not at all newsworthy.

"I genuinely don’t know his wife’s name. I know John Terry’s wife’s name. I know the story of various footballers because they’re almost tabloid-like.



"John Stones is just a consummate professional who’s never put a foot out of line, who’s done his job to the maximum of his potential for 10 years.

"He’s served Man City for ten years, for Pep Guardiola’s entire reign, in the most dominant period of club football in this country’s history.

"For some reason, and I’m not suggesting you’re part of this because I know you respect him and I know you rate him very highly, but I don’t think that people rate him that highly."

Stones has twice been named in the PFA Team of the Year during his career.



He was also included in the FIFPRO World 11 in 2023 following City's treble triumph.

Sports.title: Arsenal told the one transfer that would be biggest in Premier League history could also win them the biggest prize
Sports.content:
Arsenal told the one transfer that would be biggest in Premier League history could also win them the biggest prize

Vinicius Junior would be the biggest signing in Premier League history.

That is the view of talkSPORT host Rory Jennings who was discussing the Real Madrid star's possible move to Arsenal, which now appears to be unlikely.



4 Vinicius Junior is on Arsenal's list of targets for the summer Credit: Getty

That is because talkSPORT understands that Real boss Jose Mourinho wants the winger to remain at the Bernabeu.

Real Madrid have also opened talks with the forward in an attempt to extend his contract.

Brazil international Vinicius has one year left on his mega deal in Spain, but progress has been made on a new one, with the LaLiga giants determined for him not to leave on a free next summer.



Arsenal's interest in the 26-year-old has been internal, with the Gunners fully aware of Real's intention to keep him.

But should a new deal not materlialise, Arsenal are prepared to make the 26-year-old the highest paid player in the club's history.



And should that happen, Jennings feels it would be massive.

Speaking to on talkSPORT Drive, he said: "It would be absolutely massive for the Premier League, but you have to look at through the lense of Arsenal and what this means for Arsenal.

"They are behaving exactly as they should. Being champions of England comes with a power, it comes with opportunity, and they are making the most of it.



"If he lands at Arsenal and is the missing piece to them winning the European Cup, it immediately becomes money well spent.

"Off the top of my head, biggest signing in Premier League history.

"When Paul Pogba went to Manchester United. That was big."

4 Pogba's transfer from Juventus to Manchester United was enormous Credit: Getty

Co-host Ade Oladipo then chipped in.

"As good as Pogba was, he was never in the Ballon d'Or conversations.

"No one ever said Pogba is the best player in the world.

"When three years ago, Vinicius Jr probably was that."

Jennings added: "This is definitely up there as one of the biggest transfers that has ever happened in Premier League history.

"This is one of the biggest transfers that has ever happened in football.



"If they sign Vinicius Junior, who is at the peak of his powers, and you could argue his best football is still to be played.

"He is undeniably world-class. There is no way anyone can defy Vinicius Junior as not world-class.

"He's in the top two in his position. The only player potentially better than him in his position is Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

"For Arsenal, it would be such a statement, and I think Arsenal fans were feeling that the transfer window was underwhelming, but this is how you behave as champions.



"Vinicius Junior coming in transforms the frontline, and it is very intimidating."

4 Arsenal are looking to win back-to-back Premier League titles for the first time in their history Credit: Getty

Money, money, money

If Arsenal were to get encouragement and make a move for Vinicius, it would be an eye-watering deal.

Despite having a year left on his deal, Jennings doesn't believe he would go for anything less than £100m.



He said: "I don't think you could bid for less than £100million.

"He might have a year left, but you are not going to get him if you don't bid that kind of money.

"Real Madrid will try to woo him and try to make him stay and sign a new deal.

"Jose Mourinho wants him to stay, so you are going to have to do something to allow Florentino Perez to present this as a victory.

"They can't say he's surplus to requirements because the money needs to be big and Perez can present it to the Real Madrid faithful as a victory."



Reports suggest that in terms of wages, Vinicius is looking for around £470,000 per week, blowing the wage structure.

Bukayo Saka is believed to be the highest paid player at the club, but this would dwarf his wages.

4 Vinicius Junior is an electric forward player, who would rip up the Premier League Credit: Getty

Other huge deals

In terms of fees, there have been some massive deals in the Premier League, but it is very rare you get a true superstar player from another league moving to the UK.



Andriy Shevchenko and Michael Ballack - two icons of the game - moving to Chelsea in 2006 were notable transfers as was Manchester City's blockbuster deal for Erling Haaland in 2022 given he was one of the most sought after players in Europe.

There have also been plenty of superstar transfers within the Premier League from Alan Shearer's then-world record £15million move to Newcastle United from Blackburn Rovers in 1996 to Robin van Persie ditching Arsenal for Manchester United in 2012.

There have also been several players who've arrived in the Premier League as relatively unheralded and turned into multiple winners and legends.

Mohamed Salah, Yaya Toure and Kevin De Bruyne all spring to mind.

But when it comes to world's best players from other leagues joining Premier League sides, it is very rare.



As a result, you can see why Jennings believes it would be the biggest signing in Premier League history.

Sports.title: Roberto De Zerbi hands transfer ultimatum to Lucas Bergvall amid Tottenham exit talk
Sports.content:
Roberto de Zerbi has said he would like Lucas Bergvall to stay at Tottenham, but admitted he cannot promise him a starting role.

Sweden midfielder Bergvall is keen to leave Spurs this summer in order to get more regular game time, with several Premier League clubs chasing his signature.



5 Lucas Bergvall has made 78 appearances for Tottenham since joining in 2024 Credit: Getty

So far, the north London outfit have rejected advances from Nottingham Forest and Newcastle for the 20-year-old.

Forest have had at least one offer of £38million knocked back, while the Magpies failed with a £46m bid for Bergvall earlier this month.

Meanwhile Brighton are also keeping tabs on him, who are yet to make any formal contact with Spurs over a potential deal, but the Swede has caught the eye of their data-led recruitment team.



talkSPORT understands Bergvall has informed Tottenham chiefs of his desire to find a new club, after failing to nail down a starting berth.

Despite representing Sweden at the World Cup, the youngster cut his his summer break short to join his Spurs teammates on the club’s pre-season tour of Australia and New Zealand.



With his future still up in the air, Bergvall was handed a surprise start for his side's penalty shootout win over Sydney FC on Wednesday.

No promises

Following Tottenham's pre-season victory in Sydney, head coach De Zerbi admitted he made mistakes in his handling of Bergvall towards the end of last season, as his side narrowly avoided relegation.



And while the Italian admitted he is keen for Bergvall to stay, he reiterated his previous stance that the club will not stand in the way of players wanting to leave, and refused to guarantee him more than a squad role.

De Zerbi said: "I'm always being very clear with him and with you. I would like that he stays with us.

"I think he's potentially a top, top, top player. But then I don't want to convince anyone to stay. Tottenham is already, without me, a top club and we are not to convince anyone to stay.

5 Roberto De Zerbi has been frank about Bergvall's position at Tottenham in his first pre-season as head coach Credit: AFP



5 Bergvall started his first match of Spurs' pre-season tour against Sydney FC Credit: Getty

"He can find the space if he stays with us. The competition within the players will be very strong because we are Tottenham and we have to build a strong squad - not just 11 players - especially considering a lot of injuries we suffered in the last two, three seasons.

"Football is going in a clear direction – to compete for the highest places in the table, you have to manage 22, 23, 24 players. I don't want 24, but 21, 22 of a high level."

'He has to improve'

Bergvall made 33 appearances for Spurs across all competitions last term, scoring once and adding three assists.



However, only 17 of these were starts, and he is likely to face an even tougher task of being a regular name in the first XI in the upcoming season.

De Zerbi has strengthened his midfield options after landing Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes for a combined £185m.

And with Bergvall keen to play in a deeper midfield role, a position he occupied alongside Archie Gray in Spurs' latest pre-season game, the arrival of both new players has cast doubt over this.

5 Record signing Tonali started Spurs' pre-season friendly against Sydney FC on the bench, while Bergvall started Credit: Getty



5 Spurs beat off competition from Manchester United to secure Mateus Fernandes' signature Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

De Zerbi confirmed as much in his interview, as he then explained that Bergvall will have fight for his place here,

The Tottenham boss continued: "He wants space. He wants to play as a double pivot as a position. I can't give, for any player in the world, the place in the first XI guaranteed.

"I want to be honest with the players. I want to be clear. I don't want to make the first mistake. In terms of position, I can't give guarantees. It's right when he wants to play as a central midfielder.



"But to play as a central midfielder, sometimes it is to attack, sometimes to keep the holder, to move the ball faster.

"He has to improve."

Sports.title: FIFA pile pressure on nations over Gianni Infantino's controversial proposal to sell the World Cup - with members given just 53 days to decide whether they accept £30m offer
Sports.content:
FIFA pile pressure on nations over Gianni Infantino's controversial proposal to sell the World Cup - with members given just 53 days to decide whether they accept £30m offer

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

FIFA are attempting to pressure their 211 member associations into backing plans to sell stakes in the World Cup - just hours after the FA voiced deep concerns over Gianni Infantino's divisive proposals.

News broke on Tuesday that FIFA boss Infantino was considering selling parts of the tournament to private investors and forming a new company in a deal that could be worth around £15billion, which the governing body later confirmed in a hastily-issued statement.

In a letter to the associations, Infantino says member nations must decide on the proposal by September 19 and explains the financial benefits of approving the project.

He says that a funding package around £30million per nation will become available if associations sign up, but if they reject it their earnings will be almost 75 per cent less.

The letter from Infantino says: 'The decision on whether or not to proceed with this proposal belongs entirely to you. Should you wish to proceed this $10billion package will become available as of January 1, 2027, ushering in the next phase of our journey together.

'Should you wish to retain the status quo and reject this proposal we still have our planned expansion of the Forward programme [development money] of $2.7billion as previously presented.

'In total for the upcoming cycle starting as of January 1, 2027 each member association will have the possibility of access up to $40million per member association under this proposal.'

UEFA have responded to the letter, insinuating that FIFA are attempting to bribe associations into accepting the proposition.

'Today we have learned of FIFA's deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn,' UEFA said. 'This says everything you need to know about this plan.

'But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, UEFA knows there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme. FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It's time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans.'

The FA have deep concerns over FIFA's leaked plans to sell stakes in the World Cup

Investment bank J.P. Morgan is FIFA's financial advisor on the project while Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital is expected to lead the proposed investor group. Kushner is the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared. The Trump administration is understood to have been consulted.

FIFA hope to raise more than £3bn for the venture from a diversified, global investor group which is thought to include sovereign wealth funds.

Should their plans be successful, FIFA intend to give each of their 211 member associations a stake in the company - which they can choose to keep or sell - worth £15m.

The FA, though, are worried about FIFA's leaked plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.

In a statement, an FA spokesperson confirmed they had been left in the dark over the controversial proposals which have sparked outrage amongst the football community.

The statement said: 'We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

'Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

'When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further.'

It has been suggested that Infantino could become the commissioner of that company once his role at FIFA ends in 2031, although FIFA claim that has not been discussed.

European Football Clubs, who represent over 800 European clubs, have voiced their opposition. Crucially, the body is chaired by PSG President Nasser Al-Khelaifi, who has been touted as a potential leadership challenger to Infantino.

'European Football Clubs (EFC) notes with serious concern the sudden, unilateral media briefings and announcement by FIFA about a potential new corporate structure for the commercialisation of certain football competitions,' the statement read.

'As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in FIFA's competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude. EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.

'EFC always seeks to work collaboratively and supportively with all stakeholders – FIFA, UEFA and all confederations, national associations, leagues, player and fan associations.

'In that vein, we urge for calm and thorough consultation on all topics affecting the football ecosystem, together with more rigorous and transparent governance processes put in place to protect the game for the long term. Only in this way can we build the right institutional frameworks and relationships required to promote the true success, stability and sustainability of football.'

The European Leagues Association, of which the Premier League is a founding member, added: 'The World Cup should not be for sale. It is not the FIFA President's private equity asset. Its value is created day in and day out by leagues, clubs, players and supporters who are being left without a voice or a vote on this matter. European Leagues firmly reject this proposal.'

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also among the dissenting voices.

'Let me say this very directly,' Burnham posted on X. 'Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

'The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell.

'Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will.'

One European nation has already publicly supported Infantino's plan, with the President of the Czech FA David Trunda backing him.

'I can see the pragmatic benefits for Czech football from working in close co-operation with [FIFA president] Gianni Infantino and his team,' Trunda told Sky News.

'Of course we need more details, but my personal point of view is that I can see the positive impact of FIFA's intentions.'

FIFA want to set up a new company responsible for the 'operational delivery of FIFA tournaments', called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

They claim the plans would help advance the FIFA Forward development programme, which distributes capital to member associations. The governing body hopes to increase funding from £6m to £15m for the 2027-30 international cycle.

FIFA would need approval from the FIFA Council and majority support from the FIFA Congress (the 211 member associations) to launch the new enterprise.

Three of the six continental confederations have expressed resistance, including UEFA who released a scathing statement on Tuesday.

'This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross,' UEFA said. UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder who cares about the future of the game.

'The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell.'

CONCACAF, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean, added: 'CONCACAF was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,' their statement read on Wednesday morning.

'We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

'We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

'As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, FIFA, the Confederations and every Member Association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.

'This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the FIFA family will act in the same manner.'

The Asian federation have also stated their disappointment at the lack of consultation from FIFA.

There are major concerns over what the proposals could mean for the game, including whether FIFA could increase the frequency of tournaments to create more opportunities for financial backers to see a return on their investment.

The Club World Cup and men's World Cup are currently held every four years. FIFA have previously explored the possibility of staging both tournaments every two years.

FIFA maintain that they have a duty to control the development of this project, with external investors holding only a minority stake in FFE and having no operational role.

Sports.title: 'He's a delusional dictator who's lost touch with reality': Insiders reveal how FIFA boss Gianni Infantino went from 'pleasant and unassuming' to a 'greedy narcissist' with 'zero empathy' so drunk on power he is destroying our game
Sports.content:
The date was March 20, 2025, and a gilded ensemble had convened at a beautiful spot in southern Greece. Against the backdrop of the Ionian Sea, one of the many mysteries of Gianni Infantino was about to play out.

His reason for being at the Costa Navarino resort was a task of some importance. Same went for the rest of the group – an assortment of royals, heads of state and sporting powerbrokers known collectively as the membership of the International Olympic Committee.

As president of football’s global governing body, Infantino was part of their gang. And that was a big deal on this particular Thursday, because they were in town to elect the movement’s next leader. Seven candidates were in the running, 97 votes would be cast, and the finer detail of who ticked which box is usually lost to secrecy.

But whispers can carry on a sea breeze.

According to three prominent sources contacted by Daily Mail Sport, the shared wisdom was that FIFA’s supreme ruler sided with the Spanish candidate Juan Antonio Samaranch Jr. Evidently, Samaranch Jr’s team felt pretty sure of it.

But therein lies the intrigue, because we have also been told that figures close to a rival candidate, Lord Sebastian Coe, heard a different song in Greece. Apparently, they were given reason to believe Infantino’s vote would be his.

Gianni Infantino has been FIFA president since 2016 and will stand for re-election next year

The Swiss has been instrumental in the bloating of the World Cup from 32 nations to 48

As it transpired, neither man won, but here’s the thing: 15 months on, the two parties are still said to trust that Infantino went their way.

FIFA did not respond to Daily Mail Sport’s request for a little clarity, so what are we to do with this vignette? Is it par for the famously opaque course of sporting politics, or indicative of the confusion that forever surrounds Infantino? It’s just one thought to consider after the strangest, most politicised World Cup in recent memory and find ourselves studying the many faces of the man behind it.

Because who and what is Gianni Infantino?

Four years have passed since he took to a stage at the Qatar World Cup and offered his own answer. Addressing his audience that day, he said: ‘Today, I feel Qatari. Today, I feel gay. Today, I feel disabled. Today, I feel like a migrant worker...’

Prior to this World Cup, the portrait is somehow more surreal.

Today, it can be tempting to wonder if there is a world leader Infantino wouldn’t feel for a buck.

Today, it can feel as though Infantino has bucked football senseless.

Today, it feels prudent to query if football is safe in his hands.

It was February 26, 2016, when Infantino was elected to clean the wreckage left by the institutional corruption found beneath his predecessor, Sepp Blatter

Infantino has hungered for the limelight unlike any sporting administrator in recent memory

From presidents and sheikhs to Salt Bae, carver of steaks – the cast of individuals embraced by Infantino and presented to his four million Instagram followers is broad. But he wasn’t always so ostentatious.

It was February 26, 2016, when Infantino was elected to clean the wreckage left by the institutional corruption found beneath his predecessor, Sepp Blatter. Back then, the new guy he was largely anonymous to the outside world.

The Swiss-born son of working-class Italians and a lawyer by trade, Infantino had been the accidental candidate. He had risen across the course of 16 years to the rank of UEFA’s general secretary, but FIFA’s top job was seemingly ordained for his boss, Michel Platini.

It was only after Platini was sucked into the same investigations as Blatter that a door opened for Infantino. ‘I had dinner with Platini the week before the whole thing blew up, and he genuinely thought he was there,’ says Greg Dyke, who was the FA chairman during the Blatter demise and for the first few months of Infantino.

‘I don't quite know where the idea came from for Infantino to run, but my first impressions were that I liked him. He was a guy you could sit down with and have a chat. I never thought he was particularly political and thought he would bring a positive change.’

Dyke’s FA were among those to vote for him.

Patrick Nally’s instincts were similar to Dyke’s and date back further. Renowned as the founding father of modern sports marketing, the Englishman, 79, was one of the foremost king-makers behind Blatter’s rise at FIFA in the 1990s and he remains connected to the lever-pullers of elite sport. He first met Infantino in 2010 and found him ‘pleasant and unassuming’. He adds: ‘He didn't strike me as an incredibly political or ambitious individual, which clearly he seems to have become.’

That understatement only skims over the changes we have witnessed across Infantino’s decade on the throne. Neither his personality nor his alterations to the very fabric of football point to a leader who dwells long on where to impose his limits.

The FIFA president drew criticism for posing for selfies close to Pele’s coffin in 2023

Infantino sends birthday messages to Cristiano Ronaldo which hint at his obsession with celebrity

The question is: how closely are the two factors linked? And from there, how worried should we be?

We’ll stick with the personality traits for now, because Infantino has hungered for the limelight unlike any sporting administrator in recent memory. To look at one of his most contentious creations, the Club World Cup, is to see his name engraved into trophy. Twice.

Birthday messages to Cristiano Ronaldo sit at a trivial end of this discussion about celebrity obsession but posing for selfies close to Pele’s coffin in 2023 drew greater flak. Caught somewhere between pragmatism and fawning, Infantino’s relationships with autocratic rulers is where the chat becomes more germane to what football has become on his watch.

It hasn’t gone unnoticed that the ongoing grins of fealty to Donald Trump are an echo of what has gone before with Vladimir Putin and the ruling family of Qatar, but, like so much else, it has grown more extreme with each World Cup cycle.

To the riposte of whether such endorsements matter, some would suggest the migrant workers who built Qatari stadiums are best qualified to answer; or those elements of the Iranian football delegation denied visas to the United States.

When Infantino wore a red Trump hat at the US President’s Board of Peace meeting in February, the optics were so jarring the IOC investigated a potential breach of their principles around political neutrality. As a member of the IOC, he might have been expected to play closer attention to their sensitivities – the Winter Olympics were in progress at that very moment. Infantino was cleared, but IOC president Kirsty Coventry was unimpressed. A seasoned Olympics source tells us their relationship is ‘not close’.

A kind interpretation would argue occasional clumsiness on Infantino’s part. But is it something else? Has it morphed closer to grandiosity and delusion?

Let’s review what played out at FIFA’s congress in Vancouver in April. Having already requested – and been denied – a motorcade beyond the privileges of the Canadian prime minister, Infantino attempted to coax a handshake on stage between senior executives of the Israeli and Palestinian football associations. Predictably, they refused and Palestinian FA president Jibril Rajoub walked away in audible displeasure from an excruciating scene.

When Infantino wore a red Trump hat at the US President’s Board of Peace meeting in February, the optics were so jarring the IOC investigated a potential breach of their principles around political neutrality

Infantino cosied up to the ruling family of Qatar ahead of the 2022 World Cup

‘To me, it looks like a muppet show,’ says the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, who initially campaigned for the FIFA post after Blatter’s demise. ‘What we saw in Vancouver and that embarrassing situation around Israel and Palestine, showed me a man with zero empathy and a superiority complex that degraded the position of FIFA president.’

It might be academic to ponder why Infantino craves the spotlight. But it would also be naive to assume power has no impact on those who wield it, especially if we rewind to the environment Infantino entered in 2016. Having inherited the political gold dust of a disgraced predecessor, Infantino was almost lionised as the reformist football needed. From there, the scope to become intoxicated is self-evident.

In Nally’s mind, a key transition point will have been the World Cup in Russia in 2018, which Infantino inherited from the previous regime and placed him in proximity to Putin. What follows is a compelling theory.

‘All I can say is that power goes to one's head,’ Nally says. ‘I think Russia showed him just how powerful a position that he was in. The fact he was given one of the highest awards he could be given by Russia (the Order of Friendship Medal, patted onto his chest by Putin in 2019), and the realisation of what he had become, the penny dropped quite quickly.

‘Look at Qatar. This brought Infantino into complete contact with the most powerful families in Qatar. And then through Qatar into Saudi Arabia. He's allowed his personality and ego to suddenly think he is another leader of the world. He will see himself as being equal to a Trump. He will see himself as being equal to a Putin. In other words, it's difficult when you're being feted by these individuals for it to not have an influence. Some individuals forget the reality.’

Two things to note on the conversation with Nally. One is to declare is he remains in contact with Blatter, whose distaste for his successor was made clear by other sources used in this report.

The other is that he was speaking to Daily Mail Sport before that botched handshake in Vancouver – an episode that might lend some prescience to his speculation.

‘There is no humility there at all,’ Nally adds.

The peace prize conceived and handed to Trump is a natural bookend to this chapter. Infantino could not have forecast the invasion of Iran three months later, pitting his World Cup host against a participant, but the very belief that such a prize was his to gift will surely feature in his final legacy at FIFA.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin awards an Order of Friendship to Infantino during a ceremony to present state decorations at the Moscow Kremlin in 2019

Donald Trump is presented with the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize by Infantino late last year

There is a relevance to the conversation about ego, mainly for the way in which one explosion has been mirrored by others more fundamental to football. So much of the game has swelled on Infantino’s watch – a bigger World Cup, a bigger Club World Cup, bigger ticket prices, bigger demands on tired players, bigger takings.

We can talk at length about the other sliding-door moments of Infantino’s election win – for one, Dyke reaffirmed to us Platini was opposed to VAR – but the adaptations and the World Cup expansion from 32 nations to 48, and potentially 64 in 2030, have manifestly altered a crown jewel of sport. The qualification process and group-stages of the tournament are plainly diminished for it.

‘The expansion will dilute the quality of play,’ says Vega, capped 23 times by Switzerland. ‘This could cause massive player burnout and concerns over the welfare of the athletes.’

Few beyond those 48 nations, or entities that stand to profit from 40 extra games, have spoken in favour. Ditto the Club World Cup, which prompted the threat of strikes from players. And yet the sprawl will continue. The 2030 World Cup will be spread around Africa, Europe and South America, with guaranteed qualification for no fewer than six host nations.

A saving grace is that FIFA officials insist it is highly unlikely the tournament will swell to 64 nations, despite Infantino saying ‘every idea is a good idea’ when the thought was floated in 2025. It remains to be seen if he realises his wish of jamming in a Club World Cup every two years.

Time will tell on the wisdom of 2030 and possibly the motivation behind it. As a manoeuvre, this messy concoction opened a convenient path for an Asia host to jump a queue of continents in 2034. That being Saudi Arabia, of course. Accusations of sportswashing and profit before sense have already recommenced on that front, but multi-faceted issues in the US are the matter at hand.

The immense backlash against FIFA’s ticket prices this summer stands as the preeminent challenge to Infantino’s view of every idea being a good one.

‘He (Infantino) has changed the game for the worse,’ says Vega. ‘He completely lost touch with reality, prioritising financial revenue. Real fans cannot afford to go to the World Cup.’

'He (Infantino) has changed the game for the worse,’ says Ramon Vega, the former Spurs player who initially campaigned for the FIFA post after Blatter’s demise. ‘He completely lost touch with reality'

Infantino with Colombian singer-songwriter Shakira at a World Cup event

Other major issues sit not far beneath the surface of the approaching jamboree, and as ever will be largely forgotten once balls are kicked.

‘As the World Cup looms, it wouldn't pass any human rights smell test,’ says Minky Worden, the director of global initiatives at Human Rights Watch. ‘FIFA have been unable to secure a guarantee that armed ICE enforcement officials aren't greeting the millions of fans here.’

Worden has offered scathing views previously in these pages about what happened in Qatar and, now, she fears for US-based Haitian supporters attending the June 13 match against Scotland. Her worry is that ICE agents might scoop them up. FIFA did not respond to a request for comment on that one.

Worden is among the many to have noticed a change in Infantino. On June 20, 2016, she visited him at FIFA HQ in Zurich. ‘He kept a promise to meet in his first 100 days,’ she says. ‘But the evolution in 10 years shows there’s clearly no value system that says he has to do that anymore.’

Human Rights Watch lost patience two years ago when Saudi Arabia emerged unopposed from a curiously truncated bidding process to land the World Cup. They cut ties.

Worden’s assessment of Infantino’s tenure concludes with a reference to what played out in Vancouver. ‘The Pope isn't asking for treatment like this so where would he have gotten the idea that he deserves it?’ she asks. ‘This is delusional dictator behaviour.’

Vega used the very same description before adding: ‘He is only serving his own ego.’

As criticisms, they are withering. But those with voting rights show no sign of joining a chorus – Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023 and has been cleared to stand again in 2027 because his first term fell short of the full four years. He will almost certainly win.

Infantino is front and centre again as a bisht is put on Lionel Messi by Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, in 2022

Other than the Norwegian FA, who called out the peace prize saga and his rescinding of Folarin Balogun's red card at Trump's request, there are no vocal dissidents among FIFA’s 211 member nations. The development allowances handed their way have grown eight-fold in Infantino’s tenure and whatever private discontent exists, it has never spread to the ballot papers.

Because whatever else has been observed during Infantino’s time, there has not been a corruption scandal. And financially, the game is thriving – FIFA’s accounts a decade ago showed an annual revenue of $502million and in 2025 that was up to $2.66billion.

In this World Cup year, the projections suggest $9bn. Everything has bloated in tandem.

Today, Infantino will feel good about that. Today, we might be entitled to feel the worst of the ‘good ideas’ was to think he was ever the solution.

Sports.title: FIFA open disciplinary case against Argentina over Falkland Islands banner as three are accused of ASSAULT for 'punching' Spain stars in ugly brawl after World Cup final
Sports.content:
FIFA have launched disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over the Falklands banner displayed by players after the England match alongside a number of other alleged breaches including discrimination, racist abuse and objects being thrown by supporters.

Two Argentina players, Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina, along with Argentina coach Roberto Ayala, have also separately had proceedings opened against them over allegations of assault following the ugly scenes that marred the World Cup final against Spain.

A number of Argentina's jubilant squad, including Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez and Tottenham's Cristian Romero, lifted a controversial banner touting their country’s claim to the Falkland Islands after their World Cup semi-final win over England.

It triggered a fierce backlash in the UK, with former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer supporting calls for FIFA to open an investigation made by Business Secretary Peter Kyle at the time.

FIFA’s rules forbid the use of any political messaging at the World Cup but have previously turned a blind eye to continued references to the 1982 conflict in a song sung by the players – and posted on social media by the country’s association – in the dressing room throughout the tournament.

At full-time of a fractious match players including Manchester United’s Lisandro Martinez and Tottenham Hotspur’s Cristian Romero, held aloft a banner which read: ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’, using the country’s term for the South Atlantic islands.

At full-time of a fractious match players including Man United ’s Lisandro Martinez and Tottenham's Cristian Romero, held aloft a banner which read: ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’

Argentina midfielder Paredes, along with team-mate Thiago Almada's help, threw unused Spanish substitute Gavi to the floor in disgraceful scenes at the full-time whistle

A FIFA statement said proceedings had been opened 'in light of discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, failure to comply with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators and the throwing of objects by spectators' during several Argentina matches at the World Cup.

Several Argentina players were also involved in ugly post-match clashes with Spain's players immediately after the final whistle of their World Cup final meeting.

Spain's captain Rodri was struck by Molina as he went to celebrate with his team-mates, before Dani Olmo was punched by coach Ayala.

Elsewhere, Argentina midfielder Paredes attacked Eric Garcia by grabbing him by the neck and then, along with team-mate Thiago Almada's help, threw unused Spanish substitute Gavi to the floor in disgraceful scenes.

Paredes faces three counts of assault, Molina faces two counts (one completed and one attempted) and Ayala is charged with one count.

The trio, as well as the winger Thiago Almada and the Spanish midfielder Gavi, have also been charged with unsporting behaviour following the post-match brawl.

'In accordance with the FIFA Disciplinary Code, the respondents have now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the FIFA Disciplinary Committee in due course,' the statement said.

Sports.title: Bournemouth star Eli Junior Kroupi ruled out for three months after surgery - as Cherries attempt to fight off suitors including Barcelona and Tottenham
Sports.content:
Bournemouth star Eli Junior Kroupi ruled out for three months after surgery - as Cherries attempt to fight off suitors including Barcelona and Tottenham

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Bournemouth's pre-season plans have been rocked after striker Eli Junior Kroupi was ruled out for at least three months following surgery on a broken metatarsal.

The 20-year-old suffered a fracture to a fifth metatarsal during training camp in Austria and flew back to England ahead of undergoing surgery on Wednesday.

Kroupi had been attracting transfer attention from numerous clubs this summer with Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Tottenham and Manchester City among his many admirers.

However, Bournemouth have maintained throughout that he is not for sale.

Similarly, they have done the same with Chelsea and Manchester United target Alex Scott as they try to maintain a competitive squad for new coach Marco Rose.

Kroupi took the Premier League by storm last season after joining from Lorient. He scored 13 goals, the highest number scored by a teenager in a debut season in Premier League history, surpassing the previous record held by Robbie Fowler and Robbie Keane.

Eli Junior Kroupi has undergone surgery after breaking his fifth metatarsal during training

Meanwhile, Bournemouth have confirmed Patrick Eibenberger will join Rose’s backroom staff ahead of the new season as first-team coach.

Eibenberger leaves his role at RB Leipzig and reunites with Rose, having previously worked with him at Borussia Dortmund, Borussia Monchengladbach and Red Bull Salzburg.

Marco Kurth, assistant head coach, Frank Geideck, assistant coach, Fabian Friedrich, technical coach, and Frederic De Boever, goalkeeping coach, had already been confirmed as part of Rose’s staff.

Sports.title: Club at centre of 'Clicky Ponting' scandal break their silence on cheating storm: Saltburn CC confirm player who tricked umpires has been BANNED after he was 'knocked sideways' by outrage
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A cricketer who has become known as 'Clicky Ponting' for his role in a cheating scandal has been banned by his club – who have finally broken their silence.

Saltburn cricketer Brian Devine is accused of clicking his fingers to imitate the sound of the ball hitting the bat, to fool the umpire into thinking the batter is out.

The amateur cricket scandal has caused convulsions around the cricketing world.

Now, more than 24 hours after clips of Devine went viral, Saltburn have confirmed that the player has been banned from the club.

'This statement is issued in response to the widely publicised complaint made against a Saltburn Cricket Club member and, as a consequence, against the Club more generally,' the statement, shared on social media, began.

'We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric Club, we are fully cooperating with the NYSD League's investigation.

Brian Devine has been dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' on social media for his cricket fielding actions

Saltburn Cricket Club have broken their silence on the ordeal, revealing the player has been banned pending an investigation

'We believe that the Club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us. The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the Club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation. Initial discussions have already taken place between Club officials and the league.

'This has been a very distressing and stressful experience for all those concerned, and we would ask that this reality is borne in mind and that personal boundaries are respected, as we are an amateur club entirely run by volunteers.

'We will be making no further comment at this time.'

Devine is accused of clicking his fingers while fielding for the club to make it sound as though the ball had hit the bat when it had in fact not.

If the ball hits the bat and is then caught, it means a batter is out.

The minor league cricketer at the centre of the scandal is 'completely bewildered' to find himself engulfed by a global furore.

Friends say Devine's 'head is all over the place' after the accusation that he clicked his fingers to imitate the sound of the ball hitting the bat.

A friend of Devine's said he was not expected to play and would 'lie low' while the cheating row continues.

Amateur cricket player Devine has been caught appearing to click his fingers to make it appear that a batter has been caught behind when in fact they haven't hit the ball at all

Other incidences have been found of Devine clicking his finger in previous matches for wickets

The friend said: 'Brian is completely bewildered by the way this has gone all around the world.

'He's had an Australian podcast offering to pay his legal bills today - it's the first that he's heard that he's got any legal bills and he's hoping it won't get that far.

'His mates have been telling him to sell his story in Australia, but he just wants it all to go away and hopes he can get back to playing cricket, though at the moment that feels impossible for him.

'He woke up on Monday morning thinking the world was still the same place he'd left it the night before and suddenly his story was all over the world, in Australia, India, New Zealand and the UK of course.

'He understands why there is an investigation but the reaction all over the world to all this has knocked him sideways.'

Mr Devine, 38, a father who lives with his partner in Guisborough, North Yorkshire, has continued to decline to comment. His mobile phone number was also removed from the company website at the auction mart in Northallerton where he works.

At Saltburn Cricket Club's clubhouse, prior to their statement, journalists were angrily told to leave by a club official, who said: 'We're sick of this now, you have no right to come here.'

A Durham-based amateur cricketer named Ben Mummery, who had been tipped off about the series of events, posted footage to X, where he dubbed it 'about the worst case of cheating I have ever seen in cricket'.

Saltburn have been widely condemned on social media following multiple videos emerging

That clip had soon clocked up millions of views.

Viewers then began to trawl the archives for other similar incidents. They promptly turned up dozens, suggesting that Saltburn had been employing the cynical scam for more than a season.

In almost every one of the clips that have emerged, Devine can be seen standing at first slip, clicking his fingers as the ball whistles past.

One particularly damning video was posted by Rory Cotterill, the captain of Middlesbrough CC's second XI. He said there had been two more incidents like it in a single game they played on Saturday, June 27, which Saltburn won by 29 runs, 'leading to a 15 and 16-year-old being cheated out of an innings'. He added: 'I was at the non-striker's end at the time, unknowingly watching them cheat in real time.'

Other cricket fans to weigh in included Piers Morgan, who dubbed the club's behaviour 'outrageous cheating' and a 'shameful scam'. Several posters dubbed Devine 'Clicky Ponting' – a play on the name of former Australian captain Ricky Ponting – on social media.

Georgina Vaughan, the mother of Devine's partner Clare, said the family had been shocked by the scale of the cheating row.

She said: 'It was only a little village cricket match and now it's become this thing that's all over the news and social media.

'It has got totally out of hand and there is nothing that any of us want to say.'

Asked whether Devine was a man of integrity, she replied: 'He certainly is.'

A statement from the North Yorkshire and South Durham League read: 'The League has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25th July 2026. A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete, no further comment will be made.'

Sports.title: 'Clicky Ponting' is just the tip of the iceberg. I've played club cricket for decades and these are the wildest stories of cheating, from vaseline to elastic bands and fattening up umpires to a trail of sawdust
Sports.content:
'Clicky Ponting' is just the tip of the iceberg. I've played club cricket for decades and these are the wildest stories of cheating, from vaseline to elastic bands and fattening up umpires to a trail of sawdust

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

At the snap of a finger, Brian Devine became English cricket's Public Enemy No 1 - and 'Clicky Ponting' was born.

An investigation is underway in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League after several videos appeared to show Saltburn CC slip fielder Devine clicking his fingers as the ball passed the batsman to mimic the sound of an edge.

Devine’s aim is as clear as it is shocking – to con the umpire into giving his team a wicket. The spirit of cricket this most definitely is not, and Devine and his team’s actions have shocked the cricketing world (and his now former sponsor, the local curry house).

But Saltburn are hardly the only team over the years to bend the rules – and in some cases, openly break them.

The 2018 scandal which saw three Australian cricketers receive long bans for their part in a sandpaper ball tampering plot and Alex Carey’s controversial 2023 Ashes run out of Jonny Bairstow are high-profile recent examples in international cricket.

And similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level, too. We've gathered together the best (or worst, depending on your view) from decades' worth of experience in the glory, and shame, of club cricket.

Brian Devine, the man at the centre of the 'Clicky Ponting' club cricket scandal

Devine (circled) is being investigated by his local league, with allegations he clicked his fingers when the ball passed an opposition player's bat to simulate the sound of an edge

Vaseline assistance

Sunny Agnihotri played for West Blatchington Cricket Club between 2002 and 2008, and won the Sussex Invitation League Division 1 twice.

When they met Crawley Eagles, the opposition would put Vaseline on their bats ahead of the match. The idea was that when the ball nicked the outside edge, it wouldn’t make so much noise.

‘We asked the umpires about it and they said it’s not against the rules,' said Agnihotri. 'They were also definitely rummaging in their pockets between balls, so we knew something untoward was going on. They made it so obvious. The dark arts happen a lot.’

Local rivals Brighton Insurance would waste time when they batted first to use up the daylight.

Between a dismissed batsman walking off and a new one replacing him, you had three minutes. But on the field of play, you could still get padded up. Brighton players would throw all their equipment on the pitch and take longer than three minutes without punishment.

‘They would take double the time so that when it was our turn to bat, it would be gloomier,’ Agnihotri said.

Izzy Martin

But similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level too

It’s not always the players…

There was an umpire in the Leicestershire leagues during the late 1990s renowned for getting a twitchy trigger finger the closer it got to opening time at the bar.

When he started to get really thirsty, he would whisper under his breath: ‘Next one that hits the pads… give it a big appeal’ and, when the fielding side did, he duly obliged.

A trick of one former Leicestershire Premier Division champion team was to send beers to the umpires' room and offer them sweets while in the field in a bid to get them on-side so decisions would fall in their favour.

‘Where there’s a will, there’s a way,’ said one member of the side. Their wicketkeeper was also known for trying to kick the stumps down and appealing that the batter had been bowled.

I remember playing in a county age-group match in which one fielder on the team, who went on to become a professional, took a catch on the half-volley and celebrated as though it was clean.

Another team in the Leicestershire leagues was once accused of sending the same batsman in twice in different kit, until their plan was foiled when the star man was spotted by the home team scorer through her binoculars.

Anonymous

No matter the spread of the 'spirit of cricket', the laws are always open to a little bending

Let's all band together

I played in a match many, many years ago where three of our batsmen were given out caught behind, all of them swearing blind they never got a nick on the ball.

After some brief research, we realised the wicketkeeper had an elastic band attached to his glove, which he snapped against it to make the noise of a nick, fooling the umpire into giving it out in a similar trick to Saltburn's.

Anonymous

Saltburn CC, which has now come under international scrutiny after Devine was caught on camera

Questionable declaration

In 2017, Pembrokeshire rivals Carew and Cresselly took on each other in the final game of that year’s West Wales league season. Carew were top, Cresselly second.

Cresselly faced a difficult task that day, but not an impossible one. Carew’s lead was 21 points and a win was worth 20, but then you had the bonuses to consider – a point for every 40 runs up to 200 and a point for every two wickets.

In short, it boiled down to this: if Cresselly could win and take two more bonus points than Carew, they’d snatch the title. But Carew had a devilish plan.

As far as I’ve been told in my retracing of the steps, they even checked the rules with the umpire before the game, found their read of the situation was accurate, and set about putting it in action.

Batting first, they declared on just 18 for one. First there was shock, then revulsion. It was filthy and entirely legal.

Cresselly were welcome to the 20 points, which they achieved by knocking off the chase in just a few overs, but the opportunity for any bonuses had been snatched clean off the table. It was Carew’s title by a single point.

Riath Al-Samarrai

Saltburn weren't the first side to mimick an edge - one of our contributors played against a team whose wicketkeeper used an elastic band!

Bailout

One day, while in action for Saffron Plantationers – a village side in Quendon near Saffron Walden in Essex – I was at the crease with my team needing four runs to win.

My plan was to charge the bowler and hit the ball down the ground. I was still deep in my crease as the bowler ran in. But his delivery was short of a length, so I stepped back and pulled it for four. As I did so, however, I trod gently on my own stumps and off came the bails.

But instead of me being given out hit wicket, as I should have been, everyone at the ground watched the ball disappear to the boundary. Not seeing the bails were off, the umpire signalled four and the end of the game.

After a while, the opposition wicketkeeper noticed something off and questioned why the bails were no longer on the stumps. But I just kept walking off the pitch as technically, the game was now over.

It was one I got away with but I’m not proud of my actions – I got caught up in the moment and should have fessed up. I do seem to remember sleeping OK that night though!

Matt Gatward

Australia captain Steve Smith breaks down at a press conference in light of his side's Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal in 2018

Another cheat bites the dust

I remember playing for Eynsford at Chislehurst and West Kent one year in the Kent leagues.

Eynsford were interrupted in their victory charge by a short, sharp shower. After 20 minutes off the field to allow the pitch to dry, the umpires suggested a restart and asked Chislehurst to put out some sawdust for the bowlers to allow for better grip.

The response from the Chislehurst captain was: ‘Sorry, we haven’t got any.’

Unfortunately for him, a visiting member had seen him put a bag from the club shed into his car boot, leaving a trail of sawdust between the two locations. When called out, he had the front to say he knew nothing about it!

Anonymous

No age allowances

Not cheating as such, though by way of intimidation it comes close to the line.

I distinctly remember my senior debut in the adult leagues. As someone who had a modicum of talent and was playing Northamptonshire junior cricket at the time, I was chucked in alongside grown men aged just 13 in a bid to speed up my development.

Cricket is meant to be a sport played by gentlemen - but don't be surprised if you hear a few expletives at a village game, no matter how young the person on the receiving end is

Playing for South Northamptonshire village side Marston St Lawrence, I faced a tough task against experienced cricketers. Unsurprisingly given my youth, I struggled with the bat, playing and missing repeatedly.

I was as frustrated as anyone on the field, but my tender years didn’t stop me getting both barrels from the bowler who I couldn’t lay a bat on. I’ll never forget his words.

‘Just hit it, you c***!’ he shouted at me, his words starting off an unpleasant exchange with my more senior partner at the other end.

I was so shocked to be verbally abused at that age, I could not muster a reply. However, in the years since I've thought regularly about what I should have said.

If I had my time again, the response would have been: ‘I’m f***ing trying!’

Alex Bywater

Sports.title: Stephen Fleming in line to become England's new Test coach after Brendon McCullum sacking - as New Zealander is chosen by ECB to lead post-Bazball project
Sports.content:
England are closing in on Stephen Fleming as their new Test coach following the axing of his fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum.

Fleming, 53, is viewed as one of cricket’s great strategists, having played 111 Tests for his country, becoming their most successful captain with 28 wins.

Since quitting international cricket in 2008, he has enjoyed a successful coaching career, predominantly with Chennai Super Kings, claiming five Indian Premier League titles before quitting days after McCullum was removed from his position.

Defeat to New Zealand at Trent Bridge in what was Ben Stokes’ final international appearance meant England had not won a series for more than 12 months, forcing a re-think within an ECB hierarchy that resisted change following the deflating 4-1 Ashes defeat last winter.

The ECB declined to comment when contacted on Wednesday, but Daily Mail Sport understands he edged out Englishmen Richard Dawson and Jonathan Trott in the selection process.

One of Fleming’s first tasks will be to determine who succeeds Stokes as England captain.

New Zealander Stephen Fleming is in line to become the new England Men's Test head coach

Fleming has worked as a coach since 2009, but his only roles have come in franchise cricket, including 14 years over two spells at Chennai Super Kings

England are still looking for a new captain after Ben Stokes' retirement earlier this summer

Joe Root stepped in when Stokes was suspended for The Oval Test last month and was being lined up to work alongside McCullum until the end of next year’s Ashes.

That particular succession plan was put into place in order not to over-burden Root’s fellow Yorkshireman Harry Brook.

However, Brook revealed it would be a ‘privilege’ to lead England in all three formats, having made a success of turning around results in his 15-month captaincy of the limited-overs teams.

Appointing Brook, who at 27 is Root’s junior by eight years, now would maintain some continuity as England return to split coaching roles and avoid another captaincy switch within the next 18 months.

Fleming indicated his interest in the post immediately after mutually severing ties with the CSK organisation a fortnight ago. The franchise said it was ‘bringing to a close one of the most successful and enduring partnerships in IPL history.’

Adding: ‘The decision was reached with respect and gratitude, following a series of open and honest discussions between Fleming and the Super Kings management.’

Fleming also ended ties with Super Kings' other franchises - Joburg Super Kings in the SA20 and Texas Super Kings in the United States - where he was head coach.

His appointment would reunite him in a working capacity with McCullum, who viewed his fellow Kiwi as a mentor during their playing days.

It would also take the numbers of New Zealanders across England’s coaching set-up to four: Jeetan Patel and Tim Southee are currently spin and fast bowling coaches respectively.

Some will feel that a lack of homegrown presence is a concern, particularly after managing director Rob Key turned to Australian Marcus North as national selector.

Indeed, only two Englishmen featured on a nine-strong list of potential candidates. Not all received calls, however, suggesting that Fleming became their preferred choice after Andy Flower, the original No 1 target, turned down the chance to interview.

Fleming is well known to the English game, however, having captained Nottinghamshire to the County Championship title and also represented Yorkshire.

As a coach, he also took Southern Brave to the knockout stages of the 2023 and 2024 editions of the Hundred.

Sports.title: Angry Man United fans to challenge club after ticket touting clampdown saw thousands of accounts wrongly suspended
Sports.content:
Angry Man United fans to challenge club after ticket touting clampdown saw thousands of accounts wrongly suspended

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United supporters’ groups will challenge the club over its controversial clampdown on ticket touting at a Fans’ Forum meeting on Thursday night as criticism continues to grow.

United have come under fire over the purge, with a number of groups including The ’58, Manchester United Supporters’ Trust and The Red Army issuing a joint statement last week accusing the club of making fans feel as though they are being ‘treated as suspects’.

By bringing in an external agency using automated monitoring to find any trace of touting, United have been criticised for casting the net too wide and targeting innocent fans.

Thousands of supporters – including some as young as six – have received notification that their accounts have been suspended due to suspicious activity and their season tickets could be revoked unless they provide a satisfactory explanation.

The quarterly meeting of the Fans’ Forum on Thursday will give fan representatives an opportunity to confront United directly over the crackdown and urge the club to take a more lenient approach.

Protests have regularly been staged by Manchester United supporters clubs in recent years, with this photo having been taken last year on the 20th anniversary of the Glazer takeover

It comes as the Manchester United Muslims Supporters’ Club backed the stance taken by other groups on Wednesday.

‘Manchester United has always been more than a football club,’ read a statement from the MUMSC. ‘It was built by generations of supporters, dedicated staff, the people of Manchester, and communities around the world, who have given their unwavering loyalty to this club through every high and every low. Today, many supporters feel that bond is being broken.

‘The recent treatment of season-ticket holders has only deepened those concerns. Long-standing supporters, some with decades of loyalty behind them, have spoken publicly about being suspended or losing their season tickets.

‘After allegations of breaking club rules, while questioning whether they were provided with the evidence against them, or afforded a fair and transparent process, every supporter deserves fairness, transparency, and the opportunity to be heard.

‘Trust is built through openness, not silence. These issues do not exist in isolation; they form part of a wider feeling that Manchester United is becoming increasingly disconnected from the people who built the club.

‘We all want Manchester United to succeed again, but success should never come at the expense of the values that made this club great. The supporters, the staff, and the communities who built Man United deserve better.

‘Enough is enough. It's time to put the people of Manchester United back at the heart of Manchester United.’
