World.title: Conflict shift
World.content:
Superintendent Mark Harris, commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division, speaks about the division’s changing crime landscape during an episode of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Force4Good podcast. x

THE St Andrew Central Police Division, which is the commercial heartbeat of the Corporate Area, where thousands of Jamaicans live and work daily, is confronting a changing crime landscape, with police saying interpersonal and domestic conflicts have become a greater concern than organised gang violence.

Commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division Superintendent Mark Harris said the division has largely brought organised gang activity under control, but is now grappling with murders arising from personal disputes, many of which occur without warning and in communities not traditionally associated with violent crime. He said this shift has presented a more complex policing challenge because, unlike gang conflicts, interpersonal disputes are far less predictable.

Speaking on the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Force4Good podcast, Harris said the division recorded the largest reduction in murders across the Jamaica Constabulary Force last year and even went an entire month without a murder this February. However, he noted that while gang-related killings have declined significantly, police are increasingly being challenged by crimes rooted in personal and domestic disputes.

“Last year, I had gang issues, [but] this year, we don’t have a gang issue, we have criminals committing crimes, but it’s not associated with gangs, like 2024 and part of 2025, and believe it or not, gang conflict is easier to police than the interpersonal and the domestic issues,” he noted.

The St Andrew Central Police Division encompasses some of Jamaica’s busiest commercial, educational and transport hubs, including Half-Way-Tree, New Kingston, Cross Roads and Papine. It is also responsible for policing major national events, entertainment activities and sporting fixtures that are often held at the National Stadium, making it one of the JCF’s most demanding divisions.

The division also includes communities such as August Town and Nannyville, both of which have experienced persistent gang activity and periodic security operations over the years. August Town was placed under a Zone of Special Operations in 2020 following years of deadly gang violence, while Nannyville has repeatedly featured in anti-gang and anti-gun operations as police sought to dismantle organised criminal networks operating across Kingston and St Andrew.

Despite that history, Harris said the division’s greatest challenge is no longer organised gangs but the rise in deadly interpersonal conflicts.

“We know where the gangs are and where they operate and who they’re in conflict with, and we put police right there…but for the interpersonal things, even in Jack’s Hill we have murders [and] that is not normally a place where we have murders… and these are interpersonal, rather than gang conflict,” he explained.

He said the division is relying not only on intelligence-led operations but also stronger community partnerships to prevent personal disputes from escalating into violence.

“We go out there and do the hard policing, we still have our community engagement. We had to do those meetings at the Transport Centre to speak to students and parents and stakeholders,” Harris noted.

Meanwhile, Area Four Commander Assistant Commissioner of Police Michael Phipps said St Andrew Central remains critical to crime management across Kingston and St Andrew because of its concentration of commercial activity, major institutions and daily commuter traffic.

He noted that the division has also experienced a significant number of fatal attacks involving weapons other than firearms, reflecting the growing challenge posed by interpersonal violence.

“I can tell you here and now that St Andrew Central has had a very high number of murders resulting from the use of knives and other blunt-force trauma injuries that have resulted in death. So we see St Andrew Central as one of the most important divisions if we are to maintain control of crime across Area Four,” Phipps said.

World.title: Ed Miliband grabs Brexit reset role as he reboots UK Foreign Office
World.content:
According to one person familiar with his accession talks with Andy Burnham, granted anonymity to speak freely, Miliband extracted a promise from the incoming prime minister that he would be able to pursue his determination to address the damage being done by climate change in his new job — and also foreground international development. That's a topic sidelined by recent governments keen to cut spending to prioritize security and defense.

Miliband underlined this new focus by heading straight to Paris and Madrid for informal talks with French and Spanish counterparts Jean-Noël Barrot and José Manuel Albares this week — visiting the two countries at the heart of Europe's wildfire disasters.

At a party hosted by the left-leaning IPPR think tank on Wednesday, Miliband told guests he wants climate and the environment to have a much higher profile in the role.

He also added, pointedly: “I am a politician not a chief diplomat.” It’s a sign he intends to conduct himself with a punchy style and pursue some distinct causes.

On that score, he has been seeking advice from a senior figure across the political aisle — Ed Llewelyn, a former key advisor to ex-Prime Minister David Cameron and previous head of the Foreign Office with extensive diplomatic experience, latterly as U.K. ambassador to Rome.

Miliband has indicated he might also soon meet Cameron himself for counsel on how to “hit the ground running,” as a person familiar with the background conversations told POLITICO. The pair used to clash furiously in the House of Commons when Miliband was opposition leader, but Cameron had a second act as foreign secretary in the dying days of Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government.

World.title: France issues expulsion order against Russian TV star Xenia Fedorova
World.content:
The French Ministry of the Interior told POLITICO the order to remove her from the country was signed on Tuesday.

Xenia Fedorova did not immediately reply to a request for comment, but her lawyer told Agence France-Presse she would challenge the decision.

Fedorova headed RT France before it was shut down due to EU sanctions in 2023. She has since become a fixture on the CNews television channel, Europe 1 radio station and Le Journal du Dimanche newspaper — all owned by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bolloré.

As POLITICO previously reported, the TV star’s commentary echoing Moscow talking points on Ukraine, NATO and European security was raising concerns among lawmakers and Russian propaganda experts for months, especially ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election. Le Monde also reported Fedorova has allegedly grown very close to Bolloré, a powerful figure who has been leveraging his media empire to try and influence French politics.

In her coverage on Bolloré’s platforms, Fedorova has often accused French President Emmanuel Macron and NATO of warmongering, presenting Russia as a peaceful country looking to end the war in Ukraine. She also regularly criticizes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and depicts the country as corrupt and incapable of winning the war.

In Brussels, some members of the European Parliament have been unsuccessfully lobbying for Fedorova to be included in the EU’s Russian sanctions packages, while several lawmakers in Paris have pushed for her residence permit to be revoked.

Fedorova is now under house arrest and banned from working on French soil. However, according to Libération, the lack of diplomatic ties between Paris and Moscow will make it difficult to actually deport her back to Russia.

Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

World.title: Merz’s party picks new parliamentary group leader
World.content:
The new leader previously served as the head of Merz’s Chancellery and is a popular figure within the conservative bloc.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder congratulated Frei in a post on X: “He has the same compass as the CSU, is deeply engaged in the issues, and is a good communicator … These are the best premises,” Söder wrote.

Frei succeeds Jens Spahn, who stepped down amid a controversy over his use of a surrogate to have a child. The resignation prompted Merz to launch a broader cabinet reshuffle.

Earlier on Wednesday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier appointed three new CDU ministers proposed by the chancellor.

Former CDU Secretary-General Carsten Linnemann took office as health minister, replacing Nina Warken, who became the head of the Chancellery. Steffen Bilger was appointed transport minister, replacing Patrick Schnieder.

“Reshuffling governments is nothing unusual in the history of the Federal Republic. There have always been cabinet reshuffles during an ongoing legislative term,” Steinmeier said ahead of the appointments in a speech supporting Merz.

World.title: Brussels rises against FIFA President Infantino’s plan to bring in private investors
World.content:
FIFA chief Gianni Infantino’s close relationship with Trump has previously drawn criticism from members of the European Parliament. Earlier this month, 90 MEPs signed two letters challenging the organization over actions they said undermined the governing body’s political neutrality. Three MEPs, when asked about the matter, said that Infantino should now answer questions before Parliament.

“If the plans are true, Infantino has to explain himself,” German Green MEP Rasmus Andresen said. “We should organise a hearing with ECON and CULT involved,” he added, referring to Parliament’s Economic and Monetary Affairs and Culture and Education committees. Bogdan Zdrojewski, the European Parliament’s lead lawmaker on the European Sport Model, also told POLITICO Playbook that Infantino should also be invited to appear before lawmakers.

In a statement to POLITICO, Renew MEP Barry Andrews and Volt lawmaker Nela Riehl, the chair of the Parliament’s Culture and Education committee, said that they would introduce a proposal “to request FIFA appear before a joint hearing in the European Parliament at the soonest possible date.”

Under the proposal, FIFA would transfer its commercial rights and tournament operations to a new subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise. Private investors, led by Kushner’s venture capital firm, would acquire roughly 20 percent of that company, while FIFA would retain control.

Micallef added that the proposal raised “important competition law considerations,” which the Commission would investigate.

To help win support from FIFA’s member associations, Infantino paired the proposal with a substantial increase in development funding. If a majority approves the plan, each of the 211 member associations would be eligible for up to $20 million in one-time subsidies, on top of increased payments in the coming years. “Football is the world’s most popular sport and an extraordinary engine of human and social development,” Infantino said.

World.title: Der „große Irrtum“ von Ex-AfD-Chef Jörg Meuthen
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Der ehemalige AfD-Chef Jörg Meuthen blickt in diesem Sommer-Spezial schonungslos auf seine Zeit an der Parteispitze zurück. Im Gespräch mit Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler räumt er Fehler im Umgang mit dem radikalen Flügel ein. Die heutige AfD werde von einem völkisch-nationalistischen Kurs dominiert.

Meuthen bereut es heute, den extremen Parteiflügel um Björn Höcke anfangs als harmlose Folklore unterschätzt zu haben. Ein gemeinsamer Kurs mit Frauke Petry hätte die Partei damals in eine völlig andere Richtung lenken können. Stattdessen sei er damals rein taktische Allianzen mit den Radikalen eingegangen.

Die aktuellen Umfragehochs der Partei seien einzig der eklatanten Schwäche der etablierten Parteien geschuldet. Bei einer Regierungsübernahme in Sachsen-Anhalt würde sich die personell völlig blanke AfD jedoch schnell demaskieren. Die Partei habe schlicht nicht das Fachpersonal, um Ministerien zu führen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: BMW to cut 8,000 jobs by the end of 2027
World.content:
BMW's headquarters in Munich, Germany are pictured on July 16, 2026. | Astrid Vellguth/AFP via Getty Images

German-based workers in administrative and research and development roles will be offered a severance program.

German car manufacturer BMW is cutting thousands of jobs by the end of 2027 through a voluntary redundancy program, a corporate spokesperson told POLITICO.

Up to 8,000 jobs are expected to be culled under the program, with offers going out beginning in October, according to internal corporate sources.

The program targets German-based workers in administrative and research and development roles, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with facilitating terrorism
World.content:
Pavel Durov watches the bantamweight bout at UFC 321 in Abu Dhabi on Oct. 25, 2025. | Giuseppe Cacace/AFP via Getty Images

Moscow claims the platform allows Ukrainian intelligence services to recruit spies and support terrorist activities.

Russia charged Telegram co-founder and CEO Pavel Durov on Wednesday with facilitating terrorist activity and placed the Soviet-born Kremlin critic on an international wanted list.

The Federal Security Service (FSB) accused Durov’s messaging platform of supporting Ukrainian intelligence services. The agency claims a Telegram chatbot named “Daivinchik/Leo — acquaintances, communication and new friends” was used to recruit Russians “into sabotage and terrorist activities through deception and psychological manipulation.”

The FSB also accused Telegram of failing to remove numerous channels, chats and bots that it alleged were used by Ukrainian intelligence agencies and terrorist and extremist organizations to coordinate sabotage, terrorist attacks, mass killings and cyber fraud in Russia.

World.title: Who is Ed Miliband really listening to?
World.content:
Anne shares what she’s been hearing about the new top team at the Foreign Office and Ed Milliband reveals what his grandfather would have said about his new job.

Meanwhile, can Andy Burnham really fix Britain’s social care system? That’s the big question as the new prime minister hosts cross-party talks on one of the country’s biggest challenges.

There’s just one problem: the invitations only went out on Tuesday, and neither Kemi Badenoch nor Ed Davey will be in the room. The Conservative leader is sending the shadow health secretary in her place, while Davey will join by Zoom. Nigel Farage and the Green Party’s Zack Polanski weren’t invited.

Sam and Anne dig into what, if anything, today’s meeting could achieve.

World.title: More than half of England 'officially in drought', UK Environment agency says
World.content:
UK authorities on Wednesday declared more than half of England in drought after "record-low rain and exceptionally high temperatures".

 

The declaration follows what is set to be the driest July on record, with around just seven percent of expected rainfall nationwide and some parts of southern England seeing just one percent, according to the UK government's Environment Agency.

The UK is also currently experiencing its fourth widespread heatwave of 2026.

Describing it as a "flash drought" -- which develops quickly and is caused by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures -- it was the second consecutive summer parts of England were experiencing drought.

"Rivers are running low, farmers are having to harvest crops early, wildfire risk is increasing, and millions of people are living under restrictions on water use," the agency said as it made the announcement.

The seven areas declared in drought -- which include London, East Anglia to its northeast, all of southwest England and the West Midlands -- comprises 51.4 percent of the nation.

The Environment Agency reported that representatives of the National Drought Group, which consists of government and meteorological officials, ministers, regulators, water corporations, farmers, and others, met on Tuesday to talk about the situation.

'We are using water faster than nature can replenish it'

They examined the effects, preparations for preparation, and drought response measures in England and instructed the country's private water firms to give leak repairs top priority.

"The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it," the group's chair and director of water, Helen Wakeham, stated in a statement.

People sit at a lido in London, as a heatwave is forecast to develop in the coming days, Friday, June 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Kin Cheung) Kin Cheung/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

"A second consecutive summer drought is an exceptionally serious situation and one that will have long-lasting impacts on our environment, wildlife, and the economy," Wakeham added.

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, the Met Office, the nation's meteorological agency, announced it had finalised readings in June and that both England and the UK saw a daily temperature record of 38°C for the month.

That was higher than the 37.7C figure previously reported.

According to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Service, Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average.

Last month, Western Europe recorded its hottest temperatures with extreme heat and widespread dryness contributing to the spread and intensification of fires in France and Spain, Copernicus said.

World.title: Pro-Russian propagandist Xenia Fedorova faces expulsion from France
World.content:
France has ordered Russian commentator Xenia Fedorova to leave the country, accusing her of spreading Kremlin propaganda through French television and radio, the interior ministry said on Wednesday.

 

Fedorova, who works for the media group of a conservative billionaire, has been placed under house arrest after being notified of the expulsion order, according to a source familiar with the case.

She is required to report daily to a police station.

According to the French Interior Ministry, Fedorova's activities “undermine the fundamental interests of the state” and her presence in France “constitutes a particularly serious and current threat to public order.”

Disinformation experts have warned about the influence of Fedorova, a former journalist for Russia's state-run broadcaster RT, ahead of France's presidential election next year.

Related MEPs urge EU sanctions on former RT France head Xenia Fedorova

Her employer said it was shocked by the expulsion order, calling it “a particularly serious infringement of freedom of expression”.

Fedorova, the former head of RT France, which was banned after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, is now a commentator for media outlets owned by French billionaire Vincent Bolloré. French newspaper Le Monde has described her as a “protégé” of Bolloré

Fedorova is a regular commentator on CNews and Europe 1 and writes for Le Journal du Dimanche, where critics accuse her of echoing Kremlin narratives on Ukraine and the West.

According to French newspaper Libération, the expulsion order accuses Fedorova of acting “as a conduit for disinformation campaigns orchestrated by the Russian authorities” aimed at “destabilising public order” in France.

The order accused Fedorova of contributing to the dissemination of disinformation aimed at "manipulating public opinion" and "undermining the confidence of European citizens, and particularly French citizens, in their institutions".

World.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to overturn €71 million defamation award in sexual assault case
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and the Justice Department are asking the Supreme Court to overturn an $83 million (€71 million) defamation verdict won by writer E. Jean Carroll after she accused him of sexual assault.

 

Trump has long argued he cannot be sued over comments he made about Carroll during his first term where he disavowed knowing her and attacked her motivations for going public with her story in a recent memoir.

The Justice Department says the Westfall Act shields government employees from lawsuits over actions taken as part of their official duties, while Trump's lawyers argued that presidential immunity shields him from the €71 million award because he made the statements while serving as president in 2019.

"Absent this Court’s intervention, the sitting President is facing nearly a hundred million dollars of personal liability for conduct that was well within the scope of his federal office,” federal attorneys wrote. “That alone deserves this Court’s attention.”

“This is the first case in our nation's history in which a court has imposed damages liability on a president for his conduct in office,” the lawyers wrote.

E. Jean Carroll exits the New York Federal Court after former President Donald Trump appeared in court, Sept. 6, 2024, in New York Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Carroll testified twice before New York juries that Trump sexually assaulted her in a dressing room at luxury department store Bergdorf Goodman in the spring of 1996. The longtime advice columnist and former TV talk show host first made the allegations public in a 2019 memoir.

She later sued Trump for defamation after he accused her of fabricating the allegations to boost book sales, saying he had never met her and that “she’s not my type.” Trump has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

It's the second time Trump has asked the Supreme Court to overturn damages awarded to Carroll. In June, the justices declined to hear his appeal of a separate $5 million (€4.3 million) verdict that found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation.

A Manhattan jury awarded her €71 million in damages in January 2024. Lower courts have so far rejected Trump’s appeals to overturn the verdict, though the New York-based appeals court split over the decision and agreed to delay that payout until the Supreme Court weighs in.

In 2023, another jury said Carroll was entitled to €4.3 million after concluding that Trump had subjected her to sexual abuse in the department store encounter and for defamation for remarks he had made after his first term ended, a judgment which has been paid.

Carroll's lawyers have declined to comment on the latest Trump filing.

World.title: Italy moves to ban horse-drawn tourist carriages in Rome and other art cities
World.content:
One of Rome's oldest trades risks disappearing for good.

 

On Wednesday afternoon, a bill was presented in the Chamber of Deputies which, if passed, would ban the "botticelle", horse-drawn carriages that are particularly widespread in major tourist cities, above all Rome.

The bill, promoted by PD, Avs and M5S, calls for the repeal of article 70 of the Highway Code, which regulates "public hire services using animal-drawn vehicles", authorising their circulation.

The aim is an explicit ban on the use of animals to pull vehicles for public hire services, non-scheduled public transport as well as for tourist, recreational and ceremonial purposes.

"Individual municipal ordinances that restrict the hours and activities of the botticelle are not enough. We need to move towards a national law that abolishes botticelle and animal-drawn carriages in cities," said PD MP Patrizia Prestipino, animal welfare guarantor for Roma Capitale, during a press conference with Avs MPs Francesco Emilio Borrelli and Sergio Costa of the M5S.

The MP stresses that for years environmental associations, including Amore A Quattro Zampe, which is also promoting the initiative, have been pointing out that today's streets are not suited to animal welfare. In addition, the extreme temperatures of these days make it impossible for horses to work, given the scorching asphalt.

Throughout the month of August, in the main tourist areas of the Capital, the awareness campaign A piedi è più bello will be displayed. It is promoted by Rocco Ferraro, councillor of Roma Capitale and delegated councillor of the Metropolitan City of Rome Capital for the Environment, Ecological Transition, Protected Areas and Animal Protection, and has been produced in Italian and English.

Ferraro has also expressed his support for the bill, expressing the hope that "Parliament will seize this historic opportunity and approve a measure that will definitively end the use of horses for tourist transport in our cities. In 2026, continuing to have horses pulling carriages in the heart of the capital is a practice that belongs to the past, not the future".

World.title: Portugal: Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submit binding bids to buy TAP
World.content:
Air France-KLM and Lufthansa on Wednesday submitted binding offers to buy a 44.5% stake in TAP Air Portugal, Parpública, which manages the state's shareholdings, said in a statement quoted by Eco (source in Portuguese).

 

"As part of the third stage of the process for the reference sale of 44.9% of TAP's share capital, PARPÚBLICA, SGPS, S.A. announces that it has received two binding proposals, submitted by the interested parties invited to do so after the conclusion of the second stage of the said transaction, Air France-KLM S.A. and Deutsche Lufthansa AG," the Parpública statement says.

Parpública now has 30 days to analyse the documentation and submit a report to the Portuguese government, and may request further clarifications from the airlines. In that case, the deadline is suspended until the requested information is provided.

According to Eco, the binding proposals already specify the amount to be paid for the 44.5% stake in the airline, as well as an industrial and strategic plan to guarantee the company's sustainability and future.

Once it has examined Parpública's report, the government may decide to invite one or both of the bidders that submitted binding proposals to present a new final offer.

The deadline for submitting the two binding proposals expired on Tuesday, marking the end of the third phase of TAP's privatisation process.

The process for the partial sale of the national airline, relaunched in 2025 by Luís Montenegro's government, was narrowed down to two bidders after International Airlines Group (IAG), owner of Iberia, pulled out, leaving Air France-KLM and Lufthansa still in the running. The two groups submitted their binding offers on Tuesday.

The decree law approved by the government a year ago provides for the sale of up to 49.9% of TAP to private investors, with the state remaining the majority shareholder.

Of this 49.9%, 5% is reserved for employees, and any unsubscribed stake may also be acquired by the selected investor.

On the privatisation process, the Minister for Infrastructure, Miguel Pinto Luz, has already said he would like it to be concluded next September and has even indicated that the chosen investor could start sharing management of the airline as early as 2026 with the current board, although the actual capital injection is only expected to take place in a year's time, in the summer of 2027.

World.title: UEFA slams FIFA over Infantino's deadline for World Cup stake sale
World.content:
UEFA and FIFA have escalated their conflict after the European football's governing body issued a new scathing condemnation on Wednesday of plans to sell a stake in the World Cup tournament, one of the world's biggest sporting events.

 

"FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends," UEFA said, accusing FIFA President Gianni Infantino of pressuring national football associations into backing the proposal by setting a deadline for their support.

FIFA announced on Tuesday that it plans to create a $20 billion subsidiary to manage the World Cup and other tournaments, offering up to a 20% stake to external investors.

A letter sent to football associations worldwide, seen by British media, indicates that Infantino has given members until 19 September to support the proposal, with a $40 million (around €35.1 million) financial incentive to join the venture early.

UEFA said the deadline "says everything" about the proposal and claimed opposition to the plan is growing.

In a statement released on Tuesday, UEFA accused FIFA of putting the game's "soul" up for sale. According to media reports, European football's governing body will hold an emergency virtual meeting on Thursday to decide its next move.

Infantino's proposal involves New York-based JPMorgan, while potential investors include Thrive Eternal, founded by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared is married to Ivanka Trump, the daughter of US President Donald Trump.

FIFA insists long-term investors would be carefully vetted and would acquire only minority, non-controlling stakes, with all net proceeds reinvested in football worldwide.

The proposal must now be approved by FIFA's 211 member associations. It requires the backing of a majority of members, as well as the FIFA Council, the governing body's 37-member decision-making panel chaired by Infantino.

The plan has already triggered a backlash across Europe, with several football associations accusing Infantino of blurring the lines between football, politics and private business.

"We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details," the English Football Association, the world's oldest national football association, said on Wednesday.

EU Commissioner for Sport Glenn Micallef backed UEFA, warning that the "relentless commercialisation of football has become corrosive" in separate comments, while the newly appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the World Cup "is not a product" for sale.

World.title: France expels Russian media commentator over disinformation
World.content:
Tensions between Xenia Fedorova and the French date back to 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron accused her of spreading "defamatory falsehoods."

Russian commentator Xenia Fedorova has been ordered to leave France, the country's Interior Ministry said Wednesday. She has been accused of disseminating Kremlin propaganda on French television and radio.

According to French newspaper Liberation, the expulsion order accuses Fedorova of acting "as a conduit for disinformation campaigns orchestrated by the Russian authorities" with the aim of "destabilising public order" in France.

According to the AFP news agency, Fedorova has been placed under house arrest since the order was issued.

Fedorova is the former chief of the Russia Today (RT) in France, which was ultimately banned in the country after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

She stayed in the country and became a commentator for broadcasting outlets owned by French billionaire Vincent Bollore's media conglomerate.

According to French daily Le Monde, Fedorova has been known to be a "protege" of Bollore.

Fedorova made frequent appearances on the CNews television channel and Europe 1 radio.

She also writes for Le Journal du Dimanche newspaper, where she has been accused of spreading Kremlin talking points about Ukraine and the West.

'Serious infringement' on free speech

Fedorova's employers reacted to her expulsion saying they were astonished, adding that the move amounted to "a particularly serious infringement of freedom of expression."

The media group said it would "provide their full support ‌to Ms. Fedorova during this decision."

The commentator's lawyer Emmanuel Piwnica told AFP that his client would "immediately" file an appeal against the order.

"Xenia Fedorova is a journalist," Piwnica told AFP, adding that she has "always carried out her work in the most proper manner possible."

Macron says Fedorova 'not a journalist'

Tensions between Fedorova and the French state go back as far as 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron criticized her and implied she was not a journalist.

"When media outlets spread defamatory falsehoods, they are no longer journalists. They are instruments of influence," Macron said.

In June, Macron was again asked to speak on the subject and he said his opinion had not changed.

Experts on disinformation had previously raised the alarm about the influence of figures like Fedorova in France, ahead of a presidential election next year.

Although there is no evidence of any links between Fedorova and the Kremlin, media advocates have said she should still be regarded as an agent of influence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: K-pop's BTS opt out of new Asian music Grammy consideration
World.content:
The K-pop sensation BTS, snubbed when nominated for Grammys in the past, say they're not interested in winning a new Asian music category.

K-pop powerhouse BTS said on Wednesday that they would not submit songs for consideration for the 2027 Grammys next February.

The seven band members issued the same Korean-language note online in concert.

What's the reason BTS doesn't want to be considered this year?

They said they did not want to be included in the new Grammy category, best Asian pop music performance, that's seen as a way to categorize releases across K-pop or J-pop and C-pop from Japan and China, respectively.

Newly reformed BTS, touring to promote a new album after returning from a military service hiatus, would seem to be among the frontrunners in the category.

"We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language," the band's message read. "We thank Army [the band's colloquial term for the BTS fan base] and everyone who has always stood by us."

Critics of the new Grammy argued it could serve as an exclusionary barrier stopping Asian pop music from winning other awards. Proponents argued it was just the latest of numerous genres added to the list of more than 90 Grammy categories.

BTS performed 'Butter' at the 2022 Grammys in LA but were overlooked as the awards were doled out Image: Chris Pizzello/AP Photo/picture alliance

Has BTS won Grammys before?

No. But the band had been nominated for a total of five.

Three times they made the shortlist as the best pop duo or group performance, once they shared a nomination for best album of the year because of their contributions to Coldplay's "Music of Spheres," and also for their music video "Yet to Come."

Up until this year's ceremonies, no K-Pop act had ever won a Grammy Award.

"Golden" from the Netflix animated film "KPop Demon Hunters" won the best song for visual media, a decision that prompted elation in South Korea, despite the song's US roots and fictional performing artists.

In a sign of the band's global reach, Chile's government looked to ban BTS' visit as part of its giant American tour — until mass protests in Santiago prompted a U-turn Image: Sebastian Silva/Nexpher Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

BTS touring to promote 'ARIRANG' after military service return

BTS reformed and returned to frontline performance this year after a four-year hiatus.

They have released and are now promoting a 14-track album, "ARIRANG" — named after Korea's most renowned traditional folk song and unofficial national anthem, roughly translating as "My Beloved One."

The band has spent most of the summer in the Americas amid the World Cup and its world tour, including performing at the controversial halftime show of the World Cup final this month.

This fifth studio album follows a four-year break as the band members completed South Korea's mandatory military service and pursued solo projects.

World.title: Iran war: Egypt's difficult balancing act
World.content:
The US-Iran war has already had a negative economic impact on Egypt. Now new threats from the Houthi group in Yemen are likely to worsen that. At the same time, Egypt is trying to stay on good terms with all parties.

The Suez Canal boasts an array of impressive statistics. At 193 kilometers (120 miles) long, the Egyptian waterway is located between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and it saves ships traveling between Europe and Asia approximately 10,700 kilometers. This is why, since it was opened in 1869, the canal has become one of the world's most important trade routes.

However unrest in the Middle East has seen shipping companies increasingly avoid the Suez Canal over the past couple of years. The Houthi rebel group in Yemen has targeted shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, off the coast of Yemen. To get to the Suez Canal, ships must pass the Bab el-Mandeb and the Yemeni coast.

Recently the Houthis have again threatened to block ships passing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and there are fears that the trend to avoid the Suez Canal will accelerate.

This is a huge problem for Egypt. Fees paid by shipping companies transiting the Suez Canal are an important source of revenue for the country.

According to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, Egypt likely lost around $7 billion (€6.15 billion) from a decrease in traffic through the Suez Canal in 2024 alone. The Reuters news agency said that at times, losses could have been as much as $8 million (€7 million) in a month.

Houthis claim attacks on Saudi tankers in Red Sea To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is why the economic consequence of that loss extends well beyond shipping. Egypt has not been impacted by the Iran conflict in a major military way, but it is certainly seeing an economic effect.

Egypt loses billions on Suez Canal

"Economically, Egypt is in a very ambivalent situation," says Stefan Lukas, director of German think tank Middle East Minds.

During 2025 and 2026, revenues from canal transits actually went up again, mainly because oil from the Gulf states was transported via Saudi pipelines to the Red Sea and then onwards through the Suez Canal. This was to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, which is being blocked by Iran and the US in turns. But the new threats by the Houthis to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could interfere with this alternative route.

It's bad timing for Egypt: Rising energy prices and the International Monetary Fund's reforms are already putting tough limits on Cairo's financial flexibility.

"Higher energy prices have made imports more expensive and driven up inflation," says Hanna Voss, an expert on the region with Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation. "The uncertainty in the Red Sea and potential disruptions to the passage through Bab el-Mandeb are jeopardizing Suez Canal revenues."

The Yemeni Houthi rebels recently threatened again to attack ships going past the coast of Yemen Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu/picture alliance

Tourism into Egypt, capital inflows and the exchange rate for the Egyptian pound are sensitive to any changes. Additionally Egypt is heavily indebted and dependent on loans from the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, as well as investments and financial aid from the Gulf States.

Just how serious the situation already is, can be seen via other numbers. According to the Associated Press , Suez Canal revenues fell from $10.25 billion in 2023 to around $4 billion in 2024. During the same period, the number of ships passing through the waterway decreased from more than 26,000 to just over 13,000. Many shipping companies preferred to detour around Africa rather than risk Houthi attacks.

No short-term solution

As the US think tank Carnegie Middle East Center explains, Egypt cannot compensate for these losses on its own because of the country's current economic model. The government increasingly relies on large-scale state projects and military-controlled assets to generate growth, the think tank reports, while potentially productive investments and private growth are neglected. The result is growing dependence on foreign loans and investments.

In the short term at least, there are no new sources of revenue that could offset the decline in Suez revenues. Economic reforms, such as those required by the IMF, are also not progressing.

"Egypt has an interest in very rapid de-escalation," Voss states.

This is why Cairo supports mediation between the US and Iran, albeit less overtly than Qatar or Oman. The Egyptian government wants to secure its relationships with the US, Saudi Arabia and the UAE while simultaneously avoiding an open confrontation with Iran.

British think tank Chatham House describes Egypt's positioning as risk management. The goal is not to decide the regional power struggle but to minimize the economic damage to itself.

More than 1,500 commercial vessels have been stuck in the Gulf since the Strait of Hormuz closed in late February, when the US-Iran war began Image: Wen Xinnian/Xinhua/IMAGO

"The regime under al-Sissi is once again pursuing a two-pronged approach," Lukas from Middle East Minds explained.

Outwardly Egypt is demonstrating solidarity with Saudi Arabia, condemning the Houthis' threats and increasing security at the Suez Canal. But Egypt isn't openly opposing Iran and behind the scenes, is keeping communication channels with the Iranians open. That behavior is driven by Egypt's financial dependence on the wealthy Gulf states and the fear that the Suez Canal itself could become a target in the war, Lukas explained.

"All the neighboring states have an interest in stabilizing the regional order because they simply cannot afford a prolonged crisis," Voss added.

And that is precisely Egypt's dilemma. For Cairo, this isn't just about foreign policy. Every escalation in the Red Sea costs the country urgently needed foreign currency. Every move towards peace increases the chances of economic recovery.

"The crucial question is whether the [Houthis' threatened] blockade remains symbolic or takes effect," Lukas said.

In reality the Egyptian government has little influence on that or the course of the wider conflict. Any lasting peace or diplomacy won't be decided in Cairo but in Washington, Tehran and likely by the Houthi rebels themselves.

This story was originally published in German.

World.title: German Muslims are alarmed by the Islamist terror attack in Berlin
World.content:
The terrorist attack that struck Berlin's Pride celebration, or Christopher Street Day (CSD), late on Saturday evening has heightened fears and concerns about further Islamist attacks. Until Sunday evening, when security forces confronted 21-year-old Abdul B. and fatally shot him, most media outlets and the politicians responsible referred to a "suspected perpetrator" and "alleged motives".

Investigators are now relatively certain that the perpetrator was an Islamist, a radicalized Muslim with links to the "Islamic State" terror group. Politicians and security agencies are debating stricter laws and expanded surveillance powers. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) is politically responsible for this area.

"With shock and profound dismay, we learned of yesterday's inhumane attack on the CSD," the Council of Berlin Imams stated across various channels just over twelve hours after the attack. The Council expressed its solidarity with the victims, their relatives, and the bereaved, and thanked the emergency responders. "This act, which we condemn in the strongest possible terms, demonstrates the terrible consequences to which hatred and hostility toward others can lead. Hatred leads to nothing good."

Berlin attack: When deradicalization programs don't work To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Two days later, once the perpetrator's Islamist background had been confirmed, the Council of Berlin Imams issued a second statement, this time in greater detail. It stated that the terrorist attack once again demonstrated that "religiously motivated extremism ... poses a real threat to our society."

"As imams, we cannot emphasize often enough that terror, hatred and violence have no religious legitimacy whatsoever. Anyone who uses the religion of Islam to commit violence against people because of their identity, their beliefs or their way of life, or even to kill them, is acting in direct contradiction to the ethical principles of our religion." The term "Islamism" does not appear anywhere in the 30-line statement.

The Council of Berlin Imams explicitly condemns "all violence against queer people and members of other minorities in our society". Such direct references to queer people are relatively uncommon in comparable statements.

The Council has repeatedly faced criticism. Some politicians of the ruling center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and several experts argue that it promotes views that are at odds with Germany's liberal democratic constitutional system. Others dispute that assessment.

The Council's latest statement suggests that the imams are keenly aware of the challenges involved. They note that "radicalization rarely happens overnight". More often, it is the result of a gradual process that unfolds online and across social media platforms. The priority, they argue, must be to reach young people at an early stage and "provide them with guidance, a sense of belonging and future prospects".

No single institution, they emphasize, can shoulder this responsibility alone.

A few months earlier, one imam had told DW that, for many young people, the internet had long since become the real mosque.

Mouhanad Khorchide is the founding dean of the Centre for Islamic Theology at the University of Münster Image: Lars Berg/dpa/picture alliance

Islam is not the same as Islamism

"Some Muslims reject the term 'Islamism' because they fear that even the linguistic association with the word 'Islam' harms their religion," sociologist and religious education scholar Mouhanad Khorchide told DW.

The 54-year-old is the founding dean of the Centre for Islamic Theology at the University of Münster . He does not regard this concern as helpful: "If we categorically deny any connection between Islam and Islamism, we make the necessary substantive engagement with the issue all the more difficult."

After all, Khorchide argued, Islamists base their arguments on Islamic sources. They claim to speak in the name of Islam. In his view, it is therefore not enough simply to say that Islamist perpetrators have "nothing to do with Islam". What is needed instead is a nuanced engagement with the issue in order to "deprive Islamist ideologies of their credibility in the long term".

Berlin's Ahmadiyya community

The members of Berlin's Ahmadiyya Muslim community are devout Muslims belonging to a reform movement founded more than a century ago, whose teachings have led many Muslims to reject them as non-Islamic. As a result, they have also been persecuted by Islamists.

In the days following the attack, the Ahmadiyya mosque community in Berlin-Charlottenburg invited the public to a series of dialogue events scheduled for the coming days, as well as to an "open Friday prayer service on the topic of Islamism."

Burhan Kesici, chairman of the Islamic Council for the Federal Republic of Germany , condemned the attack "in the strongest possible terms" and expressed his sympathy. He concluded with the words: "Muslims in Germany stand for peace."

Burhan Kesici, chairman of the Islamic Council for the Federal Republic of Germany, condemned the attack in Berlin (file photo from 2022) Image: Abdulhamid Hosbas/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

Central Council of Muslims in Germany: 'we condemn all forms of violence'

Similarly, the much longer statement issued by the Central Council of Muslims in Germany (KRM) describes the organization as "deeply shaken" by the attack. "As Muslim religious communities in Germany, we condemn all forms of violence, extremism, terrorism, and contempt for humanity in the strongest possible terms," it states.

Like the Council of Berlin Imams, the Central Council of Muslims in Germany avoids using the term "queer", and states: "No one should become the target of violence because of their sexual orientation...". Addressing the perpetrator's "Islamist" motive, the Central Council describes the attack as yet another case "in which an extremist ideology misuses religious references to justify hatred and violence."

Islam and pluralism

According to Professor Khorchide of the University of Münster, many mosque communities, imams and Muslim organizations remain "stuck in an apologetic posture."

Their main concern, he says, is often "to defend Islam against sweeping accusations and to emphasize that violence and terrorism have nothing to do with Islam". Although this is "understandable in light of widespread anti-Muslim hostility", it does not go far enough, Khorchide said: "Anyone who wants to solve problems must first be willing to name them openly."

Khorchide also points to the conspicuous reluctance to mention the event itself, the "CSD," and the queer context in which it took place.

Some imams, he argues, avoid a "clear distancing from Islamism" because "on certain socio-political issues, such as attitudes toward sexual diversity or gender roles, they share conservative convictions, even though they naturally reject violence."

Precisely for that reason, he says, they must be willing to engage in self-critical reflection. "A credible Muslim voice is not one that relativizes problems," the academic says.

Eren Güvercin is the deputy chairman of the Alhambra Society advocating a pluralistic Islam (file photo from 2024) Image: teutopress/picture alliance

Eren Güvercin, deputy chairman of the relatively small Alhambra Society, is even more outspoken. Founded in 2017, the organization advocates a pluralistic Islam and has drawn criticism from established Muslim umbrella groups because of its broadly liberal orientation.

Güvercin speaks of a "deliberate decision" by many not to name "the motive behind the attack, namely Islamist hostility toward queer people," nor "the target of the attack, namely queer people and the CSD."

According to Güvercin, speaking openly about these issues would inevitably raise the question of what their own religious stance toward queer lives actually is, he told DW.

While people are generally able to clearly identify the motives behind far-right attacks, he argues that this willingness is completely absent when it comes to Islamist attacks. There is no serious or self-critical debate within Muslim communities about Islamism as an ideology, nor about hostility toward queer people or antisemitism, Güvercin says.

Muslim organizations that are unable to name problems openly will, in Güvercin's view, be unable to provide meaningful guidance. "Instead, young people find that guidance from Islamist influencers online."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: World Cup sell off: Has FIFA finally gone too far?
World.content:
A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?

"While you divide, we unite," Gianni Infantino wrote on social media on Monday, in a long missive aimed at his detractors. By Tuesday, he had united the football world — albeit in opposition to his latest scheme.

Shortly after reports emerged in UK newspapers The Times and the Financial Times on Tuesday, FIFA confirmed its plans to create a new subsidiary, named FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). This would enable it to sell a minority stake in the World Cup's operations to private investors for billions of dollars.

Chief among FIFA's proposed investors is the investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, headed by Joshua Kushner — younger brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Why is FIFA's new World Cup plan controversial?

Other than the potential conflict of interest connection to Trump, with whom Infantino has grown close, there are significant concerns about transparency, corruption and whether FIFA has the remit to make such a move unilaterally.

"The World Cup is one of the few truly global sporting events, and that comes with a responsibility beyond maximizing revenue," Bret Myers, a professor of sports business practices at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, USA, told DW.

The US connection is important, with the model echoing the way that many US sports operate. Formula 1 too went through a similar process when it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017. Greg Maffei, a former Liberty CEO, has been a "key commercial adviser" to FIFA on the FFE plan.

"North American sports have long operated within a more commercial framework, where private ownership, franchise valuations, and investor involvement are widely accepted," Myers added.

"Football, particularly in Europe, has a much stronger tradition of clubs and competitions being viewed as cultural institutions rather than purely commercial assets."

USA striker Folarin Balogun's red-card ban during the World Cup was suspended after Infantino got a call from Trump Image: Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire/IMAGO

More fundamentally, the concern is that this is the first step towards the World Cup, football's biggest prize, becoming privately owned.

"A minority investment is very different from relinquishing control," Myers said. However, it does represent a significant shift in how the World Cup is financed and managed commercially."

World football's global governors are a nonprofit organization but sit on cash reserves of an estimated $8 billion (€7.02 billion) after a World Cup that saw ticket prices skyrocket.

Given FIFA's remit lies in developing football, rather than purely profiting from it, there is a sense that this is a move designed to shore up Infantino's power and, perhaps, encroach on the turf of the continental football federations he failed to include in the planning.

How do Infantino and FIFA aim to sell the plan?

FIFA has promised to invest profits back into the game, mostly by offering all 211 member associations a flat fee of $20 million in 2027, rising to $24 million by 2035. Associations must decide whether to accept those payments by September 19 or risk them being reduced or retracted.

"The president controls this huge pot of money and uses it to reward those that are loyal to him, that support him, and punish those that are not supportive of him," Miguel Maduro a former chairman of FIFA's Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee, told DW.

"FIFA could do lots of good things with money. But there is no system of checks and balances and accountability to make us sure that the money is actually going to be well spent by all national football associations. Everything that that's happened in the past makes me suspicious of how this money will end up being spent."

What has the reaction been from the footballing world?

Almost universally negative. National federations, world leaders and fan groups have all come out against the idea, with federations particularly peeved about the lack of consultation.

But perhaps the most surprising reaction came from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), who released a statement confirming it was "not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed" by the way in which it was released. Asia and Africa, are where Infantino's main power base lies, as together they have 101 of the 211 national associations — with each getting a vote on the president.

The close friendship between Infantino and Trump has raised alarm bells for some Image: Kai Pfaffenbach/REUTERS

Similar misgivings were expressed by a number of powerful national football associations, including Germany's DFB.

"A line is being crossed here. There is a strong consensus among the member associations on this matter, as evidenced by several conversations I have had in recent days with Aleksander Ceferin [president of Europe's football governors UEFA] and other colleagues," said Hans-Joachim Watzke, a DFB vice president.

"If European football stands united in opposing these plans, it carries significant weight."

Who might oppose FIFA's World Cup plans?

UEFA seems in the best position to lead any revolt and has hit out at the plans, saying football is "not FIFA's to sell." It was a strongly worded statement of the type UEFA has released several times in recent months as its battle with FIFA plays out in public. Reports suggest UEFA will meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss their options.

Maduro backs UEFA's stance but said he'd like the current climate to serve as an opportunity for broader reform.

"I don't think UEFA has the same severity of problems that we find in FIFA, but I do think it also suffers from serious governance problems and that they need to be addressed," he said.

"Simply getting rid of Mr. Infantino but leaving the entire structure and model of governance of sports will be removing a couple of bad apples but leaving the tree that produced them in place."

Aleksander Ceferin's UEFA has been a strong critic of FIFA in recent years Image: Mike Egerton/PA/picture alliance

How could this change football?

That the AFC and the CONCACAF (which governs North, Central America and Caribbean football) have criticized the way the latest plans were released, may have strengthened UEFA's hand in any thoughts of breakaway or boycott.

It may also lead to the continental federations uniting to find someone to oppose Infantino in next year's presidential election or in threats of boycotting next year's Women's World Cup.

But Maduro thinks such talk is often designed to appease the public before intentions are quietly shelved.

"What we've seen so far for the most part is that these statements, where they distance themselves from these kinds of initiatives of FIFA, are made under the pressure of public opinions. But then they actually never follow through."

Maduro went on to say that UEFA's increasingly strident opposition to FIFA is, at least in part, a reaction to an increased threat to its own highly lucrative Champions League. Should the proposed changes go through, Maduro expects World Cups to be more frequent and a further expansion of FIFA's recently expanded Club World Cup.

"They will want to transform that into the big international football competition of clubs instead of the Champions League. That's what they will try to do because it will be in their commercial interest," he said.

World.title: Germany news: Temperatures to soar amid new heatwave
World.content:
07/29/2026 July 29, 2026 German official defends deportation of non-criminal to Afghanistan

The German government on Wednesday defended its decision to deport an Afghan back to their homeland despite not being convicted of any crime.

On Tuesday evening, the latest in a series of deportation flights from Germany to Afghanistan took off, carrying 31 Afghan people.

But unlike previous flights, which saw only criminals deported to the Taliban-run country, Tuesday's flight was the first to include a person not convicted of a crime.

On Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that those on the latest flight were mostly "serious offenders who had committed crimes such as murder, rape and acts of violence," but admitted that "the designation of 'convicted offender' does not apply" to one of the passengers on board.

The government has said that it prioritizes deporting individuals convicted of serious crimes.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Wednesday that the government aimed to "begin with deporting people who have been convicted and those who pose a threat" but that it was also possible "to put people on deportation flights who are not criminals."

Dobrindt said on Tuesday that "people who have no right to stay in the country can also be subject to deportation if there are no signs they have integrated in Germany."

As a member of Chancellor Merz's conservative party, Dobrindt defended the government's actions and said it would continue to pursue a strict immigration policy with a "firm stance."

Refugee rights groups sharply criticized the deportation, and Tuesday's flight, which set off from Leipzig, was accompanied by protests of about 250 people, according to officials.

World.title: BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs
World.content:
Nearly half of BMW's German staff will receive a voluntary redundancy offer in the carmaker's bid to reduce staff by about 8,000 people.

BMW aims to cut staff by up to 8,000 positions by the end of 2027, according to company sources.

The German carmaker said the reduction would primarily target office jobs, while production line workers will be spared from cuts.

"The workforce will ultimately be reduced by around 8,000 people by the end of 2027," an anonymous source told the AFP news agency. "We're planning on the basis of that."

The Munich-based automaker hopes to achieve the cuts through natural staff turnover as well as a voluntary redundancy scheme. The latter would be aimed at all employees in Germany not directly involved in production, who could choose to accept severance packages in a period from October 2026 to the end of 2027.

The company currently employs 84,000 staff in Germany, and roughly 154,000 globally.

The latest German carmaker to announce job cuts

BMW is the latest German car company to announce job cuts, following similar moves by rival brands Volkswagen, Mercedes and Volkswagen-owned Audi.

Germany's prestigious car industry is struggling amid stiff competition from Chinese carmakers, US tariffs, and narrower profit margins from electric cars.

BMW was long considered one of the sector's more resilient players. The planned cuts come after the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.

Last year, BMW's vehicle deliveries in China were already at their lowest level since 2017, and they fell 30% year-on-year in the three months to June.

On Thursday, BMW is due to announce its earnings for the first half of 2026.

World.title: Europe wildfires: Spain lets people return, France faces extreme heat
World.content:
Spain lifted evacuations for Avila province, a day after doing so in parts of the Madrid area. To the north in France, temperatures rose again, with extreme heat warnings in much of the country, including Gironde.

As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France struggled to contain a blaze four times the size of Paris, scientists warned that extreme wildfires were becoming more frequent worldwide.

New heatwave could worsen France, Spain fires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Evacuees allowed to return in Spain

Spain started lifting evacuation orders for various places in the Avila province on Wednesday, having taken similar steps in the Madrid province on Tuesday.

Interior Minister Francisco Martin Aguirre announced progressively reduced restrictions for a variety of places after conditions overnight allowed firefighters to make gains, saying tens of thousands had been able to return home.

Sanchez: 'Next 12 hours will be very important'

"Today, I believe we are closer to that final objective" of "defeating the fire," Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told reporters in televised comments at a command center in the town of Navalarnero near the fire zone.

"Things are progressing favorably, with the greatest of caution," he said, predicting that "the next 12 hours will be very imporant — they will be decisive for consolidating the work that has been done."

For a week, Spain has been fighting two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills west of Madrid.

However, authorities remain on alert, with highs consistently above 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) forecast every day in the Madrid area this week.

Spain's meteorological agency AEMET warned of a new stretch of high temperatures starting on Wednesday Image: Cordon Press/picture alliance

Heat warnings across most of France, including fire flashpoint Gironde

On France's southwestern Atlantic coast, temperatures and winds picked up once more on Wednesday, threatening to fan the flames.

Temperature warnings were in place for most of the country, with the most severe on the eastern border and in the southwestern areas hardest hit by fires, including the Gironde region. The Meteo France weather service forecast highs of 40 Celsius in the Bordeaux area in the afternoon.

Thousands of French firefighters, with support from elsewhere in Europe, are trying to control the fires in Gironde Image: Mohamad Salaheldin Abdelghani Alsayed/Anadolu/picture alliance

French authorities have been forced to relocate around 220,000 people in total amid the fires, many of them from holiday resorts on the coast — like Lacanau and Grand Cohot on Tuesday.

More than 2,200 firefighters and over 20 aircraft remained mobilized, backed by crews from across France and European partners.

"We strike quickly and strike hard at any new smoke emissions," Gironde fire commander Matthieu Jomain said.

The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.

While new fires were reported in France's Gironde, authorities in Landes said the advance of the wildfires had stopped Image: Jeanne Accorsini/SIPA/picture alliance

Climate change exacerbating wildfires

Scientists say climate change is fueling hotter, drier summers that are intensifying wildfires across Europe. The warmer temperatures are also extending fire seasons and making these blazes harder to control, straining the resources of European nations.

Currently, the European Union only coordinates the deployment of extra resources pooled from its member states when a ​country requests emergency help. As fires on the continent grow more extreme, however, the bloc called for greater investment in forest management and wildfire prevention.

Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brussels is purchasing its own permanent firefighting fleet.

"Climate change ​is accelerating. So, our response must evolve just as quickly," Hadja Lahbib, the EU's Crisis Management Commissioner, told Reuters.

World.title: La Comunidad de Madrid compra un ático de lujo en Chamberí para que lo use Ayuso como “oficina” temporal
World.content:
Ayuso: "Yo no me estoy comprando nada, insisto, y no se me está comprando nada"

La Comunidad de Madrid ha comprado un ático de 485 metros cuadrados en Chamberí, una de las zonas más caras de la capital, para que lo use la presidenta Isabel Díaz Ayuso “durante la rehabilitación de la Real Casa de Correos, cuyos trabajos comenzarán en agosto”, según le ha respondido este martes una portavoz a EL PAÍS. La noticia se conoce tres meses y medio después de la adquisición del piso y solo después de que este diario planteara la pregunta tras descubrir la compraventa, que aparece en el Registro de la Propiedad.

La portavoz solo ha precisado que Ayuso trabajará en el inmueble “con un mínimo equipo” y no ha respondido otras cuestiones planteadas ―si Ayuso también planea vivir en él, el precio de la compra, las razones por las que se había guardado este secreto o por qué no se ha optado por alquilar un inmueble―. Tampoco queda claro a qué obras se refiere. La Real Casa de Correos, sede de la presidencia madrileña, concluyó el año pasado las obras de restauración de su fachada.

Tras la publicación de la noticia, una fuente de la máxima confianza de la presidenta ha explicado a este diario que la decisión sobre el uso del ático como oficina “no está tomada al cien por cien”. Ha dicho que van a reformar el inmueble y decidirán sobre el traslado en octubre o noviembre. También ha añadido, tras ser preguntado por ello, que no piensan destinarlo a residencia presidencial.

La compra fue realizada el 14 de abril por la empresa autonómica que comercializa suelo público y gestiona las oficinas propias, Planifica Madrid. Esta agencia, presidida por el portavoz del Gobierno y consejero de Presidencia, Miguel Ángel García Martín, no había incluido esta inversión en el presupuesto para este año. El valor de mercado de un ático de estas características en esa zona privilegiada ronda los seis millones de euros.

El ático del paseo del General Martínez Campos de Madrid, que en abril fue comprado por el Gobierno regional. Claudio Álvarez

El ático se encuentra en la planta novena de un portal del paseo del General Martínez Campos, un edificio residencial en una de las principales arterias del acomodado distrito de Chamberí. El bloque colinda con el Museo Sorolla, a tan solo 300 metros del paseo de la Castellana. La vendedora ha sido la economista y escritora Astrid Gil-Casares, según dos fuentes conocedoras de la operación. Una pareja residía en el inmueble como inquilinos.

La vivienda mide 485 metros cuadrados, de los cuales 199 corresponden a la terraza. Varios pisos del edificio pertenecen a familias de aristócratas y, según un empleado del bloque, ninguno está destinado a oficinas.

El gasto sorprende porque no estaba previsto en el presupuesto para 2026 de Planifica Madrid, que sí detalla minuciosamente otras operaciones de venta de inmuebles o de inversión en obra nueva. El Consejo de Gobierno tampoco ha concedido una extensión de crédito para la compra de esta vivienda (algo necesario para incurrir en este tipo de gasto) y, lo que es más importante, Planifica Madrid no ha informado de la adquisición en su página de transparencia, actualizada por última vez el pasado lunes 20 de julio, y donde se enumeran las actuaciones abiertas más relevantes.

Planifica Madrid es dueña de diez edificios enteros destinados a oficinas y un local, que luego arrienda, en casi todos los casos a distintos departamentos de la Comunidad de Madrid. En su mayoría son inmuebles históricos en el centro de Madrid con distintos grados de protección, como la Consejería de Sanidad (Calle Aduana, 29) o la de Cultura y Turismo (Alcalá, 31).

El registrador de la propiedad de la zona ha denegado a EL PAÍS la solicitud para conocer la identidad del vendedor, argumentando que el solicitante debe tener “un interés directo, legítimo y patrimonial”. No obstante, dos fuentes que conocen esta compraventa han indicado que se trata de Gil-Casares. Esta escritora estuvo casada hasta 2016 con Rafael del Pino Calvo-Sotelo, el presidente de Ferrovial y segundo hombre más rico de España,

El precio pagado por el ático es una incógnita, pero varias fuentes sugieren que puede haber rondado los seis millones de euros. Para tener una idea del monto, habría que multiplicar los 486 metros cuadrados por el precio del metro cuadrado en el código postal del barrio de Almagro, donde se ubica la vivienda, que según el portal del Notariado es de 9.414 euros. Esto supone 4,5 millones de euros. A esto habría que añadir un plus por tratarse de un ático que depende principalmente del tamaño de la terraza. Esta en concreto, de 200 metros cuadrados, es tan grande que el precio puede ser muy superior. En los portales inmobiliarios se ofertan áticos con grandes terrazas por precios que oscilan entre los cinco y los siete millones de euros.

La terraza de casi 200 metros cuadrados es tan grande que uno de los expertos inmobiliarios en Almagro, el gerente de la oficina de Don Chamberí en Paseo General Martínez Campos, responde que nunca ha visto algo así: “Yo no conozco un ático así. No creo que exista”.

Empresa con pasado oscuro

Planifica Madrid es la heredera de Arpegio, la empresa pública que se vio inmersa en un gran escándalo conocido como el caso Púnica, y que está judicializado. Esta sociedad protagoniza una de las piezas del macrocaso por haber participado en presuntas irregularidades cometidas en la adjudicación de suelo público y contratos de infraestructuras. En aquellos años era consejero de la empresa Francisco Granados, hombre de confianza de Esperanza Aguirre. La pieza que pertenece a estos presuntos amaños fue enviada en mayo a juicio. Allí se sentará Granados, que ya ha sido condenado por otros delitos.

La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, y el consejero de Presidencia, Justicia y Administración Local, Miguel Ángel García Martín, durante un pleno en la Asamblea de Madrid el 2 de julio. Gabriel Luengas (Europa Press)

La empresa está adscrita a la Consejería de Presidencia de García Martín, tiene una plantilla de 90 empleados y su presupuesto para 2026 es de 127 millones de euros. Su consejero delegado es desde julio de 2023 Pedro Corbalán Ruiz, que antes había tenido puestos en la administración autonómica dentro de los sucesivos gobiernos del Partido Popular.
