World.title: Before China’s First Emperor: Unearthing the Long Rise of the Qin
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018803/Before China’s First Emperor: Unearthing the Long Rise of the Qin
World.content:
Wang Hui still remembers everything about the sensational tomb-robbing scandal that launched his career.

It was the early 1990s, barely a decade into China’s transition from planned to market economy, and grave robbing had become a lucrative cottage industry in the Chinese countryside — a rare way for villagers to get rich. So when a local farmer in northwestern China’s Gansu province uncovered bronzes while digging for oracle bones, it kicked off a feeding frenzy.

The looters who descended on the site — now known as Dabuzi — were embedded in a highly specialized chain covering target scouting, excavation, transportation, trafficking, and smuggling. At its peak, there were reportedly tens of thousands of grave robbers and dealers in Dabuzi and the surrounding Lixian County. Their numbers were so great that they generated entire side businesses, with people setting up camp near the tombs to sell them water, food, and cigarettes.

Finally, in 1993, the problem became too big to ignore. After the influential China Youth Daily published a shocking expose on the extent of the problem — priceless artifacts being sold off for pennies on the dollar and entire tomb complexes stripped bare — the Gansu provincial government dispatched an archaeological team to the area to crack down on looting and salvage what they could.

“When we arrived, the entire area looked like a battlefield, full of massive pits,” recalls Wang, a member of the archaeological rescue team and now a professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University. “As we dug, we used the cigarette boxes we found inside the tombs to guess who had been there. Expensive ‘Hongtashan’ and ‘Ashima’ brand cigarettes — those were probably smoked by antiquities dealers. ‘Benma’ and ‘Fenghu’ were for the local villagers, while cheap brands from elsewhere meant laborers from across China.”

The looting of Dabuzi was catastrophic: It scattered countless artifacts across the world and triggered nearly two decades of repatriation work by Chinese authorities. But northern China is filled with ancient burial sites, and there was little reason at first to think the tombs themselves were of any special importance.

It was only after the team started digging that they realized the robbers had stumbled onto one of the most important Chinese archaeological discoveries of the past century: the Xichui necropolis, the first royal burial ground of the Qin people.

Although famous for unifying China after the chaos of the Warring States period (475–221 BC), very little is known about the Qin’s early history. Originating in a remote backwater far from China’s ancient heartland, the Central Plains, they appear only rarely in surviving histories from the period.

That left historians and archaeologists to piece together fragmentary evidence from oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. In this context, the discovery of Xichui changed everything, bringing new attention — and new resources — to a millennia-old mystery: Why was it the Qin, and not any of their rivals, that unified China?

Holes in the history books

In 230 BC, a Qin army swept out of the Hangu Pass and into the Central Plains, the heartland of Chinese civilization.

Over the next nine years, the other six of China’s seven remaining Warring States fell, one by one. By 221 BC, only Qin remained. With China unified for the first time in centuries, the Qin king proclaimed a new dynasty — and gave himself the title of Qinshihuang, or the Qin’s “first emperor.”

Qinshihuang’s empire would outlive him by only four years, collapsing in 206 BC before being replaced by the longer-lived Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220). But the title — and the scope of his conquests, which stretched from Liaoning in the northeast to the coast of the Gulf of Tonkin in the south — would largely endure for the next two millennia.

The speed of the Qin’s rise was extraordinary, and the reasons for it have been the subject of intense debate among generations of Chinese scholars.

But due to a lack of textual sources from the Qin itself, the terms of this debate were largely set by later histories — most notably Sima Qian’s monumental “Records of the Grand Historian” and Jia Yi’s celebrated essay “On the Faults of Qin,” both written during the ensuing Han.

These accounts, composed well after the fact, generally attribute the Qin’s success to the “Shang Yang reforms”: a series of institutional and economic policies promoted by the fourth-century BC Legalist philosopher Shang Yang. Together, they are credited with growing the Qin’s population, strengthening its military, and making the Qin the most powerful of the Warring States.

If that narrative seems too tidy — a single set of reforms magically transforming a poor state into the most powerful war machine in Asia — many historians would agree. The Qin’s rise from a marginal tribal polity to the state that unified China took more than eight centuries. By the time of Shang Yang’s reforms, Qin was already a major player in Warring States-era politics.

Nor was Shang Yang the only reformer of the Warring States era. But his reforms took root in a way few others did. Why? What was Qin like before he came on the scene? And how was it, unlike the other states, able to break the stalemate and impose its will across China?

The lack of reliable sources hasn’t stopped modern scholars from trying to reconstruct early Qin history. As early as a century ago, the great historian Wang Guowei attempted to apply his famous “dual evidence method” — corroborating transmitted texts with newly unearthed materials such as oracle bone and bronze inscriptions — to trace how the Qin people gradually expanded eastward.

Yet, with little archaeological evidence to go on, research into Qin’s early and middle periods remained stalled for decades — until the tomb-robbing incident at Dabuzi.

It took nearly a decade to confirm the site as the Qin royal tombs, but with Xichui as a starting point, Chinese archaeologists could finally begin systematically tracing Qin history.

Progress was fast. In 2004, shortly after returning to China from doctoral studies in Japan, Wang — then deputy director of the Gansu Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology — formally launched the “Early Qin Culture Archaeological Survey, Excavation, and Research Project.” In the decades since, archaeologists have made rapid progress: uncovering the earliest known Qin remains, pinpointing the first county ever established by the Qin, and identifying most of the nine capitals founded by the Qin as they pushed eastward from the western frontier into the Central Plains.

And the more Qin relics they uncover, the more archaeologists and historians have come to question the picture painted by Sima Qian and Jia Yi.

“Tigers and wolves”

For most Chinese people, the phrase that comes to mind when speaking of the Qin is “a state of tigers and wolves.”

Sima Qian was the first to use the term in relation to the Qin. In his “Records of the Grand Historian,” the phrase appears twice. The first time, it’s attributed to the great poet Qu Yuan, then serving as a minister to a rival state, who uses it to try to dissuade his king from making an official visit to Qin. Later, Su Qin, a Warring States strategist, invokes the same label to rally the other six states into a last-ditch alliance against the Qin’s overwhelming power.

But how did Qin become such a formidable opponent?

Historical texts provide only a sketchy account. Sima Qian, for instance, describes the Qin’s origins as follows: The distant ancestors of the Qin people were descended from Zhuanxu, grandson of the Yellow Emperor and one of China’s legendary Five Emperors. They had once been a major tribe under the Shang (c. 1600–1046 BC) kings before being relocated to the western frontier after the rise of the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1046–771 BC).

During this period, a chieftain of this tribe, Feizi, was granted the fief of Qin in recognition of his skill in horse breeding. After the Western Zhou fell, Duke Xiang of Qin escorted the Zhou king to the new capital and was enfeoffed as a feudal lord, officially making Qin one of the states of the Eastern Zhou (c. 770–256 BC).

The archaeological record backs up some of these details. To start, early Qin material culture shows clear links to the Shang and Zhou. The layout of Qin ancestral temples, the style of its palace architecture, and the types of bronze ritual vessels used all follow Zhou tradition, while its large burial pits — including dog sacrifices, chariot-and-horse pits, and even human sacrifices — reflect Shang practice.

But archaeologists have found something else: evidence that the Qin people intermingled closely with the various non-Chinese tribes known as the “Western Rong.”

“Rong” was a broad term used by people of the Central Plains to describe various non-Zhou groups, many of which were quite different from each other.

One of the most important of these was the Bronze Age Siwa culture, centered in what is today southern Gansu.

Current archaeological evidence suggests that, after the Qin moved west, they developed a close but complicated relationship with the Siwa and other tribes inhabiting the region, one that gradually evolved from coexistence to conflict and finally to Qin domination.

When the Qin first moved westward, they initially settled in the Liya site in present-day Qingshui County, Gansu. It was at Liya — currently the earliest identified Qin cultural site — that Liang Yun, a professor at Northwest University and a key member of the Early Qin Culture Project, unearthed a paired burial containing the bodies of a man and a woman.

The woman’s grave contained Qin-style pottery, while the man’s contained Siwa-style artifacts — an arrangement that Liang believes points to intermarriage between Qin and Siwa peoples.

“When the Qin first arrived (in Gansu), they had little foundation there and could only survive in regions where indigenous power was relatively weak,” he says. “This burial indicates that relations between the Qin and Siwa populations were relatively harmonious at the time — or at the very least, there was intermarriage.”

But circumstances changed after the Qin expanded further into nearby Lixian. Unlike Qingshui, Lixian was densely populated by Siwa communities and rich in resources such as salt, gold, and copper. Competition over land and mineral wealth between Qin and Siwa led to repeated clashes and eventually resulted in the extermination of the Qin branch living in Lixian, Liang says.

Fortunately for the Qin, another Qin group had remained in Qingshui. Their leader secured military support from the Zhou, then led the Qin back into Lixian, where he avenged their defeat and established a new capital.

From that point onward, Qin gradually subdued the Siwa, either destroying them outright or incorporating them into Qin rule.

Liang argues that this experience — and later, frequent warfare against nomadic peoples looking to expand from the Eurasian steppe — left Qin fundamentally different from the more established states of the Central Plains.

The Qin’s rise was extraordinarily difficult; its territory had to be seized bit by bit from western tribes, and several Qin rulers died in battle. “The Qin were deeply committed to militarism and expansion,” Liang says. “If you compare a state to a person, then the Qin’s interactions with the Western Rong were its childhood experiences — they shaped its ‘cultural genes.’”

In other words, Qin had already developed a strongly militarized culture more than four centuries before Shang Yang’s reforms.

“Many people see Shang Yang’s reforms as the cause of the Qin’s rise,” Liang adds. “In reality, they were the result. Why did (the Qin leaders) embrace Shang Yang? Why were these reforms successful in Qin? Because the conditions were already there. Qin’s political culture was inherently suited to strengthening centralized authority and military power.”

From west to east

The Qin were certainly adept at warfare, but wanting to unify the realm was one thing — actually achieving it was another. So how did Qin pull off the impossible: vanquishing multiple entrenched rivals in a series of devastating campaigns, all in just a decade?

Once again, the answer may lie in the soil of China’s northwest.

Among the major Warring States, the Qin are often portrayed as the most geographically marginalized. Although Qin’s rivals recognized its military strength, the elites of China’s Central Plains regarded it as uncivilized and culturally backward — a belief that persisted even as the Qin expanded inexorably eastward.

But this belief, dutifully recorded and largely accepted as true by later historians, is being overturned by recent archaeological discoveries. What the Central Plains states saw as “uncultured” may in fact have been the fruit of Qin cultural and technological exchanges with Eurasian steppe cultures.

Long before the Han dynasty envoy Zhang Qian opened formal diplomatic contact with Central Asia in the second century BC — generally viewed as the beginning of the Silk Road and China’s integration into Eurasian trade networks — early Chinese states had begun developing commercial and cultural ties with the steppe.

And the Qin stood at a pivotal node on this East-West corridor. What eastern elites considered the periphery may have actually been a central location in an emerging cross-continent exchange of technologies and ideas.

For example, archaeological evidence shows that, while the Central Plains states remained fixated on traditional materials like bronze and jade, the Qin had developed a taste for the gold artifacts popular on the Eurasian steppe.

Likewise, Qin animal motifs tended toward naturalism, in stark contrast to the abstract, stylized animal decoration found on Central Plains ritual vessels of the same era. In the sacrificial pits at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum, archaeologists have found 46 examples of bronze waterfowl — swans, geese, and cranes — each life‑size, posed differently, and strikingly realistic. Even more remarkable is a solid gold camel figurine, so finely wrought that even its toenails are perfectly realized.

The influence of steppe cultures wasn’t limited to art. The Qin’s position also gave them a crucial technological edge.

Take metallurgy, for example. The Qin were early adopters of multiple important metalworking techniques. For centuries, the Central Plains region had favored the “lost-wax casting method” for casting ceremonial and military objects: melting metal, pouring it into a mold, and allowing it to cool and solidify. But gold pieces unearthed from Dabuzi demonstrate Qin mastery of a different process: the repoussé technique, in which gold is heated until soft and repeatedly hammered to stretch it into thin sheets or into the desired shape.

Breakthroughs in one area spawned others. Beyond metallurgy, the Qin built large-scale water conservancy projects such as the Zhengguo Canal and Dujiangyan — still functional today — which dramatically boosted agricultural yields. They invented the two-shaft chariot and introduced the “exotic livestock” of the northwest — donkeys and mules — as pack animals, improving carrying capacity and efficiency. Their craftspeople also invented new materials, including “Chinese purple,” a synthetic pigment that requires precise control of firing temperature and proportions of raw material to produce.

According to research by Wang Zijin of Northwest University, by the late Warring States era, Qin held a leading position over the other six states in multiple technological fields, including water conservation, transportation, and machinery.

They also had a highly advanced state system that enabled the deployment of these technologies at scale.

Archaeologists have found evidence of an early quality-control process known as wu le qi ming, in which artisans were required to carve their names on the objects they produced so their supervisors could trace each item back to its creator.

Perhaps the best-known example is the “Lü Buwei Halberd,” forged in the second half of the first millennium BC. Its inscription identifies four individuals involved in the weapon’s manufacture: the highest supervising official, the workshop master, the workshop assistant, and the individual craftsman who produced it, suggesting that Qin weapons production operated under a highly structured chain of accountability.

Excavations at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site have likewise shown that Qin bronze trigger mechanisms were produced to tight specifications. Components made by the same workshop group were interchangeable, while different types of crossbows were distributed systematically across different sections of the battle formation. This suggests that Qin had achieved standardized, interchangeable, large-scale weapons production — a factor now regarded as a key military advantage in Qin’s wars of unification.

“In my view, Qin’s greatest technological advantage over the six states was not any single invention, but the establishment of a large-scale standardized production system,” says Qian Wei, Dean of the Institute for Cultural Heritage and History of Science & Technology at the University of Science and Technology Beijing. “That organizational innovation was the decisive factor behind Qin’s victory.”

Systemic change

The Qin’s moment of glory lasted less than a quarter-century: a decade to conquer the six Warring States, then 15 years for it to all fall apart.

Yet the Qin’s legacy has endured — its achievements and failings remembered, debated, and ceaselessly revisited.

That’s not just because it was the first empire to unify much of what is today China, or because of its standardization of writing, currency, and weights and measures. Much of its importance stems from its political system, which centralized imperial authority through a commandery-county administrative structure — a governing logic that would shape China for more than two millennia.

Unlike the nobility-based system of the earlier Zhou dynasty, which was based on blood ties, the commandery‑county system was centrally administered. Officials at all levels were directly appointed, evaluated, and transferred by the central government. That allowed central power to reach down through the bureaucratic apparatus, from prefecture to county to township to village, and from there to every household in China.

The question of how this system evolved has long puzzled scholars, with some arguing it wasn’t an indigenous invention at all, but another technology the Qin borrowed from the Western regions — specifically the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

This seemingly far-fetched idea has a certain logic. If the Qin interacted extensively with the Western Rong and other steppe nomads during its rise, then it may also have encountered — directly or indirectly — civilizations further west.

The late Sinologist Jao Tsung-I was one of the first to suggest there may have been some connection between Qin and the Achaemenids. As evidence, he pointed to a linguistic coincidence. After unifying China, Qin referred to commoners as qianshou (“black-headed people”), a phrase previously unseen in Chinese sources. In the Cyrus Cylinder, created in the 6th century BC in honor of the Persian conquest of Babylon, Persian subjects are likewise referred to as “black-headed people.”

Does that mean the Qin had been influenced by Persian norms? Jao chose his words carefully, merely expressing “some suspicion” of a link between the two, without reaching a firm conclusion.

Another scholar, the late Duan Qingbo — former director of the excavation team at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum — was bolder. He repeatedly proposed that the political civilization of the Persian Empire may have influenced the Qin’s imperial institutions. In his view, Qin policies such as the commandery-county system, codified laws, imperial roads and relay stations, the standardization of weights and measures, script unification, the use of grandiose imperial titles, and the implementation of large-scale construction projects all bore striking similarities to the policies of the Persian king Darius I (c. 550–486 BC).

But Duan’s views have gained little support from other scholars.

According to Wang, the founder of the Early Qin Culture Project, similarities between the two empires merely reflect the comparable challenges they faced. Both Qinshihuang and Darius I ruled vast territories populated by diverse peoples and cultures. Given the circumstances, centralization was a natural choice, as were standardization, road construction, legal codes, and other forms of administrative integration.

“Look at the roads, for example,” Wang says. “The Roman Empire also built extensive road systems. Does that mean Rome copied Persia?”

Wang adds that many core features of Qin political culture took shape in the state’s early developmental stages. Take its approach to ethnic conflict: Through centuries of exchange and warfare with the Western Rong, the Qin developed a sophisticated approach to managing conquered populations. What began as military conquest and forced relocation gradually expanded to include conciliation, trade, and reward systems. Administratively, the Qin governed tribes through specialized structures, including subordinate states and frontier districts known as dao.

“This approach was later used extensively during Qin’s unification of China,” Wang notes.

Northwest University’s Liang acknowledges that the Qin likely did have some exchanges with Central and Western Asia. At Yuandingshan cemetery in Lixian, for example, archaeologists unearthed a bronze model chariot with wheels that suggest it was Central or Western Asian in origin.

“But that’s it,” Liang says. “Aside from a few luxury items, there is no evidence that the Qin Empire was influenced by Persia.”

More evidence can be found in the Qin’s burial customs. Funerary rituals often reflect core aspects of a people’s identity. “The state religion of Persia was Zoroastrianism, which holds that burying corpses pollutes the earth,” Liang says. “That is why Persian royal tombs are cut into rock. In stark contrast, Qin tombs were dug deep into the earth — the deeper, the better. The two worldviews are polar opposites.”

As for the commandery-county system, Liang has no doubt it was a Qin invention. In fact, he led the archaeological team that identified the first-ever county established by the Qin. “That was more than 2,700 years ago,” he notes. “More than a century before Darius I.”

Liang is more interested in other questions, such as where the Qin originally lived and how they served the Shang. And while scholars now have a relatively clear picture of the Qin’s repeated capital relocations during its eastward expansion, the locations of one or two capitals remain debated.

These questions have been unresolved for centuries, but new archaeological discoveries are finally putting them within reach.

“Don’t be impatient,” Liang says. “Remember, the Early Qin Culture project has only been going on for a little over two decades — that is far too short by archaeological standards. The Qin people walked a path of more than 800 years.”

World.title: China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.content:
After decades spent working, raising families, and putting personal ambitions on hold, two Chinese women in their 50s returned to school thousands of kilometers from home.

In Athens, 58-year-old Ella Wang found a new sense of purpose at university, studying Greek archaeology, history, and literature. While in New Zealand, 54-year-old Zhao found herself overwhelmed by an English program that was far beyond her level.

Both studied alongside classmates young enough to be their children, but their experiences could hardly have been more different. Yet both are part of a growing number of Chinese retirees looking overseas for education.

Having spent their working lives during China’s reform era, many now have greater financial security, more control over their time, and familiarity with overseas education after sending their own children abroad.

China already has about 105,000 universities for older adults, but overseas programs that combine learning with international travel have a particular appeal for retirees seeking cultural experiences beyond the classroom. EF Education First, one of the world’s largest international education providers, estimates that China’s broader overseas education market for older adults will reach 1.2 trillion yuan ($167 billion) by 2030.

Yet for those entering education systems designed around younger students, the challenge is finding a classroom that fits.

Lesson learned

Zhao discovered that within days of arriving in New Zealand.

She had enrolled in what she believed was a beginner English program. EF had assessed her at A1, the lowest level, and shown her an A1 textbook before she left China. But when lessons began, every available course was beyond her level, and teachers spoke only English.

“It was completely incomprehensible,” Zhao told Sixth Tone.

After one lesson, she returned to the same room for the next class, only to find it empty. The class had moved, but she had not understood the instructions. On another occasion, a teacher called on her, and she did not understand the question.

Zhao had paid about 160,000 yuan for tuition and an eight-month homestay. After retiring from Shanghai’s flower industry, she hoped the program would teach her enough English to travel while she was still healthy. EF’s promotional videos had shown students studying, immersing themselves in local culture, and traveling around New Zealand.

She soon considered quitting. The experience, she felt, had been “overly romanticized” by overseas education providers. “I completely broke down and burst into tears,” Zhao said. “I couldn’t tell my family how miserable it was. I only said I missed them.”

Zhang, 56, had enrolled in a six-week program at the same school and found the pace equally punishing. “It was like I hadn’t even learned to stand, and they were already asking me to run,” she said.

Both had hoped to learn practical English: how to read a menu, take a bus, ask for directions, and order food. Instead, their classes focused on subjects such as history, biology, and mathematics. Another Chinese retiree in the same course quit after three days.

Zhang began to question what she was struggling for. “Do I really need to learn history, biology, and math at this age?”

That mismatch has led some Chinese education providers to design programs specifically for retirees. Yao Xiaoqiong, head of private education provider New Oriental’s Global Campus Center, told Sixth Tone that one- to three-year courses remain difficult for many older students. Instead, the company offers two- to four-week overseas programs, including art courses in the UK and culinary courses in France.

The programs require no prior language skills and include 10 hours of preparation before departure, as well as interpreters and coordinators during the trip. Yao said older clients generally seek cultural immersion and hands-on learning rather than degrees.

Zhang encountered some of that outside the classroom. When she got lost or struggled to understand bus announcements, strangers stepped in to help.

But keeping up with the course consumed her. Zhang studied until 11 p.m. and woke at 4 a.m. to prepare. In class, she relied on a translation app but still “couldn’t keep pace with everyone else.” Younger students often avoided partnering with her for group work.

By the end of the program, she was physically and mentally exhausted. She still hoped to return to New Zealand one day as a tourist. “But this time, I just don’t have the mood to travel,” she said.

Zhang said the program did not match how it was promoted, and planned to file a complaint with EF. The company did not respond to Sixth Tone’s requests for comment.

Zhao’s longer course gave her more time to adjust. Gradually, she learned to manage the classes, grew more confident, found time to hike, and made local friends through a church.

“Now I’ve made it through,” Zhao said. “I’m mentally much stronger.”

Second chance

At the University of Athens, 58-year-old Wang found her way back to an undergraduate thesis she had never considered complete.

Titled “God, Humanity, and Their Destiny,” the thesis at the time fell short of the university’s highest assessment. At her defense, a professor told her she would need “at least another 30 years of life experience” before she could fully develop its argument.

In 2023, while staying at her family’s holiday home in Athens, Wang came across an English-taught undergraduate program in Greek archaeology, history, and literature. More than 30 years had passed since her professor’s remark. “If I finish the archaeology and literature courses here,” she recalled thinking, “maybe I can write the essay better.”

Born in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Wang had worked as a Chinese teacher, an advertising executive, and later in publishing before retiring. With one child in college and the other already working, she was free to spend part of the year in Athens.

Most of her classmates were born around 2006. “The last students I taught were born in 1983 and 1984,” she said. “Now, their children are my classmates.”

Keeping up with them meant learning more than history. Wang typed with two index fingers and struggled to navigate the university’s online systems.

During her first semester, Wang’s daughter arranged to work remotely from Athens, helping her practice English and navigate campus life. Reading textbooks on a screen made Wang “dizzy,” so she ordered printed copies and asked her husband to bring them to Greece.

The effort showed. While many students skipped lectures, Wang rarely missed one. She sat in the front row, stayed after class to ask questions even when she could not fully follow the answers, and spent weekends catching up on coursework. Before long, she was using AI to review her exams and identify mistakes.

She even won over classmates by showing them photos of her cats. “No one can resist kittens,” she said. She also discovered that gray hair was no obstacle to using her student ID for a 10% discount at KFC.

Studying the Peloponnesian War changed how Wang thought about conflict. She began to see the same struggle playing out beyond ancient Greece. “One side wants to preserve the existing order, while the other wants to change it,” she said. “That’s how many conflicts in the world work.”

She came to see traditional expectations around family and marriage as part of that same order. She wanted to break away from them, while her husband, who benefited from the arrangement, was more comfortable preserving it.

“My life used to be a multiple-choice question with only one correct answer,” Wang said. “Work, love, marriage. There was always something I was supposed to do at each stage, and I was carried along by society. People were always defining me: whose daughter I was, whose student I was, whose wife I was, whose mother I was.”

“Now my definition comes from myself,” she said. “I no longer care about those labels. I even have a new name: Ella. I’m Ella.”

Wang has thought about becoming a museum guide or writing a memoir after graduation. But she said those plans matter less than what she has already discovered. “The biggest thing I’ve gained over the past two years is realizing that learning itself is the goal, not a means to something else. I just enjoy learning.”

Sometimes, Wang still thinks of her hometown’s long winters in Xinjiang. As the eldest of four daughters, she helped her parents prepare vegetables for the cold months ahead. Surrounded by piles of produce, she longed to play with other children but could not leave.

“My body was confined by labor, but my thoughts were free. They had already traveled thousands of miles around the world,” she said.

Decades later, Wang feels she has finally caught up with those childhood dreams.

“Now I am standing in the open field of life,” Wang said. “I am lonely, but I am free. It is the solitude of freedom.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Ella Wang in Athens. Courtesy of Wang)

World.title: China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018814/China-Developed ALS Therapy Shows Early Trial Promise
World.content:
Chinese researchers have reported encouraging early results for a domestically developed experimental therapy targeting a genetic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In a six-patient trial published this month in Nature Medicine, the drug was generally well tolerated and reduced key disease-related biomarkers.

Called RAG-17, the therapy uses small interfering RNA, or siRNA, to suppress SOD1, a gene whose mutations can cause ALS. By reducing production of the harmful protein associated with the mutation, the drug is designed to target a biological driver of the disease.

ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that destroys the nerve cells controlling voluntary movement, gradually impairing a patient’s ability to move, speak, swallow, and breathe. The disease gained wider public attention through campaigns such as the Ice Bucket Challenge, but it remains incurable.

China has an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 people living with ALS, with about 23,000 new cases diagnosed each year. Around 2% of patients carry SOD1 mutations, the only genetic form of ALS with an approved targeted treatment. Tofersen, the first approved therapy targeting SOD1-related ALS, received U.S. approval in April 2023 and was approved in China in September 2024.

RAG-17 was jointly developed by a team led by Wang Yilong at Beijing Tiantan Hospital and researchers led by Li Longcheng at biotech company Ractigen Therapeutics.

In the trial, six patients with SOD1-related ALS received repeated injections of the drug into the fluid surrounding the spinal cord over several months. Researchers reported no serious adverse events. Two participants experienced mild muscle tremors that later resolved.

The treatment produced substantial reductions in two disease-related biomarkers. SOD1 protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid fell by more than half, while plasma levels of neurofilament light chain, a marker of nerve-cell damage, also declined.

The changes indicate that RAG-17 reached its intended target.

In preclinical studies, RAG-17 delayed disease progression, preserved motor function, and extended survival in rodent models of SOD1-related ALS. Tests in macaques also found sustained suppression of the SOD1 gene in the central nervous system.

The Chinese research team said a larger clinical trial of RAG-17 is now underway.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Shijue Focus/VCG)

World.title: Why Sara opposes changing sequence of presenting evidence in her trial
World.content:
'An alteration of an established order of presentation of evidence at this stage will not only violate the respondent's constitutional rights but also weaken the integrity of the proceedings,' the defense lawyers argue

Vice President Sara Duterte has made it clear — she is opposed to changing the sequence of the evidence in her impeachment trial.

She filed a formal opposition before the impeachment court on Tuesday, July 28.

The next day, on July 29, the Senate impeachment court ruled that the status quo will be preserved and the sequence will remain the same. The prosecution will have to finish presenting its evidence on the four articles of impeachment, after which the defense will have its turn to present its own evidence.

Apparently, Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero asked the parties if they are open to changing the current order of the presentation. Escudero, however, said that if one of the parties disagrees, then the status quo remains.

“We shall finish with the evidence-in-chief of the prosecution for all the articles of impeachment that they will not withdraw…. Thereafter, we will hear the evidence-in-chief of the respondent for all the articles that remain or all the articles that evidence will be presented by the prosecution,” Escudero ruled on Wednesday.

But what are Duterte’s reasons for opposing this? Is sequence really a big deal?

Constitutional violation?

In sum, Duterte raised four main arguments:

It violates concepts of fair play and due process

It goes against what was agreed upon during the pre-trial conference

It defies the Senate impeachment court’s pre-trial order

It shifts the burden of proving the accusations from the prosecution to the respondent

The defense cited Article III, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution: “No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws.”

According to Duterte’s lawyers, this constitutional guarantee ensures that a respondent will be given a fair and reasonable opportunity to know the allegations against him/her. This also ensures that she will be informed about the alleged evidence against her and she will be able to prepare a comprehensive defense strategy.

“Requiring the respondent to present evidence per Article before the Prosecution has fully presented its case-in-chief for all Articles undermines this constitutional guarantee and will deprive her of the opportunity to be fully informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against her and the evidentiary basis supporting them, if any,” said the defense’s reply.

“Thus, to alter the established order of trial at this juncture will constitute an arbitrary departure from the respondent’s right to due process, protection against capricious proceedings, and the tenets of fair play,” it added.

The defense lawyers also argued that the burden of proof lies with the prosecution. They said that if the prosecution fails to discharge this burden, “the accused need not even answer any of the charges and must be acquitted.”

For the prosecution, its proposed sequence “allows [Duterte] an immediate opportunity to address the evidence presented on a particular article before the proceedings move to the next, while enabling the impeachment court to receive and evaluate all evidence relating to each charge in a more comprehensive and self-contained manner.”

Should stick to pre-trial order

The Duterte camp argued that the pre-trial order issued by the impeachment court should govern the impeachment proceedings.

“Considering that the purpose of pre-trial is to take the trial of the case out of the realm of surprise and maneuvering, any deviation from this agreed upon sequence will undermine the binding force of the Pre- Trial Order and render the entire pre-trial proceeding meaningless. Modifying a pre-trial order during trial indubitably results in manifest injustice,” said the defense team.

“An alteration of an established order of presentation of evidence at this stage will not only violate the respondent’s constitutional rights but also weaken the integrity of the proceedings,” it added.

During the impeachment trial of former chief justice Renato Corona, the defense presented their evidence only after the prosecution rested its case.

In criminal proceedings, the defense also presents its evidence only after the prosecution’s presentation.

Meanwhile, defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa refuted insinuations that the defense opposed the change in sequence because they have no witnesses.

“That’s not true,” said Poa. – Rappler.com

World.title: Even the Senate compound isn’t safe from thieves
World.content:
INSPECTION. A police officer holding an orange umbrella bearing Mark Villar’s name inspects the area where the theft happened on July 29, 2026.

A flat screen television, printers, and other office supplies were stolen inside the Senate compound

It seems even the Senate compound is not safe from thieves.

Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Alfred Corpus on Wednesday, July 29, said a flat-screen television, two printers, tables, and other office supplies were stolen from inside the Senate compound.

The stolen items don’t belong to the Senate.

They are owned by the House of Representatives’ CongressTV. These items were kept inside the network’s tent set up at the Senate compound’s parking lot.

CongressTV has put up a makeshift office inside the Senate compound to cover the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

CongressTV is a digital broadcast channel, launched by the House of Representatives, in partnership with state-run People’s Television Network in January 2024. In October 2024, it was transferred to the Intercontinental Broadcasting Corporation or IBC.

Play Video

Corpus, a retired police major general, said they are still confirming the exact time of the incident, but estimated that it happened in the early hours of Wednesday, amid heavy rain.

Corpus said there are CCTV cameras in the area where CongressTV was stationed, but that the tent obstructed the view of the cameras. It’s hard to see where the suspects may have entered.

The Pasay City Police are already investigating the incident and have identified persons of interest, Corpus said. On Wednesday afternoon, a police officer holding an orange umbrella bearing Mark Villar’s name was seen inspecting the area.

Corpus said they are considering deploying additional security personnel and installing more CCTVs in the compound.

The incident happened days after a suspected improvised explosive device was found about 150 meters from the Senate gate on Monday, July 27, before the opening of the second regular session of the 20th Congress. The Senate session opened at 10 am that day. On the same day, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. also delivered his fifth State of the Nation Address.

A few weeks before this, a shooting incident happened inside the chamber.

For a country where billions in public funds meant for flood control projects have allegedly been plundered, is it really surprising that even the Senate compound is not spared from theft? – Rappler.com

World.title: Glen Hansard, Oscar-winning Irish musician, dies in motorcycle crash
World.content:
Hansard had released a number of albums under his own name and as a part of duo The Swell Season with fellow Oscar winner and 'Once' co-star Marketa Irglova

DUBLIN, Ireland – Irish musician Glen Hansard, who won a Best Original Song Oscar in 2008 for the indie film Once and was lead singer for rock group The Frames, died in a motorcycle crash at the age of 56 early on Wednesday, July 28, his management company said.

Fans paid tribute online and Prime Minister Micheal Martin said he was deeply saddened to hear of the death of “a talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland’s cultural landscape over many years.”

The singer-songwriter began busking on the streets of his native Dublin as a teen before forming the popular Irish band The Frames in 1990.

He released a number of albums under his own name and as part of duo The Swell Season with fellow Oscar winner and Once co-star Marketa Irglova.

The pair’s performances in the low-budget movie shot on handheld camcorders where a street musician falls in love with a young Czech immigrant, and their Oscar-winning duet “Falling Slowly,” brought Hansard’s music to a wider audience.

The film, which featured a number of other songs composed and performed by Hansard and Irglova, was turned into a hit Broadway musical version that won eight Tony Awards in 2012.

Accepting his Oscar from presenter John Travolta, a stunned Hansard said: “What are we doing here? This is mad.”

His only acting experience prior to Once was as a band member in Alan Parker’s 1991 hit The Commitments.

“With broken hearts we announce the passing of Glen Hansard who passed away, in the early hours of this morning, following a road-traffic accident in Dublin,” ATC Management said in a statement that thanked emergency services.

Irish police said a man in his 50s had died after a single-vehicle motorcycle collision in the west of Dublin. Emergency services were alerted shortly before 4:30 am and the man was pronounced dead a short time after being treated at the scene. – Rappler.com

World.title: Did Senator-judge Pia Cayetano just amplify a misleading video of Chel Diokno?
World.content:
Senator-judge Pia Cayetano, who loves to read and lecture, should perhaps revisit the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability for lawyers

Did Senator-judge Pia Cayetano just help spread disinformation?

For someone who has repeatedly reminded everyone how much homework she does before every impeachment hearing, Cayetano’s Facebook post is raising eyebrows.

Cayetano — a lawyer and 1991 graduate of the University of the Philippines College of Law who ranked seventh in her class — shared a 57-second spliced video of House prosecutor Chel Diokno last Friday, July 24.

The clip shows Diokno answering Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s questions about issuing subpoenas for Vice President Sara Duterte’s financial records. But it cuts out the rest of Diokno’s explanation, leaving viewers with the impression that the prosecution admitted it was accusing Duterte without evidence.

The video also carried the overlay text: “Nagbabakasakali lang? Walang mga ebidensiya pero nag-aakusa na!” (Just taking a shot in the dark? No evidence, yet already making accusations!)

House prosecution spokesperson Jay Tolosa called the post “concerning and alarming” during a press briefing on Wednesday, July 29.

He warned that it could reinforce the perception that members of the impeachment court — who are supposed to remain impartial — have already formed an opinion on the case.

On Wednesday, Tindig Pilipinas, a coalition of civil society groups, also wrote the Senate committee on ethics and privileges, asking it to investigate Cayetano and the video she shared.

What Diokno actually said

The full statement as recorded in the Senate’s journal records last July 20 shows Diokno saying: “And iyong tinutukoy po ninyong fishing expedition, iyon ay maaaring sabihin nating nangyari only if the party requesting the evidence or documents ay nagbabakasakali lang — baka may makuha tayo dito. In our case, I have to disagree that there was any sort of fishing expedition because based on what the committee on justice and later the plenary of the House found was sufficient, there was enough cause to proceed with the case.”

(What you are referring to as a “fishing expedition” could be said to have occurred only if the party requesting the evidence or documents was merely taking a shot in the dark — hoping they might find something there.)

The same statement can be heard in the Senate’s livestream of the impeachment trial proceedings.

It would be hard for the lady senator to miss this exchange between her brother and Diokno because she was present during the said hearing. Could she be hard of hearing or guilty of selective hearing?

In a Facebook post, Diokno also immediately provided the full context of his remarks.

Diokno explained that a “fishing expedition” would apply only if investigators were merely hoping to stumble upon evidence.

“Hindi tayo nagbabakasakali lang,” he said, adding that the prosecution relied on Anti-Money Laundering Council records that allegedly showed billions of pesos passing through the accounts of Duterte and her husband. (We are not merely taking a shot in the dark.)

According to Diokno, the subpoena was sought so both the prosecution and the defense could examine the bank records during the trial. He noted that the House could not have legally obtained those records before the impeachment proceedings because doing so without a court order would have violated Duterte’s rights and due process.

Where did the spliced video clip come from?

The video shared by Cayetano bears a watermark resembling “Lapu-Lapu.”

A reverse image search traced the same logo to the Facebook page Bisaya na Pud, created in February 2016. The page has consistently published pro-Duterte content, including AI-generated videos.

The page previously uploaded a similarly edited clip, although the post has since been deleted.

Rappler sought Cayetano’s comment, but she has yet to respond as of writing. This story will be updated once she replies.

Throughout the impeachment trial, Cayetano has repeatedly emphasized the hours she spends reading hundreds of pages of documents before every hearing.

Yet she apparently failed to verify a video lasting less than a minute before sharing it with her more than 1.1 million Facebook followers.

The video has since amassed 4.4 million views and has been reposted by more than 17,000 Facebook users. Dozens of pro-Duterte accounts have also amplified it.

At the start of the impeachment trial, every senator-judge took an oath to remain impartial.

Under Section 38 of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, “a lawyer shall not knowingly or maliciously post, share, upload or otherwise disseminate false or unverified statements, claims, or commit any other act of disinformation.”

Given how often Cayetano reminds everyone about the importance of reading, perhaps it’s worth revisiting the oath she herself took and what the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability for lawyers says. – Rappler.com

World.title: Meralco chair Pangilinan: Power industry ‘may not survive’ if asked to absorb system loss
World.content:
The warning comes from the chairman of Meralco — the distribution giant that posted a record P50.6 billion in core profit in 2025 — who says forcing the power industry to absorb system loss costs could run into tens of billions of pesos

MANILA, Philippines – Manila Electric Company (Meralco) chairman Manny V. Pangilinan warned that the Philippine power industry “may not survive” if President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s order to remove system loss charges from consumers’ electricity bills is carried out in full.

Asked whether he would bow to the President’s order, Pangilinan did not exactly say yes. He said he wanted to talk to Marcos first.

“I think we should talk. We’re sympathetic. He’s under pressure too,” Pangilinan told reporters on Wednesday, July 29, referring to the spike in energy costs following the Iran war.

Play Video

Pangilinan argued that Meralco’s distribution rate had been unchanged since July 2015, and that recent increases in electricity bills came from other parts of the power supply chain.

“The increase in the bill hasn’t come from us. Others have moved up,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.

But Marcos’ directive could put Meralco and other utilities on the hook for system losses that consumers currently shoulder. And, according to Pangilinan, that could put them out of business. (READ: Meralco: Some system loss unavoidable, urges careful EPIRA reform)

“If we’re not allowed to charge, we have to absorb the losses coming from the system loss,” Pangilinan said.

“It’s a big bill for the industry,” he added, estimating that the cost could reach “tens of billions of pesos. We may not survive.”

The losses ‘will not disappear’

System loss is the difference between the electricity entering a power network and the amount eventually metered and billed to customers.

Some of it is technical and unavoidable: electricity encounters resistance as it travels through wires and transformers, causing part of the energy to be converted into heat.

But system loss also includes nontechnical losses such as electricity theft, illegal connections, and metering problems. The Department of Energy has said most nontechnical losses may be attributed to pilferage, although the breakdown varies across distribution utilities and electric cooperatives.

At present, consumers shoulder system losses within limits set by the Energy Regulatory Commission. Meralco estimates that system loss can account for about 5% of your monthly bill.

But in Marcos’ recent State of the Nation Address, the President said he wants consumers to stop paying the entire charge, including both technical and nontechnical losses and the value-added tax imposed on them.

“The whole system loss is what was the directive of the President na i-remove,” Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said a day later, confirming the order. “Hindi partial, hindi ‘yung nontechnical lang, kun’di ‘yung buo po (Not just partially, not just the nontechnical, but the whole thing), technical and nontechnical.”

Asked what his general take was on Marcos’ push to lower electricity rates, Pangilinan said Meralco was “one with the President.”

“But first, we have to address [what] are the causes of the sudden rise in electricity. But—” he said, before pausing for several seconds, “I’d better stop there.”

Later, the Meralco chairman would clarify that the problem lies partly in the law of physics.

“The system losses are still there. It’s not going to disappear. So, who’s going to pay for that?” Pangilinan said.

This will be the headache that the Congress and regulators will have to address: who among the generators, the transmission operator, the distribution utilities, or even the taxpayers will absorb the cost?

Meralco clashes with NGCP

Pangilinan also bristled at the suggestion that the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) does not have transmission losses. Any electricity delivered through wires will experience some energy loss, he argued.

“Meron sila, it’s embedded in their generation. Hindi totoo na wala silang (It’s not true that they don’t have) transmission [cost],” he said, punctuating his rebuttal with a curse.

This was in reaction to a statement by the NGCP that the grid operator doesn’t directly bill Meralco for transmission technical system losses.

“NGCP does not charge or bill our customers, for example distribution utilities like Meralco, for system loss,” an NGCP representative told Rappler.

“We only charge for the delivery of power and for ancillary services, which is a pass-through charge and remitted entirely to ancillary service suppliers,” the representative added.

Meralco is not struggling today

Whatever the future impact of the reform, Meralco is hardly on life support right now.

The company’s gross revenue rose 16% to P283.7 billion in the first half of 2026, while reported income climbed 11% to P26.3 billion. Consolidated core net income reached P26.5 billion, up 3.8% from a year earlier.

The revenue figure does need a bit of context: a large portion reflects generation, transmission, and other charges that Meralco collects from customers and passes on to power suppliers and the grid operator, rather than income the company keeps. Meralco’s regulated distribution business accounts for only part of its total revenue, while its profits also come from power generation and other businesses.

The Energy Regulatory Commission is also set to decide soon, by August or September, on a possible rate reset that could raise Meralco’s distribution charge.

Still, coming from a group that earned a record P50.6 billion in core profit in 2025, Pangilinan’s warning is likely less of an immediate forecast of corporate collapse and more like an aggressive opening position in negotiations. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Fox Silica’? Presidential aspirant Sara Duterte has no clue what Pax Silica is
World.content:
Asked if she knows anything about Pax Silica, Vice President Sara Duterte says, 'wala' and that she 'cannot comment'

The candidate to beat for 2028, Vice President Sara Duterte, has no idea what the United States-led Pax Silica initiative is and has no comment on it — for the time being.

The veep was at The Hague, in the Netherlands, on Tuesday, July 28, to visit her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and entertained questions from supporters and vloggers outside of the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) detention center.

There, she was asked, “Do you know anything about [Pax Silica]?”

Her response was a brief moment of confusion over the wording of it and a quick “Wala. Ako? (Nope. Me?) I cannot comment on that.”

Perhaps, it was the frequent non-essential trips abroad that have kept her too busy to know about an issue that has put the entire country on edge for months over sovereignty and artificial intelligence (AI), but one can only assume what is going on in the mind of the presidential aspirant.

Pax this, Pax that

In December 2025, the US formed the Pax Silica coalition to compete against China’s rise in the tech manufacturing sector. The Philippines joined on April 17, becoming the thirteenth country to join the coalition.

At the core of the country’s participation is the hosting of an AI industrial hub on a 1,618-hectare property in New Clark City, Tarlac. Both the Philippines and the US are still planning to identify the appropriate setup for the development of the hub, but intend to go about it with a “joint governance” approach, according to the US embassy.

Still, civil society organizations and concerned groups have raised concerns over the possible negative impact of the AI hub that include, but are not limited to, water insecurity due to high water demand for cooling systems, probable displacement of indigenous peoples and farming villages, and high energy consumption in affected areas.

Groups like the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan have called for the abolition of the country’s participation in the Pax Silica initiative, describing the program as “war production disguised as development.”

Meanwhile, Akbayan Partylist Representatives Perci Cendaña, Chel Diokno, and Dadah Kiram Ismula have filed a House resolution to urge the lower chamber to conduct a probe into the Pax Silica initiative.

Even Energy Secretary Sharon Garin expressed concern over the planned AI industrial hub, telling Rappler in an exclusive interview that the project cannot simply plug its full demand into the Luzon grid without exposing households and businesses to serious risk.

Two sides of the AI coin

While the Vice President made her unfamiliarity over the issue clear, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself was no better at addressing the criticisms of Pax Silica.

In his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, Marcos merely pitched the potential of the Pax Silica initiative to bring the country closer to the global AI stage.

“The Pax Silica Industrial Hub will create an ecosystem that will have AI at its core. It will bring quality jobs to our people, accelerate our industrial competitiveness, and revitalize our economy,” he said.

As of this writing, the Vice President has not made any further comment on the planned AI industrial hub or its effect on the Philippine economy. Nor has she given any signs of a response to the memes made after her viral “no comment” video.

If the veep is serious about taking over Marcos Jr.’s job in 2028, and if there are any odds that her ongoing impeachment trial would sway in her favor, then at the very least, she ought to perhaps read up on the Pax while she’s off to her next flight abroad. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Energy Modernization: Balancing Affordable Power and Long-Term Reliability
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is undertaking one of its largest energy infrastructure upgrades to address a key challenge: maintaining affordable electricity while ensuring a reliable supply for a growing economy. Through the National Project on Modernization of the Energy and Utilities Sectors, the country plans to expand generation capacity, upgrade aging networks and digitalize energy management.



The challenge of affordable electricity

Kazakhstan remains among the countries with relatively affordable electricity prices, with an average household tariff of US$0.056 per kilowatt-hour. However, low tariffs can limit resources for infrastructure renewal, creating a trade-off between maintaining consumer affordability and attracting the investment needed for a reliable energy system, according to analysts at the EconomyKZ.org Telegram channel.

Kazakhstan’s electricity prices are significantly lower than in many developed economies. Average household tariffs stand at US$0.406 per kilowatt-hour in Germany, US$0.447 in Ireland and US$0.466 in Bermuda. However, higher prices in these markets often reflect additional costs related to grid modernization, environmental policies and energy transition measures. The comparison highlights a broader challenge for Kazakhstan: ensuring affordable electricity while investing in new generation capacity and upgrading aging infrastructure.

Expanding capacity and securing supply

The modernization program aims to introduce 7.3 gigawatts (GW) of new and upgraded generating capacity by 2029, with total investment of 6.2 trillion tenge (US$13 billion). Of this amount, 6,484 megawatts (MW) will come from new facilities, while 825 megawatts (MW) will replace outdated capacity.

Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said the program will allow Kazakhstan to fully meet domestic electricity demand starting in early 2027 and achieve a surplus of 1.3 billion kilowatt-hours by the end of the same year.

The planned additions include five gas turbine units at the Zhambyl State District Power Plant with a combined capacity of 210 megawatts (MW) and a combined-cycle facility at the Mangystau Nuclear Power Plant with a capacity of 160 megawatts (MW). A further 4 gigawatts (GW) of capacity is planned for 2028-2029, creating a stable reserve and expanding export potential.

Upgrading networks and improving resilience

The modernization effort also focuses on reducing infrastructure risks. By 2029, Kazakhstan plans to reconstruct 77,500 kilometers of electricity networks and 1,600 kilometers of heating networks. The upgrades are expected to reduce average wear levels of electricity networks from 74% to 45% and heating networks from 52% to 42%, improving reliability and reducing losses.

Several projects have already been completed, including the modernization of the Tekeli energy complex and the launch of a 240 megawatts (MW) combined-cycle power plant in the Kyzylorda Region.

Digitalizing the energy system

Digital transformation is another part of the reform. The Ministry of Energy is developing the EnergyTech platform to integrate data from energy facilities, improve monitoring and increase operational efficiency.

The introduction of smart meters, automated management systems and a cybersecurity center covering more than 200 energy facilities is intended to improve transparency, reduce technical losses and strengthen system security.

Looking ahead

Kazakhstan’s energy modernization reflects a broader challenge faced by many countries: ensuring affordable energy while financing the infrastructure required for long-term reliability.

The success of the program will depend on the timely completion of new-generation projects, the modernization of networks and the ability to improve efficiency without creating excessive pressure on consumers. If implemented as planned, the reforms could strengthen Kazakhstan’s energy security, support industrial growth and increase its role as a regional energy supplier.

World.title: How Kazakhstan Plans to Double Infrastructure Repairs and Improve Energy Reliability
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to significantly expand repairs of its aging energy and utilities infrastructure under a 13 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) national modernization program, with the government aiming to double the pace of network upgrades while increasing the use of domestic manufacturers, officials said at a July 28 government meeting.

Launched at the end of 2024, the National Project on the Modernization of the Energy and Utilities Sectors is designed to reduce the deterioration of engineering infrastructure, improve the reliability of energy supply and public utilities, and strengthen long-term investment in the sector.

Investment and repairs

Deputy Minister of National Economy Assan Darbayev said the project’s institutional framework was completed in 2025 through legislative amendments and the launch of a digital platform overseeing implementation. The project now covers 247 regulated utility companies.

Between 2025 and 2029, Kazakhstan plans to invest 13 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) in the initiative, allocating 6.8 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) to utilities infrastructure and 6.2 trillion tenge (US$13 billion) to the energy sector, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The investment is expected to finance the repair and modernization of 84,000 kilometers of engineering networks, add 7,309 megawatts of generating capacity, and build or modernize 27 power generation facilities. By 2029, the government aims to reduce the nationwide average infrastructure wear rate to 40% and cut accident rates by 25%.

Darbayev said financing for the housing and utilities sector has doubled in 2026 compared with the previous year. The government has also secured 625 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) in financing from six international financial institutions for projects scheduled this year, which officials say will help attract long-term capital while reducing pressure on utility costs.

The government repaired 6,600 kilometers of engineering networks in 2025. This year, it plans to increase that figure to 12,000 kilometers with planned financing of 1.138 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion), marking the project’s transition from institutional preparation to large-scale construction and modernization works.

Improving utility networks

A key objective of the program is improving the financial and operational condition of utility companies operating aging infrastructure.

According to Darbayev, eight utilities were removed from the government’s highest-risk category in 2025, with another eight expected to improve their status this year. By 2029, authorities aim to move 70 utility companies out of the critical-risk category.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said implementation of the national project remains under the personal oversight of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and instructed regional administrations to accelerate modernization efforts. He also directed the National Economy Ministry and other government agencies to ensure the effective use of investment allocated under the program.

Priority for local producers

The modernization program is also expected to boost domestic industrial production.

Minister of Industry and Construction Yersayin Nagaspayev said procurement rules give priority to Kazakh manufacturers. Only companies included in the national register of domestic producers are eligible to participate in project tenders, while procurement is conducted through a dedicated electronic platform designed to give suppliers greater visibility into future demand.

Around 500 domestic manufacturers have been registered as potential suppliers for the national project. According to Nagaspayev, 27 projects are currently in the construction phase, with procurement of construction materials already underway.

Officials said demand for domestically produced equipment and materials under the modernization program is expected to reach approximately 2 trillion tenge (US$4.2 billion) by 2029.

World.title: UK-Kazakhstan Partnership Enters New Phase: But What Will It Mean in Practice?
World.content:
ASTANA — International agreements are often measured by the ceremony surrounding their signing. Their real value, however, is measured years later: by investments made, businesses launched and partnerships that would not have happened otherwise. The entry into force this July of the Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (SPCA) between the United Kingdom (UK) and Kazakhstan raises precisely that question. Beyond its diplomatic significance, could it become the framework that reshapes how the two countries work together?

British Ambassador to Kazakhstan Sally Axworthy said exactly that: the agreement is more than a diplomatic milestone. Rather, “it is a signal of intent.”

“The UK is open for business. The SPCA gives our companies, universities and innovators a stronger platform to work together, invest and deliver practical results. From critical minerals and energy to education, technology and sustainable growth, this agreement sets the course for the next chapter of UK-Kazakhstan cooperation,” she said.

Her remarks reflect a broader shift in the bilateral relationship. Rather than focusing on a handful of traditional sectors, the agreement creates a framework for cooperation across industries that are becoming increasingly important in today’s economy.

From resources to value creation

The timing is notable. Global competition for critical minerals is intensifying. Countries are looking to build more resilient supply chains, diversify economic partnerships and secure access to strategic resources. Kazakhstan, with its mineral wealth and growing role in Eurasian connectivity, finds itself increasingly at the center of those conversations. In this context, the SPCA appears less like the beginning of a relationship than its natural evolution.

The UK and Kazakhstan have been strategic partners since 2013. Over the years, cooperation has expanded across energy, financial services, aviation, education and environmental protection. British expertise contributed to establishing the Astana International Financial Centre and its English law-based court, while educational partnerships have steadily expanded. Yet the global economy has changed considerably over the past decade, and so have the priorities of bilateral cooperation.

That shift was already becoming visible in 2023. At the time, British Trade Commissioner Kenan Poleo described the growing bilateral agenda as “a wave of activities”: extending beyond a single visit to include critical minerals, agriculture and education. Three years later, the SPCA gives that trajectory a formal institutional framework.

For years, Kazakhstan attracted international interest largely because of its natural resources. Today, the conversation is increasingly shifting toward what happens after those resources are extracted. How can they be processed? Where can additional value be created? Which technologies and expertise are needed to move further up the industrial value chain? The SPCA provides a framework for exactly those conversations.

The first projects emerging under this new framework already offer a glimpse of where the partnership is heading. One of the clearest examples — the recently announced five-year, $107 million agreement between the UK’s Maritime House and Kazakhstan’s Zhezkazganredmet illustrates that shift. The project will expand cooperation in rhenium recycling and is expected to support an additional $30 million investment in Saran to produce metallic rhenium from secondary raw materials.

At first glance, it is simply another investment announcement. In reality, it reflects a broader trend. Rhenium is used in high-performance aerospace manufacturing and other advanced industries, making it a strategically important material. Rather than focusing solely on exporting raw materials, projects like this point toward industrial cooperation built around technology and higher-value production. In other words, the conversation is gradually shifting from extracting resources to creating more value from them.

That direction is hardly new. In an interview with The Astana Times last December, British Ambassador Sally Axworthy said the UK sees Kazakhstan’s ambitions extending beyond resource extraction.

“We understand that Kazakhstan wants not just to be a producer of raw materials, but also to process,” she said, referring to cooperation in critical minerals as an area where both countries could build long-term partnerships.

The agreement entering into force now provides a stronger institutional foundation for those ambitions. Critical minerals, however, are only one part of the story. Trade and connectivity are beginning to tell a similar one. Just days before the agreement entered into force, Kazakhstan launched its first multimodal shipment of mineral fertilizers from Ekibastuz to the UK via the Middle Corridor.

The new route, linking Kazakhstan with the UK through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan and Georgia before reaching the Port of Felixstowe, expands export opportunities for Kazakh producers while diversifying supply chains between the two countries. The shipment is significant not only because it opens another export route. It also demonstrates how the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route is becoming part of a broader economic relationship between Kazakhstan and its Western partners.

Taken separately, a shipment of fertilizers and a rhenium recycling project may seem unrelated. Together, they tell a different story. One reflects the movement of goods, the other the movement up the value chain. Both suggest that UK-Kazakhstan cooperation is becoming broader, more practical and increasingly tied to resilient supply chains.

Investing in people, not just projects

Education tells a similar story. While critical minerals and transport reflect the economic dimension of the partnership, education represents its long-term investment in human capital. The two are more closely connected than they may initially appear.

Education has long been one of the strongest pillars of UK-Kazakhstan relations. For more than three decades, the Bolashak Scholarship has helped shape a generation of Kazakh professionals, with the UK emerging as one of its principal destinations. More than half of all Bolashak scholars have studied at British universities over the lifetime of the program, while nearly 6,000 alumni have received their education in the UK. Today, many of those graduates work across government, business, academia and the private sector, creating long-standing professional and people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Yet the relationship is evolving once again. Instead of only sending students to Britain, British universities are increasingly coming to Kazakhstan. The UK has become one of Kazakhstan’s leading partners in higher education. Since De Montfort University opened the country’s first British university campus in 2021, the UK’s academic presence has expanded steadily. Coventry University and Cardiff University have since established campuses, with Cardiff becoming the first Russell Group university to open a branch in Central Asia. Further British institutions are expected to open this September.

The expansion reflects a broader agenda pursued by both governments. Education featured prominently during high-level bilateral talks held by Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev in London earlier this year, alongside critical minerals, trade, logistics and digital transformation, underscoring its role as a strategic pillar of the partnership.

Ambassador Axworthy believes education and industrial cooperation are closely linked.

“Education and standards play a critical supporting role,” she said, noting that Cardiff University’s Astana campus offers programs in geological exploration while the UK is also working with Kazakhstan through the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative.

“These are the things that give businesses confidence to come and invest,” she added in her December interview with The Astana Times.

Viewed separately, critical minerals, new transport routes and university campuses may appear to belong to different stories. Taken together, however, they point in the same direction. Kazakhstan is seeking not only investment, but also knowledge, technology and skills that allow the country to move further up the value chain. In that sense, education becomes part of the same long-term economic strategy as industrial cooperation.

As British Ambassador Axworthy described the SPCA as “more than a diplomatic milestone” and “a signal of intent.” That may ultimately prove to be the agreement’s greatest significance. A single agreement rarely transforms strategic partnerships. They evolve through investment decisions, research collaboration, educational exchanges and new trade routes. In many ways, the SPCA recognizes a partnership that had already begun moving in this direction. What happens next will determine whether it becomes simply another bilateral agreement or the foundation for a more mature economic partnership between the United Kingdom and Kazakhstan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Advances Regional AI Ambitions Through New Technology Hub
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to establish another international technology hub dedicated to artificial intelligence and startup development, expanding its network of innovation platforms as the country seeks to position itself as a regional AI hub through global partnerships, talent development and private investment.

The initiative was discussed during Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov’s July 27 meeting with Balaji Srinivasan, founder of the international technology community Network School. The two sides explored cooperation in artificial intelligence, startup development and technology entrepreneurship, including plans to establish an international innovation hub in the Akmola Region with future expansion into Alatau City.

The project reflects Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of building a comprehensive AI ecosystem that extends beyond infrastructure to include education, innovation, international partnerships and talent attraction.

The initiative comes as Kazakhstan continues to strengthen its international profile in artificial intelligence. Earlier, the country became a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), underscoring its ambition to contribute to global AI governance while developing its own innovation ecosystem.

A privately funded innovation ecosystem

Unlike many technology initiatives led by governments, the proposed Network School project would be financed entirely through private investment.

During the meeting, the parties discussed establishing Network City in the Burabai area—a technology-oriented community designed to bring together entrepreneurs, engineers, software developers and researchers. The concept combines educational programs, coworking spaces, startup accelerators, hackathons and international conferences within a single innovation ecosystem.

A memorandum on establishing the Network School initiative in Kazakhstan has already been signed with the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, marking the first practical step toward implementation.

Srinivasan said Kazakhstan has significant potential to integrate into global networks of talent and investment, highlighting opportunities for cooperation with international technology communities.

Building on existing foundations

The proposed hub would complement Kazakhstan’s expanding digital infrastructure rather than replace existing institutions.

In recent years, the government has invested heavily in projects including Astana Hub, the Alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Center, Tomorrow School, TUMO, and the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz.
