Together, these initiatives form the backbone of the country’s strategy, which aims to accelerate digital transformation and artificial intelligence adoption across the economy.

Bektenov emphasized that attracting international expertise remains a strategic priority, noting that Kazakhstan views the development of human capital, science and innovation as long-term drivers of economic competitiveness.

Competing for global talent

The Network School initiative reflects a broader trend among countries seeking to compete not only for technology companies but also for highly skilled professionals capable of developing new AI applications.

By bringing internationally recognized innovation communities to Kazakhstan, policymakers hope to accelerate knowledge transfer, expand opportunities for local entrepreneurs and integrate the country more closely into global technology networks.

The emphasis on education is particularly significant. Rather than focusing solely on attracting established companies, the initiative aims to develop a pipeline of engineers, founders and researchers while connecting them with international investors and technology leaders.

World.title: Parliamentary Election Campaign Rolls Across Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Political parties stepped up campaigning nationwide in the first week of Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral parliament. Since the campaign officially began July 23, parties have held tours, public forums, sporting events and meetings with voters to promote their platforms ahead of the Aug. 23 vote.

Adilet launches nationwide caravan

The Adilet party kicked off one of the largest outreach initiatives of the campaign on July 24 by sending mobile caravans across Kazakhstan.

Over the next month, the caravans are expected to visit more than 100 cities, district centers and villages, traveling more than 14,000 kilometers. Around 200 party representatives, including Kurultai candidates, campaign staff, experts and activists, will participate in the project, with organizers expecting to meet more than 10,000 voters.

The campaign focuses on increasing household incomes, strengthening regional economies, improving public services, accelerating digitalization and supporting entrepreneurship. Party representatives are also gathering public feedback on proposed legislative reforms.

During a visit to the Turkistan Region, Adilet candidates met with artisans and tourism industry representatives to discuss the development of the creative economy, traditional crafts and domestic tourism. The party proposed granting artisans formal legal status, arguing that craftspeople preserve Kazakhstan’s historical heritage, cultural identity and national traditions while contributing to economic growth.

Aq Jol engages business community

The Aq Jol Democratic Party held a large business forum in Almaty on July 24, bringing together more than 200 representatives of small, medium-sized and large enterprises, industry associations and business experts.

Discussions centered on tax reform, reducing administrative barriers for businesses, preventing unlawful inspections and improving financing programs for small and medium-sized enterprises. Participants also emphasized support for domestic manufacturers and policies aimed at import substitution.

According to the party, the forum was designed to establish direct dialogue with entrepreneurs and develop legislative proposals to strengthen Kazakhstan’s business climate.

Auyl focuses on rural healthcare

Representatives of the Auyl party, which advocates for stronger rural communities, met with healthcare workers on July 25 as part of their nationwide campaign.

Party members outlined proposals to strengthen the agricultural sector, improve rural infrastructure, enhance education and workforce training in the regions, and expand support for rural entrepreneurship and agricultural science.

Baytaq promotes green agenda

The Baytaq Green Party launched its campaign with an environmental marathon at Astana’s Triathlon Park on July 24.

More than 200 party members, candidates, activists and supporters participated in the 2.5-kilometer run. Organizers said the event was intentionally scheduled early in the morning, when traffic is lighter and air quality is at its best, to highlight the party’s environmental message.

The next day, the party presented its election platform outdoors in Astana’s Green Belt during a meeting with employees of Astana Ormany, the organization responsible for maintaining the capital’s protective forest belt.

Party representatives emphasized issues including air quality, access to clean drinking water, food security and the creation of green jobs, describing environmental protection as directly linked to public health and quality of life.

People’s Party highlights creative economy and energy

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan launched the campaign with the release of its official anthem, “Halqymmen Birge” (Together with My People), along with a music video.

The party said the creative format reflects its support for Kazakhstan’s creative economy, noting that the video features footage from its real projects, public events, and community initiatives.

During campaign visits to Pavlodar, party candidates met with employees of Pavlodarenergo and participated in a women’s forum.

Speaking to energy sector workers, party chairman Nursultan Shokanov stressed the importance of protecting labor rights while investing in modern energy infrastructure.

“Reliable energy supplies are the foundation of industrial growth and investment,” he said, adding that Kazakhstan should develop its own advanced technologies rather than relying solely on imported solutions.

Social democrats call for pension reform

The Nationwide Social Democratic Party organized a public sporting event, the Freedom Marathon, on July 25.

Participants completed the course using Nordic walking poles, symbolizing solidarity between generations. The event highlighted one of the party’s flagship campaign proposals, gradually lowering the retirement age to 58 for women and 60 for men.

According to the party, pension reform should guarantee every retiree a dignified standard of living. Party representatives said respect for older generations is a measure of a society’s maturity. They also argued that lowering the retirement age could be financed by reducing government spending, bringing more businesses out of the shadow economy and introducing fairer taxation for large corporations, rather than by cutting social benefits.

Respublica begins campaign in Karagandy

The Respublica party launched its nationwide campaign in Karagandy on July 25. Party candidates met with more than 1,000 residents during the first day, including farmers, entrepreneurs, students, factory workers and civic activists. Similar meetings are planned across Kazakhstan throughout the campaign.

Speakers focused on developing domestic manufacturing, supporting small and medium-sized businesses, creating new jobs, expanding digitalization and improving education while promoting equal opportunities. During the regional visit, party representatives also toured agricultural enterprises and manufacturing facilities and met with business leaders and young people.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan’s Non-Oil Economy Sustain the Country’s Growth Momentum?
World.content:
ALMATY – As oil production temporarily softens, Kazakhstan is increasingly relying on construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture to maintain economic momentum. Government officials argue that strengthening these sectors will not only offset weaker hydrocarbon output in the short term but also lay the foundation for more diversified and resilient long-term growth.

The strategy was at the center of a July 27 meeting of the government’s economic growth headquarters chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, where officials reviewed progress across key industries and outlined priorities for the remainder of the year.

Shifting the growth model

The government’s emphasis on non-resource industries reflects a broader effort to reduce Kazakhstan’s dependence on hydrocarbons. While oil continues to play a central role in the economy, authorities increasingly view construction, manufacturing, logistics and agriculture as the main engines capable of sustaining growth during periods of lower energy output.

Analysts note, however, that expanding output alone will not be enough to transform the economy. Analyst and policy expert Sobir Kurbanov argued that many regional value chains remain underdeveloped despite their potential.

“Value chains are there, but neither competitive nor complementary,” Kurbanov said, pointing particularly to agriculture and tourism. According to him, fragmented production, weak logistics, inconsistent standards and limited regional coordination continue to prevent Central Asia from developing cross-border industries capable of generating higher-value exports and creating sustainable jobs.

According to Zhumangarin, construction also remains the fastest-growing sector, with officials expecting strong performance through the first seven months of the year. The highest growth is projected in the Ulytau, Abai and Kyzylorda regions, supported by ongoing infrastructure investment.

Manufacturing has also emerged as one of the strongest contributors to economic expansion. Industrial output increased by 9.8%, driven by machinery production, which rose 23.2%, chemicals (19%), food processing (14.7%) and light industry, where production nearly doubled with an 89.2% increase. Authorities expect this momentum to continue in the coming months.

Domestic demand and logistics

Trade has remained another important pillar of growth. Total trade turnover reached 36.2 trillion tenge (US$67 billion), while the physical volume index rose 5.7% during the first half of the year. To sustain this trajectory, regional authorities have been instructed to accelerate the implementation of regional trade development roadmaps, including the launch of new investment projects.

Transport presents a more mixed picture. Although overall freight volumes continue to grow, expansion has been constrained by lower shipments of oil and natural gas. In response, the government plans to place greater emphasis on Kazakhstan’s role as a Eurasian transit corridor by maximizing rail and road transport capacity.

Agriculture’s expanding role

Agriculture is expected to remain another important contributor to economic growth this year, supported by the ongoing harvest campaign, livestock development and record levels of concessional financing for the agricultural sector.

One notable trend is the growing contribution of modern dairy farms financed through preferential lending programs launched in 2024 and 2025. Many of these facilities are now reaching full production capacity, contributing to higher milk output. According to Zhumangarin, during the first half of 2026, Kazakhstan produced 1.9 million tons of milk, a 2.4% increase compared with the same period last year.

Authorities also expect higher production of food and beverages as agricultural output expands.

Infrastructure as a long-term growth driver

Looking beyond short-term economic indicators, Zhumangarin stressed that Kazakhstan’s long-term growth strategy continues to rely on large-scale infrastructure development.

“In this regard, it is necessary to prepare high-quality projects now, which will ensure long-term economic effect and are provided for by the system of regional standards: facilities of healthcare and social sphere, paying special attention to bridges, crossings, key transport highways and energy facilities, funded by the republican budget,” he said.

While the government sees infrastructure investment and the expansion of non-oil industries as the foundation for long-term growth, analysts highlight that deeper structural reforms must accompany physical investment.

“Central Asia’s future path of development appeared to be less dependent on geopolitical shifts but more on the internal fundamentals,” Kurbanov said.

He argues that stronger institutions, higher productivity, investment in human capital, climate resilience and practical steps toward regional integration will ultimately determine whether the region can translate today’s economic momentum into sustainable long-term growth.

The approach reflects the government’s broader objective of combining immediate economic stimulus with investments designed to strengthen Kazakhstan’s long-term productive capacity. Rather than relying solely on commodity exports, policymakers increasingly see infrastructure expansion and the development of competitive non-oil industries as essential for sustaining future growth.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Rail Freight Growth Puts Infrastructure Expansion in Focus
World.content:
ALMATY – Freight volumes on Kazakhstan’s rail network continued to grow in the first half of 2026, underscoring the country’s expanding role in regional trade. But as cargo flows accelerate, the focus is shifting from record volumes to whether rail infrastructure can keep pace with demand.

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) transported 157.1 million tons of cargo between January and June, a 3.5% increase compared to the same period last year. Domestic freight reached 82.2 million tons, while export shipments rose by 2.9 million tons to 45.6 million tons, reflecting stronger external demand for Kazakh commodities and agricultural products.

The latest figures build on the company’s record performance in 2025, when KTZ transported 319.8 million tons of cargo, up 5.5% year-on-year, driven by growth in exports, transit and imports.

Exports remain the key growth driver

Much of the increase continues to come from export-oriented industries. Coal remained the largest cargo category during the first half of the year, with 51.3 million tons transported, including 15.9 million tons exported.

Agricultural shipments also continued to expand. Rail transport of grain increased 10% to 7.3 million tons, while grain exports climbed 11% to 5.6 million tons. Even faster growth was recorded in higher-value agricultural products. Exports of processed grain products reached 1.1 million tons, up 20%, while feed shipments surged 51% to 2 million tons, reflecting Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to move beyond raw commodity exports.

Freight volumes also increased across other major industrial sectors, including oil products (13.3 million tons, +3.7%), iron ore (11.6 million tons, +15.1%), ferrous metals (8.1 million tons, +8.8%), non-ferrous ores and construction materials.

The figures suggest Kazakhstan’s rail network is carrying a diversified export basket while supporting domestic industrial activity.

Capacity expansion moves beyond new railways

To accommodate rising freight flows, KTZ has focused on expanding capacity through infrastructure upgrades, digitalization and fleet renewal rather than relying solely on new rail construction.

The company says artificial intelligence is already helping monitor 22,000 kilometers of railway infrastructure through its Smart Diagnostics system, allowing engineers to predict track defects up to 87 days in advance and significantly improve maintenance planning.

Automation projects now cover 3,000 kilometers of rail lines to increase capacity across seven major corridors.

KTZ has also introduced a unified digital wagon management platform, which the company estimates saves up to two billion tenge (US$3.7 million) annually by reducing empty wagon movements and improving fleet utilization. In parallel, it is deploying Wabtec’s Kinetix system, enabling rolling stock to be inspected while trains remain in motion.

Rolling stock expansion is also accelerating. Subsidiary Kaztemirtrans, which currently operates more than 39,500 freight wagons, plans to purchase 13,000 additional freight cars between 2027 and 2031, including 10,000 gondola wagons, 2,100 covered wagons and 900 grain hoppers. Between 2023 and 2025, the company already added 3,000 new gondola wagons manufactured domestically to transport socially important cargo such as coal and grain.

Building a logistics hub requires more than higher freight volumes

Alongside domestic investments, KTZ is strengthening international partnerships to improve multimodal connectivity. During a June 23 business conference in Brussels, the company signed a new cooperation agreement with A.P. Moller – Maersk to expand container transport along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor. Discussions with DHL Global Forwarding focused on developing integrated multimodal services linking China, Central Asia, Türkiye and Europe.

KTZ is also expanding supporting infrastructure, including the first phase of a new container hub in Aktau Port and the KIF Warehouses logistics complex on the Kazakh-Chinese border.

According to IFC Regional Head of Industry for Infrastructure and Natural Resources for the Middle East and Central Asia Laura Vecvagare, the investments reflect the scale of the challenge facing Kazakhstan.

“Kazakhstan’s rail network extends more than 16,000 kilometers, ranking among the top 30 countries globally by network length,” she wrote in her opinion article for the Astana Times.

“However, structural constraints remain, including extensive single-track segments, limited electrification, asset depreciation, growing loads and border bottlenecks. These challenges translate into slower rail movements and longer dwell times, which limit throughput on busy routes, require costly workarounds and constrain Kazakhstan’s full potential as a transport and logistics hub,” she added.

Vecvagare noted that the government has adopted the Railway Transport Development Program 2029, while KTZ is preparing a major investment program for 2025-2029 to modernize core infrastructure.

“The scale and urgency of these investments call for blended support, combining public commitments with private capital mobilized through trusted partners,” she said.

For Kazakhstan, steadily rising freight volumes are therefore only one part of the story. Sustaining growth will depend on whether investments in infrastructure, rolling stock, digital technologies and international logistics partnerships can remove long-standing bottlenecks and enable the rail network to handle increasing trade flows across Eurasia.

World.title: Türkiye and Kazakhstan Need Processing Alliance, Not Another Extraction Rush
World.content:
At the Astana Mining and Metallurgy Congress in June, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said Kazakhstan wanted to become a regional hub for processing and higher-value manufacturing. That should force Ankara to revisit the mining memorandum signed in July 2025, which emphasised joint exploration and production. If bilateral co-operation ends at the mine mouth, it will already be behind Kazakhstan’s own industrial policy.

Türkiye and Kazakhstan need a processing alliance, not an ore-for-machinery bargain

Joint work should extend from beneficiation and metallurgy to alloys, permanent-magnet materials, processing equipment, recycling and environmental control. If Kazakhstan supplies concentrate while Türkiye imports the refined chemicals, magnets or specialised components needed by its factories from established producers elsewhere, both will remain outside the most strategic stages.

The excitement around Kazakhstan’s mineral potential makes this distinction urgent. In April 2025, the government announced an estimated rare-earth resource of more than 20 million tonnes at the Zhana Kazakhstan site, including neodymium, cerium, lanthanum and yttrium. The estimate still requires confirmation as an economically recoverable reserve. Even if confirmed, geology alone will not create industrial power. Refining concentration continued to rise in 2025 and that planned magnet production in diversified regions amounts to only about one-third of expected rare-earth mining capacity by 2035. The bottleneck is what happens after extraction.

That middle of the chain is technically demanding. Ore must be characterised, concentrated, separated and refined before it becomes high-purity metal, alloy powder or a usable component. Plants also need specialised equipment, laboratories, water treatment and reliable maintenance. These activities create engineering knowledge and supplier demand; an offtake agreement does not.

The two countries have complementary starting points, but neither should exaggerate them. Kazakhstan has operating mines, metallurgy and trained engineers. Türkiye has an export-oriented machinery industry and is developing rare-earth processing knowledge through the Beylikova pilot plant and the Rare Earth Elements Research Institute. It is not yet a substitute for the countries dominating separation, advanced magnets and specialised equipment. A credible alliance would bring in technology partners from Japan, South Korea, Europe or Southeast Asia where necessary, rather than present dependence as self-sufficiency.

The division of labour should follow industrial logic. Beneficiation and primary metallurgy will usually make more sense near Kazakh deposits, avoiding the shipment of low-grade material and retaining local value. Turkish firms can supply process machinery, power electronics, automation, precision parts and environmental systems, while Turkish industrial clusters provide demand for refined metals, alloys and magnet materials. Joint laboratories should qualify outputs for automotive, machinery, energy and electronics customers. Technology licences and engineering teams should be shared, instead of leaving one side with the mine and the other with the purchase order.

Southeast Asia makes this more than a bilateral Central Asian project. ASEAN’s Minerals Cooperation Action Plan for 2026–30 explicitly seeks upstream-to-downstream development, technology adoption and stronger human capacity. Indonesia’s nickel policy has shown that domestic processing can be created quickly, but also that foreign-led technology and excess capacity can accompany the boom. Malaysia, meanwhile, is seeking investment in environmentally responsible rare-earth processing and super-magnet production. The lesson is not to copy an export ban, but to build capabilities that can enter several regional supply chains without allowing one foreign operator or market to control them.

A Türkiye–Kazakhstan alliance could serve those chains selectively. Kazakh tungsten processed into hard-metal powders and Turkish cutting tools could supply machinery users in Thailand, Viet Nam and Malaysia. Rare-earth materials, once commercially proven, could support motor and electronics production, while recycling partnerships with ASEAN firms recover magnets and metals from end-of-life equipment. This would offer Southeast Asian manufacturers another supplier relationship without pretending that Kazakhstan or Türkiye can replace China across the whole chain.

Environmental rules must be part of the commercial model. Mineral separation can consume substantial energy and water and generate hazardous residues; weak oversight would turn strategic ambition into a local pollution problem. Each project should publish water and emissions baselines, tailings plans, closure finance and traceability data. Recycling should begin before large waste volumes arrive. The IEA expects secondary supply’s contribution to key energy minerals to rise from roughly 10 per cent today towards 20 percent by 2040, but only if collection and recovery systems are built beforehand.

The strongest objection is cost. New refining projects outside dominant suppliers face higher capital expenditure, scarce equipment and uncertain prices. The IEA estimates capital costs can be 20 to more than 150 percent higher, with operating costs around 50 per cent higher on average. A complete national value chain is therefore unrealistic. A selective bilateral chain is not: it should focus on products with confirmed deposits, contracted buyers and a credible technology route.

Ankara and Astana should establish a Türkiye–Kazakhstan Critical Minerals Processing Alliance under their High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council. Its first portfolio should test three projects: a tungsten-to-tooling line; a rare-earth separation and magnet-material pilot contingent on verified ore economics; and a platform for recovering valuable metals from metallurgical waste, used equipment and electronic scrap. A joint project-preparation facility should complete technical studies, environmental assessments and offtake negotiations before public finance is committed.

Support should be released against measurable outcomes: qualified local suppliers, engineers trained, recovery rates achieved, water reused, process knowledge shared and sales to third markets. Extraction-only projects should not receive strategic incentives. ASEAN buyers and technology firms should be invited into selected projects, while Kazakhstan and Türkiye retain diversified ownership, transparent procurement and access to operational data.

A mining agreement can secure tonnes. A processing alliance secures competence. If ore leaves Kazakhstan while Turkish factories continue buying the decisive materials and technologies from dominant refiners, the partnership will merely rearrange the route of dependency. It becomes strategic only when Kazakh resources, Turkish industrial capability and external technology produce materials that factories in Europe and Southeast Asia buy repeatedly.

The author is Mehmet Enes Beşer, a researcher focusing on ASEAN, and a graduate of Sociology in Boğaziçi University. He is the ASEAN Coordinator at Vatan Party (Türkiye) and a member of the Editorial Board of Teori magazine.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Five fined and four jailed in Tbilisi activists’ case
World.content:
A court in Georgia has concluded hearings in the cases of 10 activists detained outside Tbilisi City Hall on 26 July. Four were sentenced to administrative detention, while five were fined. Proceedings against one remaining activist have been postponed until 31 July.

What happened

The incident began when activist Tornike Toshkhua staged a solo protest outside Tbilisi City Hall holding a banner reading: “Bidzina d*ck? Yes – No.” The slogan referred to Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Police detained Toshkhua at the scene.

Tornike Toshkhua

In response, a group of activists gathered outside Tbilisi City Hall carrying banners with the same slogan to express solidarity with Toshkhua. Within minutes, police began detaining them as well. In total, nine more people were arrested alongside Toshkhua.

They have been charged with using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders.

Fines and detentions

The activists began appearing in court from the afternoon of 28 July, before the 48-hour detention period had expired.

The first ruling was delivered in the case of Vaso Beridze. The judge fined him 5,000 lari ($1,850), rejecting the Interior Ministry’s request to place him under administrative detention.

In the case of Ia Melitauri, the Interior Ministry sought the maximum administrative detention, but the judge sentenced her to five days in custody instead. Police accused Melitauri of using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders. The judge found no evidence that she had disobeyed police and convicted her only of petty hooliganism.

Melitauri had previously been found guilty twice of administrative offences involving disobeying police and insulting a police officer. A third offence under the same provision carries criminal liability.

According to people present at the hearing, Melitauri told the court she had been mistreated by police following her arrest and showed the judge injuries she said she had sustained during her detention.

The hearing in the case of the third detainee, Tornike Tikaradze, was postponed until 31 July. Tikaradze did not attend the hearing in protest.

Another judge heard the cases of seven other activists and, after several hours of witness testimony and reviewing video evidence, delivered the following verdicts:

Tornike Toshkhua was fined 3,000 lari ($1,110);

Mariam Mekantsishvili was fined 6,000 lari ($2,220);

Nato Bolkvadze was sentenced to five days of administrative detention;

Shako Bagdoshvili was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Lasha Dgebuadze was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Marine Nanava was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850);

Sandro Sekhniashvili was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850).

Scuffle outside the courthouse

Several reports of scuffles between members of the public and court bailiffs emerged throughout the day as the hearings were under way.

Videos circulating on social media showed bailiffs forcibly removing people from the courthouse.

During the final hearing, activist Ruska Mchedlidze and lawyer Marika Arevadze said court bailiffs used force against them.

Ruska Mchedlidze

“Zonder bailiff Davit Matiashvili and other zonder bailiffs physically assaulted me in the courtyard of this unjust court. Yes, I spat at them, and yes, I spat at them again after the assault, once I was outside the gates.

These bruises will heal, but everyone will remember his disgrace forever. His, and that of the other zonder bailiffs carrying out unlawful orders. There were around 20 police officers standing there, watching as these aggressive men assaulted me, and not one of them intervened,” Mchedlidze wrote on social media.

Activist Lado Jakhua also shared footage showing several court bailiffs dragging Ruska Mchedlidze out of the courthouse courtyard.

Tbilisi activists sentenced over protest

World.title: Opposition grows in Abkhazia over monument to citizens killed in Ukraine war
World.content:
A group of Abkhaz politicians and public figures has spoken out against plans to erect a monument in Sukhum to citizens of Abkhazia who were killed while fighting in the war in Ukraine.

They appealed to the republic’s president, Badra Gunba, and the city authorities to cancel or postpone the decision, which was approved by the Sukhum City Assembly at the initiative of the city administration.

The appeal was signed by former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia, People’s Artist Batal Jopua, historian Guram Gumba, former education minister Adgur Kakoba, Akhyatsa civic organisation head Akhra Bzhania, and former leader of the Aruaa veterans’ movement Ilya Guniya.

The signatories argue that any memorial erected in the Abkhaz capital should commemorate historical events only after they have stood the test of time.

“Fighting is still under way, people are dying, yet the local authorities in Abkhazia have taken the unprecedented decision to erect a monument to a war that has not yet ended.

“No one knows how, when or on what terms these two closely related peoples will first reach understanding and then reconciliation. But that will inevitably happen. Only then, years later, will we be able to return to the question of creating a memorial to this historical event,” the appeal says.

The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Dictator wants to be liked by everyone. Those who don’t like him must be neutralised’
World.content:
Transparency International Georgia researcher Zviad Koridze believes that Georgia’s current system of governance is built on fostering civil confrontation and deepening divisions within society. In his view, authoritarian regimes rely on social polarisation and the portrayal of people with different opinions as enemies in order to maintain power.

Koridze said that Georgian society still retains the capacity to resist, and that, ultimately, it is civic engagement that will serve as the main force pushing back against these processes.

On 26 July, MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several supporters, announced the creation of a civic movement that will “respond immediately” to issues involving ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. According to Kartvelishvili, the movement will be “highly active, well-organised and constructive”, and any “patriotic Georgian” will be able to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

Zviad Koridze: “the system of governance that has taken hold in Georgia — Bidzina Ivanishvili’s dictatorship — regards civil confrontation as its natural state, just like any other dictatorship. Without it, those in power cannot consolidate their rule. They cannot persuade citizens that their continued grip on power and authoritarian governance serve the public interest. To do that, they need civil confrontation.

“All dictatorships are structured and develop in exactly this way. They need to identify groups and segments of society whose views differ from those of the autocrat. Then another social group must emerge to confront and suppress them. That is the language of civil confrontation.”

“When parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that we do not need to join the European Union because we should have the right to make our own decisions, that is clearly not his independent position but Bidzina Ivanishvili’s. Papuashvili’s role is to voice that position and to support the creation of precisely these kinds of vigilante groups. He is expected to welcome their emergence. He sees this as a form of sovereign governance, and that is exactly why he does not want Georgia to join the European Union.

“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: Inside the Labor Party meeting where Victoria's new premier was elected
World.content:
The French polished cedar doors of the Labor caucus room are thick, but not think enough to stifle the chaos behind them on Tuesday.

Having calmly announced her resignation as premier earlier that morning, Jacinta Allan was now yelling.

Her ally Steve Dimopoulos was making plenty of noise too.

And the journalists and camera operators huddled outside, jostling for prime position, were within earshot.

Almost two hours after they walked in, about 70 Labor MPs spilled out in to the halls of parliament with Ben Carroll their new leader.

Factional warfare broke out once doors closed on the Labor Party caucus on Tuesday. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

In the haggling, they had to cast their vote to avoid a drawn out contest three times — once "on the voices" and then twice by a show of hands after failing to tally the numbers correctly.

"They couldn't figure out how many people had voted for it," an MP said to explain the yelling.

"The process was a shambles."

It was a commonly-used descriptor for the day.

The leadership challenge that 'destroyed' Socialist Left

Colleagues sympathetic to the now departed premier said Ms Allan raised her voice only to maintain some order in the farce, while others were interjecting and speaking over one another to grumble about the process.

Many had thought Mr Carroll's leadership was a fait accompli, having held the majority support of the room after Ms Allan had publicly declared that he would receive her full support should he emerge as premier.

Instead, she added her signature to the nomination of her loyalist, Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny, setting up a challenge that threatened to drag a contest out for more than a month and destroy any lingering possibility of a fourth term of a Labor government.

Sonya Kilkenny announced her intention to contest the leadership vacated by Jacinta Allan. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

It was a move most of Ms Allan's own Socialist Left (SL) faction had no idea was afoot, after their own "very, very, very tense" and even venomous meeting moments.

The Socialist Left has for years enjoyed dominance in Labor’s factions — blocs within the Labor Party of MPs and powerbrokers aligned on policy and other interests. It was home to former premier Daniel Andrews.

But elevating Mr Carroll — a candidate from the Right — at the expense of Ms Allan has left it in tatters.

"This has destroyed the Socialist Left," one of its MPs said.

"SL is utterly imploding."

MPs had been feeding out updates to the collection of reporters. Gabrielle Williams, also from the Left, will be deputy. Wait, Steve Dimopoulos is contesting too. Ms Williams has won the ballot but she's also been elected interim premier so the entire Labor membership can cast their votes on a leader.

For a brief period on Tuesday Gabrielle Williams was interim premier, before the Labor caucus changed course again. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Both deputy candidates were from the Left, and — while the Right voted as a bloc — the SL splintered.

One person in the room even voted informally for the deputy. Someone put a 'tick' next to retiring upper house president Shaun Leane's name, in what was a presumed gag.

Cracks in the Left had already opened under Jacinta Allan. She hoped to promote Tim Richardson to cabinet in her April cabinet reshuffle, but was overruled in a fractured vote that instead elevated Paul Hamer.

Mr Richardson is now expected to progress to cabinet in Ms Allan's absence.

Jacinta Allan talks to reporters. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Several Labor sources told the ABC that, in order to end a protracted leadership fight, Ms Kilkenny withdrew her candidacy with four conditions.

She would keep her portfolios, Mr Richardson would enter cabinet, there would be no bloodletting, and Mr Carroll's leadership would be unanimously supported.

The move was always viewed as a proxy means of "blowing the joint up" for Ms Allan on her way out, anyways, or to shore up cabinet positions.

Ms Kilkenny withdrew her candidacy at 11.55am, almost two hours after entering and just five minutes before parliament was due to begin for the week.

Sonya Kilkenny withdrew her challenge after receiving reassurances about her future in the cabinet. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Labor's new leader gets to work immediately

The new Premier Ben Carroll immediately announced a royal commission into alleged corruption in the construction sector — something Ms Allan had long refused — and asked his department secretary to begin work on "exhaustive" terms of reference.

The promised strengthening of the anti-corruption watchdog will also happen this term, he said, and stronger law and order reforms will come.

Mr Carroll has previously said he believed police stations, some of which have closed to focus resources on the front line, should be open all-hours.

He even had a cup of tea with Chief Commissioner Mike Bush on his first night on the job.

Ben Carroll immediately announced a royal commission into the construction sector after being elected leader. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

By Wednesday, legislation was introduced to parliament to establish workplace protection orders to stop abuse and violence directed at retail and hospitality staff.

Unions had been frustrated by Ms Allan's pace to pursue this reform, though she was expected to bring the legislation before the November 28 election and further consultation is still required.

"We have wanted it faster than this, but we're very pleased that the new premier is making it a priority matter in his first two days," SDA state secretary Michael Donovan told reporters.

Even Ms Allan's prized Suburban Rail Loop is now in doubt, though Mr Carroll on Wednesday said he would not be cancelling any contracts.

He has always barracked for the delayed Airport Rail.

"These are matters for cabinet. Everyone knows there's not a stronger supporter for Airport Rail … than me," Mr Carroll said.

A cast of ministers and MPs arriving at parliament on Wednesday trumpeted the leadership change as a "new start".

An "exciting opportunity for our new Labor government", Minister for Children and Disability Lizzie Blandthorn said.

Environment Minister Enver Erdogan called it a "new chapter".

Environment Minister Enver Erdogan was all smiles after Tuesday's caucus meeting. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Ben Carroll was moving on from Jacinta Allan's approach, backbencher Dylan Waight explained.

"They're clearly different people, and they'll be different leaders. But I think Ben will be an amazing leader," he said.

As Mr Carroll got started on changing course and caucus worked on bandaging up fresh wounds, Ms Allan was seen out by supporting staff and MPs.

They gathered at a Labor favourite — the Union Club Hotel in Fitzroy — singing "solidarity forever".

World.title: Jared Leto denies sexual misconduct allegations after documentary
World.content:
Jared Leto has denied sexual assault and misconduct after four women made allegations about the Hollywood actor and singer in a new documentary released by the BBC.

In a documentary called 'Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret', four women described encounters that took place between 2002 and 2016 when the actor was in his 30s or 40s. He is now 54.

In the documentary, one of the women said she was sexually assaulted in a motel bathroom when she was 17. Another said the Hollywood star threatened her with sexual assault when she was 19.

A third said she had underage sex with the star in California when she was 17, which would be classified as statutory rape. A fourth said Leto made sexually explicit phone calls to her when she was 16.

Four others described "strange and often very sexual phone calls from Leto," the BBC said.

In a statement released on Wednesday afternoon, local time, Mr Leto denied the claims made in the documentary.

"I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false," he said in a statement.

One of the women, Isabel, alleged she was sexually assaulted in a motel room when she was 17, while another accused him of having underage sex with her when she was 17.

A third, Alex, alleged Mr Leto said she would wake up in the middle of sex if she fell asleep on a chaise longue in his hotel room.

A fourth accused Mr Leto of making repeated sexually explicit phone calls to her when she was 16. She subsequently refused to sign a non-disclosure agreement that she received, the BBC investigation found.

Mr Leto is a prominent face in Hollywood, having starred in multiple films including Dallas Buyers Club and Suicide Squad.

But it is not the first time he has faced allegations about his conduct away from the camera.

Last year, US outlet Air Mail reported the accounts of nine women who accused him of sexual impropriety, allegations he strenuously denied at the time.

World.title: Why Jim Chalmers is cautious but upbeat
World.content:
There were no bold declarations about corners being turned or missions being accomplished.

After delivering a pre-election prediction that "the worst of the inflation challenge is behind us", only to see inflation then steadily rise, Jim Chalmers is now more cautious.

Yet the Treasurer was undeniably upbeat yesterday. He welcomed data showing inflation running slightly below where both his department and the Reserve Bank expected it to be just a few months ago.

Headline inflation fell for the third consecutive month to 3.8 per cent. Underlying inflation remains at 3.6 per cent.

Still too high, to be sure. But fears of another interest rate rise have eased. Some economists reckon the Reserve Bank will now sit tight for the rest of the year.

That's a reprieve for stretched households and businesses. And a major relief for the government, which itself identifies cost-of-living frustration as the main source of fuel for One Nation.

The Treasurer was undeniably upbeat as he welcomed data showing inflation running slightly below where both his department and the Reserve Bank expected it to be just a few months ago. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'The trend is clearly our friend'

Slightly lower inflation means slightly less revenue flowing into government coffers via bracket creep, but Labor is far more concerned about the economic and political pain high inflation always manages to inflict.

"The trend is clearly our friend," notes independent economist Chris Richardson.

"So far we have dodged a number of bullets," he tells this column, notably the price of oil not surging quite as high as some initially feared.

The important caveat, however, are the words "so far".

Richardson sees two main risks.

The first is beyond Australia's control.

"We are somewhat reliant on the compromising ability of both Trump and the Revolutionary Guard," says Richardson, pointing to the highly volatile situation in the Middle East.

Even as the inflation figures were being welcomed in Australia yesterday, the conflict between the US and Iran appeared to be escalating once again. Saudi Arabia joined the US in conducting strikes against Iranian proxy forces in Iraq, marking Riyadh's direct entry into the war. It follows Saudi claims of attacks on its oil facilities by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

Loading...

Spending into the gap

The second risk to domestic inflation, as Richardson sees it, is the government itself.

If inflation is seen to be easing, will the government feel it has more wiggle room to "spend into the gap"?

Whether it's energy rebates, fuel excise relief, student debt relief, cheaper medicines, or tax cuts, Labor has taken pride in its willingness to spend, even if critics say it's only made the inflation problem worse.

The decision to halt fuel excise relief this week, however, is a sign of some restraint.

Despite the ongoing risk of another spike in oil prices, the treasurer was clear yesterday about the plan to phase out the remaining 16-cents-a-litre excise discount.

"That fuel excise relief will end at midnight on Sunday," he said.

The government needs inflation to keep falling without the headline rate being artificially forced lower by an expensive excise cut. It also needs its various efforts to boost productivity to start showing some results.

Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock delivered yet another warning this week about "persistently weak productivity growth", which she said has "weighed on real incomes and growth for many years".

Motorists lose fuel discount Drivers will lose the fuel excise discount as planned, despite escalating pressure on global oil prices and warnings the world has depleted reserves.

As Chalmers has often noted, boosting productivity involves dozens of practical reforms, rather than one magic bullet. Every little bit helps.

This is no doubt one of the reasons why the Treasurer was so effusive about the "outstanding" new Premier of Victoria, Ben Carroll.

Chalmers was notably quick to endorse the first decision of Carroll, a fellow traveller from Labor's right faction, to call a royal commission into alleged corruption in Victoria's building industry.

He backed the premier's move without even being asked.

"The reason why we support that is because it's consistent with our zero tolerance at the federal level for corruption," the treasurer revealed.

It's the first time we've heard that.

Federal Labor had long adopted a stony silence as former premier Jacinta Allen refused to call an inquiry. Even as more claims of CFMEU-inflated contracts came to light, the Albanese government refused to offer a view as to whether a royal commission might help.

Cleaning up the construction sector in Victoria could well deliver national productivity benefits across the building industry by lowering costs, something Chalmers would surely welcome.

Loading

The treasurer is on board

The federal government will also be keenly anticipating the new premier's pending decision on the future of the enormously expensive Suburban Rail Loop.

This contentious project is also blamed by some analysts for pushing up costs across the construction industry.

The Commonwealth could easily redirect the whopping $6 billion it's already committed to the project.

Not everyone in federal Labor is convinced the change of leadership in Victoria is a good idea this close to the state election in November. The jury is still out. Some privately fear there will be aftershocks and recriminations. Others say it was a pragmatic move that obviously gives Labor a fighting chance.

The treasurer, looking for anything that might help the national economy, is clearly on board.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: 'The winner is Zelenskyy, not Putin': The inland sea where two wars collide
World.content:
A large inland sea connecting military supply lines through Russia and Iran could now be a pivotal theatre for two major wars that are usually thought of as separate.

Over the weekend, Kyiv's main domestic intelligence agency, the SBU, said Ukrainian drones hit a Russian missile boat as well as two cargo ships in the Caspian Sea that "were under international sanctions and were used to transport military cargo between Iran and Russia".

Iranian officials immediately disputed the assertion, saying Ukraine hit a commercial vessel carrying iron and killed one sailor.

As the two sides fought over the origins of the targeted vessels, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei vowed revenge and summoned Ukraine's top diplomat in Tehran in protest, in what appeared to be a sign of the two wars colliding in a new front.

A satellite view of the Caspian Sea, a major inland lake bordered by five countries including Iran and Russia. (Supplied: NASA Earth Observatory)

For more than five months, global attention has been focused on another Middle Eastern waterway, the Strait of Hormuz, as the Iranian regime threatened freedom of navigation of commercial ships and placed pressure on the world's energy markets.

But analysts say the latest attacks in the Caspian Sea indicate the Ukraine war and the Iran war are not isolated theatres, but parts of an "emerging Eurasian conflict system in which Russia and Iran are mutually dependent".

And it is through a 371,000-square-kilometre area that those two conflicts intersect, Basil Germond, professor of international security at Lancaster University, told the ABC.

The Caspian Sea is the largest landlocked body of water in the world and is bordered by Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Iran.

Because of its geographical position, it is often out of reach and off the radar of most of the world, but historically it has been an important East–West trading route, dating back to Imperial China and the Silk Road.

Russia has long used it as a platform for "long-range power projection" and as a sanction-immune bridge to its ally, Iran.

"This sea is not a sea where Western powers can really exercise any form of leverage," Professor Germond said.

Since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Caspian Sea has become even more important as a "safe haven" for Russia's Black Sea-based naval forces to relocate after major attacks.

But Ukraine's intervention over the weekend has likely shattered the assumption of safety in the inland sea.

Zelenskyy just scored an 'own goal' The Ukrainian president's decision to fire his popular, tech-savvy 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week baffled many. Analysts say what happens next could be pivotal to the war.

Analysts say Kyiv's ability to project more than 692 kilometres from Ukraine's nearest border into Russia and Iran's "safe space" indicates the two conflicts remain in danger of colliding and escalating.

And with the Caspian Sea now in play, what happens in this theatre next could have ramifications for not just one war, but two.

Why Ukraine is targeting Iran

Tensions between Iran and Ukraine have existed for some time and largely centre around Tehran's support for Russia's military campaign.

Russia has developed strong ties with Iran during its war with Ukraine. (Reuters: Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

Since 2022, Iran has supplied lethal long-range attack drones that Moscow has used to degrade Ukraine's air defences and target its power and water infrastructure.

The supply of these crucial weapons, called Shaheds, has been facilitated via the Caspian Sea through Russian and Iranian ports.

"The import of drones or drone components from Iran [through the inland sea] up until quite recently was considered as a safe route," Professor Germond said.

"But that has changed now."

Russia has since developed its own version of the drones with special enhancements, and begun manufacturing them in-country, making it less reliant on Iranian drone shipments.

But the collaboration between the two nations is not limited to one side. In exchange for Iran's equipment, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Russia of providing Tehran with satellite surveillance of Gulf states and US military bases in the region to help it coordinate attacks.

"It's clear that the two countries are collaborating militarily," Professor Germond said.

"Being able to rely on its allies [Iran] is instrumental in enabling [Russia] to continue their war and also to sustain their war economy."

By targeting the Caspian, however, Kyiv is attempting to disrupt that partnership and distract its enemies by forcing them to divert their much-needed war supplies to other areas.

"If Ukraine is targeting Russian or Iranian assets in the Caspian, then the Russians, and the Iranians for that matter, have to reallocate air defense systems in the Caspian. So then they can't use that elsewhere," Professor Germond said.

Yet after the attacks, Mr Zelensky said Ukraine should avoid actions that could open an additional front in the space.

"We must be careful. We must do everything to ensure that under no circumstances do we open a new front, but we must be honest. The Iranians and the North Koreans have already attacked us," he told Sky News.

He warned Ukraine would be prepared for any development from Iran.

The Caspian Sea might be in the global spotlight because of Ukraine's recent strikes, but it has been targeted before.

Last August, Ukraine conducted a long-range drone attack on a supply ship in the Caspian port of Olya, which it claimed was loaded with drone components and Iranian munitions.

And in March, Israel targeted dozens of Iranian assets along the Caspian coastline, including missile boats, a shipyard ‌used ⁠to build and repair vessels, and a command centre.
