"What Ukraine is trying to do is to show that they can exercise … [a] type of leverage there, because if vessels in the Caspian think it's too dangerous, if there are many attacks, then the two countries, Russia and Iran, will have to rely on a terrestrial route that's less good for many reasons," Professor Germond said.

If the tactic sounds familiar, it is because Tehran has used a similar strategy with great effect in the Strait of Hormuz.

The tankers that reignited the war The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers.

Ukraine's strikes fell on the eve of Mr Zelenskyy's visit to the United States, and Professor Germond said the timing of the two events is significant and may have been designed to generate support for Kyiv within the Trump administration.

Ahead of his visit, Mr Zelenskyy had warned of Russia and Iran's close military collaboration and told Sky News that Tehran had been responsible for transferring new technologies to Moscow.

"I think in the current context, it's quite obvious that it's a way to demonstrate to Trump that the winner is Zelenskyy, not Vladimir Putin," Professor Germond said.

"Zelenskyy is currently managing to convince Trump that he's the strong man, and that's important because Ukraine still depends on weapons and support from the West in general, the US in particular," Professor Germond said.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) relies on military aid from Donald Trump and the US. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The Ukrainian leader met with Mr Trump on Tuesday, local time, and said the two leaders discussed securing more air defence capabilities for Kyiv and "several other ideas that could help".

Russia's economic lifeline

For some time now, technologies and materials relevant to sustaining both Iran and Russia's war economies have moved through the Caspian Sea.

That is partly because it is insulated from Western sanction pressure, with a treaty of cooperation struck between the five countries that border the Caspian stipulating that no nation can grant entry to third-party military assets.

"It means that none of those countries around the Caspian Sea is allowed to ask, for example, the US to send military assets to the Caspian. It wouldn't be legal," Professor Germond said.

The Caspian Sea therefore functions as a critical node for Russia and Iran.

"For Russia, because of the sanctions since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Caspian Sea has become more important for trade. And for Iran, it's the same," Professor Germond said.

For its part, Iran has vowed Ukraine's attack will not go unanswered.

In a post on X, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the strikes on ships "a blatant UN Charter violation" and claimed it had been "done at Israel's behest to drag Europe into its war". He offered no evidence to support the allegation.

Mr Araghchi said he had also discussed the incident with both the European Union's top diplomat Kaja Kallas and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

He said he made clear that Ukraine's action "cannot go unanswered".

World.title: See how the price of everything has changed with inflation
World.content:
The cost of most everyday items is up. Here's by how much.

Good news: inflation has eased slightly. Bad news: it continues to remain stubbornly high.

With annual inflation this week coming in at 3.8 per cent, it has cooled the prospect of an interest rate hike in August.

But the figure is still higher than what the Reserve Bank of Australia and the federal government would like.

Below, we've tracked exactly what's going on with prices, from rent and eggs to holidays and insurance.

It's worth noting electricity sits first and foremost on the list. Its big, all-at-once jump is largely due to the removal of various government subsidies that had helped people cover soaring power costs mostly caused by the war in Ukraine.

sits first and foremost on the list. Its big, all-at-once jump is largely due to the removal of various government subsidies that had helped people cover soaring power costs mostly caused by the war in Ukraine. You'll also notice a decrease in the price of automotive fuel . Surging oil prices due to the Iran war prompted the federal government to cut the fuel excise. Sadly, for many, that's a discount which is set to expire on August 2.

. Surging oil prices due to the Iran war prompted the federal government to cut the fuel excise. Sadly, for many, that's a discount which is set to expire on August 2. Use the controls to select different time periods and categories.

About the data

Data is from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), specifically the June 2026 Consumer Price Index release, retrieved via the ABS Data API. The ABC published a version of this article last quarter using data from the March release.

The change over three months and one year is calculated from monthly CPI data.

The monthly CPI series is relatively new and only available for all categories since April 2024, so the figures displayed when "Since COVID" is selected use quarterly CPI data from the same June 2026 ABS release.

In the category "Other food products" n.e.c. stands for "not elsewhere classified".

World.title: Solar is cheap, but building enough of it can be difficult
World.content:
When it comes to domestic solar and battery installations, Australia is a trendsetter.

More than four million homes now have rooftop solar, and in the past year more than 450,000 household batteries were installed. At times during the day, there is so much solar energy in the grid that in some states power is being offered for free during a midday window.

But to truly transform our economy requires solar energy to be installed cheaply and at an industrial scale, according to a new white paper by the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA).

"Work is well underway to make sure that we achieve our goals in cell and module efficiency, which is a critical thing to unlock," ARENA CEO Darren Miller said.

" What's been harder is getting momentum in the deployment of solar at scale at very low costs. "

ARENA has set an aspirational goal known as 30-30-30 — solar panels with 30 per cent efficiency, installed at 30 cents per watt, by 2030. Even if Australia doesn't hit every part of that target, Mr Miller said it helped focus attention on the scale and speed of deployment needed to make solar cheap enough for new industries.

Solar panels themselves are now a relatively small part of the overall cost of building a solar farm.

"The large majority of the cost structure is those heavy civil works, the pouring of concrete, the drilling of holes for pilings, the steel, the cables, and obviously the manual labour involved," Mr Miller said.

To help, ARENA has been investing in technologies and companies designed to automate construction, such as robotic solar panel installers, automated piling systems, and modular solar arrays that can be deployed quickly.

Drones are another technology ARENA is investing in, helping to automate monitoring of large solar projects. (Supplied: ARENA)

Putting a dozen solar panels on a suburban roof is a world away from installing millions more across the vast expanses of the Pilbara.

Until now, these projects have been largely carried out by teams of itinerant workers, if they can be found.

But a company called Luminous Robotics is trying to streamline the process, according to Mr Miller.

"They have these autonomous robots called Lumis that can move around a solar field and place modules in the right positions and then ultimately place those modules onto the racks without human intervention," he said.

"We have a shortage of skilled workers that we can deploy in remote areas.

" So the more robots we can use as part of skilled labour, the better. "

Lumi robots helping to lift and install solar panels. (Supplied: Luminous Robotics)

That is not to mention the more than 30-kilogram weight of each solar panel a person might have to lift over and over again in 40-plus temperatures.

"Robots can do a much better job in a much safer way at picking and placing modules on racks, with humans being quality control, control of the robots, and ultimately doing those fine-grained bits of work that robots can't yet do," Mr Miller said.

There is also an Australian company ARENA has backed called 5B, which trucks in prefabricated concertina-style solar arrays to site and unfolds them with a forklift, bypassing the need to build foundational infrastructure.

Alice Lang, 5B's chief of staff and a solar photovoltaic engineer herself, said traditional solar farms were often built by taking "all of the sticks and bits and pieces and nuts and bolts to site" and assembling them there.

The company is based in Adelaide, where the arrays are prefabricated and loaded into shipping containers.

The 5B Maverick is an accordion-style prefabricated solar array that can be deployed in under an hour. (Supplied: 5B)

Ms Lang said once logistics were organised and a site had been prepared, some companies using the technology had been able to install about one megawatt of solar in a day with a team of just four people. That is four people installing enough capacity to supply the annual electricity use of roughly 300 homes.

"Rather than hundreds of people lifting modules above their heads and putting them onto an array, you would see someone in a forklift unrolling a solar array," Ms Lang said.

She pointed to the Bellevue Gold project in Western Australia, where 5B's technology has been used as part of a hybrid energy system with solar, wind and storage to help decarbonise its mining operations.

The Bellvue gold mine in Western Australia runs on 80-90 per cent renewable energy, and uses 5B solar arrays. (Supplied: ARENA)

While solar panels have become cheaper globally, Australia has struggled to match China's rapid decline in project costs. Utility-scale solar installations in Australia still cost around one-and-a-half times as much as they do in China.

China turns into the world's first electrostate China has put its economic might behind renewable technologies in a desire to stop relying on imported fossil fuels.

Ms Lang said Australia's role was not to copy China's manufacturing scale, but to play to its strengths.

"Australia still has is these incredibly strong research institutions and these connections between research institutions like UNSW and other universities and industry to find ways to make use of the technologies that we are developing in building the economy that we all want," she said.

A renewable global economy

The vision of the ARENA white paper is more than just decarbonising Australia's electricity system. It argues ultra-low-cost solar could help underpin future industries like green iron, hydrogen production and critical minerals processing.

That would require enormous amounts of low-cost renewable electricity, but Climate Energy Finance director Tim Buckley said Australia was well placed to become what he described as a renewable energy superpower.

Inside mining's 'messy' energy transition BHP and Rio Tinto have put their two battery-electric trucks on show, but is an aversion to risk stifling meaningful change?

"We've got some of the best wind and solar resources in the world," he said.

"We have huge capital reserves in the superannuation system, and we are a trusted export partner to North Asia in particular."

Mr Buckley said cheaper renewable energy could do more than generate electricity, potentially supporting more processing and manufacturing onshore instead of simply exporting raw resources.

"Rather than just aluminium, we export green aluminium," he said.

" Rather than iron ore, we export green iron, and rather than lithium spodumene, we export lithium hydroxide powered by firmed renewables. "

Australia currently has about 12 GW of utility-scale solar connected to the National Electricity Market (NEM).

The average daily electricity demand across the NEM, which excludes Western Australia and the Northern Territory, is a fraction of what would be needed to power those new export industries.

In the future, ARENA's Darren Miller envisages something closer to a parallel energy system, with thousands of gigawatts of solar built in remote areas to support mining and manufacturing.

Due to the abundance of unused landmass and sunshine, Mr Miller sees a unique opportunity for Australia.

"The opportunity set here around ultra-low-cost solar and the opportunity to play a global role in commodity markets towards net zero is an order of magnitude bigger than the opportunity to decarbonise our grid," Mr Miller said.

" We see an opportunity for 1,000 gigawatts of solar to be deployed in remote areas of Australia making these green commodities. "

'Vested interests' stall progress

While the ideas are inspiring, Australia is not China, and the democratic process can be slow and bureaucratic.

Batteries now cheaper than gas for peak demand power supply Falling battery costs and a data centre-fuelled dash for gas have overturned decades of accepted wisdom.

"Planning, coordination, social licence for transmission lines, the time it takes to get environmental approval, those are the barriers and the challenges around the speed of deployment of solar," Mr Miller said.

But for Tim Buckley, a former banking analyst, the challenge is less about engineering and more about investor confidence.

"We're not a communist state, we don't have a dictator, but what we do have is a messy democracy, and we have vested interests," he said.

" We're a major fossil fuel producer and vested interests are getting in the way of the science, and they're getting in the way of investor confidence. "

Renewable energy now contributes to roughly 50 per cent of electricity demand in Australia, transforming the grid. Now Darren Miller wants to transform the economy.

"There will be nothing more important to Australia's economic advantage going forward towards 2050 than very, very cheap electrons made at scale in Australia."

World.title: Australians fork out $4 million for failing to vote in federal election
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of Australians who failed to cast their vote at last year's federal election have paid millions of dollars in penalties.

The ABC can reveal the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) dished out "apparent failure to vote" notices to more than 1.3 million people following the 2025 poll.

All enrolled adult Australians must vote in federal and state elections under the nation's compulsory voting policy.

About 90 per cent of eligible Australians voted in the 2025 election.

But those who fail to fulfil their civic duty in elections face a $20 administrative penalty, or they could cop a fine of up to $330 if the matter is referred to court.

As of May, 207,000 people had elected to pay the administrative penalty, which means they have collectively forked out about $4.15 million.

The money from the penalties goes into the federal government's consolidated revenue fund.

The AEC is pursuing some people who failed to vote through the court system. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Quarter of a million excused from voting

More than 250,000 non-voters, as of June, will not be punished by the AEC after providing a "valid and sufficient" reason for not casting their ballot.

The AEC also confirmed 710,000 electors had not responded to their apparent failure to vote notice by the relevant deadline.

"A failure to respond can of course occur by choice, due to a recent residential move or due to other practical reasons," the election watchdog said in a statement, adding electors may be punished for not providing a valid reason.

"Like all legal matters, we weigh up a number of factors before commencing any action."

The AEC said court action against non-voters had "progressed" and many were finalised, however final figures were not yet available.

Compulsory voting rare around the world

The 1.3 million notices issued for the 2025 poll is similar to the roughly 1.27 million notices given out following the 2022 election.

Australian National University associate professor in politics Jill Sheppard described compulsory voting as a "net good".

"The obvious good is that it gets everyone involved in elections," she said.

"And in Australia that means, even if you feel like the parties don't necessarily speak for you, even if you feel like you're unrepresented by people in Canberra, you still feel engaged with the political process.

"The downside of compulsory voting is that the parties assume that we will always turn out to vote, no matter how boring or how unresponsive or how out of touch they may seem, and that can breed laziness."

ANU political scientist Jill Sheppard says Australia is one of very few countries that has compulsory voting. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Dr Sheppard also pointed out compulsory voting across the world was "so rare" — and said Australians were amongst the most active voters in democratic countries.

"At any given time, less than two dozen countries in the world would have some form compulsory voting," she said.

" To combine compulsory voting with such a liberal democracy is even rarer. "

According to the AEC data, the electorate of Durack in Western Australia had the highest number of apparent failure to vote notices, with 20,000 issued.

Rounding out the top five seats with the most non-voters were Leichhardt, Kennedy, Forde, and Herbert — which are all located in Queensland.

The electorate where the smallest number of notices was issued was Franklin in Tasmania, where fewer than 3,500 people did not turn up to the polls.

This was followed by Clark, also in Tasmania, and then Corangamite, Kooyong, and Menzies — all located in Victoria.

World.title: Drug company backdown sees lifesaving cancer treatment offered for free
World.content:
Women with breast cancer or endometriosis will have free and continued access to a lifesaving drug, after a pharmaceutical giant bowed to widespread pressure and committed to supplying the medication in Australia indefinitely.

Before the eleventh-hour backdown, the ABC spoke to several women who were contemplating removing their ovaries because they were so fearful of the prospect of going without the drug.

As revealed by the ABC last month, AstraZeneca, the maker of lifesaving breast cancer and endometriosis medication goserelin 3.6mg implant, said it would pull the drug from both the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and the private market in November.

Cancer and endometriosis drug discontinued Patients have been left frustrated and scared after learning that a life-saving breast cancer and endometriosis drug is to be pulled from shelves.

AstraZeneca said the Australian price for the product, sold as Zoladex, was too low "making it unsustainable to supply the medicine on the PBS".

The move triggered criticism from advocates, patients and the broader public and a Change.org petition calling for urgent action gathered more than 42,000 signatures in a matter of weeks.

AstraZeneca had initially promised to set up a six-month access program to provide the medication for free to those without alternative treatments.

However it has since announced it would supply the medication indefinitely to those whose doctors determine there are no other suitable treatments available.

"This includes patients who are currently prescribed and patients who may need to be prescribed the implant as a treatment option after 1 November 2026," an AstraZeneca spokesperson said.

Pharmaceutical commentator Paul Cross said the nature of pricing negotiations meant it was likely more financially advantageous for AstraZeneca to supply Zoladex in Australia for free, than create a low pricing precedent for other countries.

Diabetics pay thousands of dollars a year for drug still not on the PBS The "broken" process behind listing medication on the PBS contributes to hundreds of thousands of Australians with diabetes missing out on subsidised lifesaving medication, according to the peak industry body.

He said international reference pricing — where governments can use lower prices in other countries as a negotiating benchmark — was probably a factor behind the company's decision to remove Zoladex from the PBS.

"It's quite possible that because it's been provided for free it's not included in the benchmark and that's one of the workarounds," he said.

Mr Cross, who worked as an advisor on the PBS for the Howard government and used to be a pharmaceutical executive, said Australia could become increasingly vulnerable to decisions made to keep prices high overseas. That could include drugs being withdrawn from sale in Australia.

"International reference pricing has been a feature of the global pharmaceutical industry for many, many years," he said.

"Because you've got two behemoths now in the US and China being far more assertive on pricing, I think it's fair for Australian patients who are already accessing medicines to contemplate whether they could be the next group to be impacted."

'If I don't have Zoladex… game over'

The medication, delivered monthly as a pellet injected under the skin, stops a patients' ovaries from producing oestrogen, a hormone which promotes the growth of many forms of breast cancer and can fuel endometriosis.

Katie Elson said because her type of cancer was hormonally fuelled, stopping Zoladex could cause it to grow out of control and claim her life. (Supplied)

Victorian public servant Katie Elson has had breast cancer twice and said because her type of cancer was hormonally fuelled, stopping Zoladex could cause it to grow out of control and claim her life.

At just 31 she said the uncertainty surrounding the drug's availability meant she had considered removing her ovaries.

"It's either that or die," she said.

" If I don't have Zoladex, my cancer will spread, I'll produce oestrogen again and then game over. "

Ms Elson said despite AstraZeneca's latest decision, she remained fearful about accessing the drug.

"It does feel like they could still pull the carpet from under us at any time," she said.

"I will definitely still consider a hysterectomy, which is sad, but how can you trust a drug company that says one thing and then switches overnight?"

'Groundbreaking' cancer drug no longer available at public hospitals Men with aggressive prostate cancer who were being treated with a groundbreaking drug have been told the therapy is no longer available at public hospitals.

Other women, like Ella Somerville Glover from Sydney, have also considered surgical options.

The 35-year-old research scientist was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2020 and has been on Zoladex since then — taking a break to have her son, who is now just over one year old.

"Anything I can do, no matter the side effects, I'm happy to do it if it gives me a better chance," she said.

Cancer treatment was a long, bumpy road for Ms Glover that involved surgery, chemotherapy and radiation, before she started hormone therapy.

Ella Somerville Glover, 35, has been on Zoladex for about six years — taking a break to have her son, Pippin. (ABC News: Mary Lloyd)

She said finding out she might not be able to access the drug she was relying on to keep her cancer free had created anxiety for herself and her family.

Before the full access scheme was announced by AstraZeneca, she spoke to her oncologist about surgically removing her ovaries.

It was a choice she was uncomfortable with: she wanted another child, but also wanted to ensure she watched her son grow up.

"Your focus is so on the baby that you've got and making sure that you're here for them," she said.

PBS lifeline for MS patients Health Minister Mark Butler has accepted independent advice for a rapid review of MS drugs to ensure they remain available on the PBS.

An estimated 8,600 patients were dispensed Zoladex in the first three months of the year, according to health department figures.

The drug is also available as a 10.8mg dose administered every 12 weeks, but that formulation is currently only approved and on the PBS in Australia for prostate cancer patients.

That means any woman prescribed the drug to treat breast cancer would have to pay about $700 for each dose privately.

Many of the women the ABC spoke to said they could not afford that.

"It feels like to the people who are reliant on Zoladex, like a big middle finger," Ms Elson said.

Rachelle Panitz, CEO of advocacy group SoBrave, said uncertainty about Zoladex had added to an already stressful time for many women.

She said there were still aspects of the access program they wanted to clarify.

AstraZenca announced it would supply Zoladex indefinitely to those whose doctors determine there are no other suitable treatments available. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"We just need some reassurance about whether that is going to be something long-term or if we can actually rely on that," she said.

The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC), which advises the government about what goes on the PBS, will meet today to discuss listing an alternative medication, known as triptorelin, which also suppresses hormones like oestrogen and testosterone.

'They should realise the people this impacts'

The federal government has recently been in several protracted, high-profile stand-offs with major pharmaceutical companies over the way the PBS works.

In April, Eli Lilly withdrew diabetes drug Mounjaro from the PBS listing process, arguing the price Australia was willing to pay was too low.

MS drugs facing PBS uncertainty The latest PBS stoush means thousands of people with MS are at risk of being forced to pay $33,000 a year for lifesaving medication.

Earlier this month, a pricing dispute with two major drug manufacturers who make multiple sclerosis medications sparked fears people with MS would have to pay tens of thousands of dollars to access life-changing treatments. The government later confirmed the drugs would remain on the PBS.

When drugs are placed on the PBS, patients are able to receive their medications at a small portion of the cost: currently $25, or $7.70 for concession card holders.

US pharmaceutical companies have long been lobbying against the scheme, arguing its pricing processes undervalue innovation and threaten billions of dollars in lost sales.

A 2024 review of the PBS — known as the Health Technology Assessment (HTA) review made several recommendations aimed at streamlining processes and expediting the time it takes to list medicines on the scheme.

An advisory group is guiding the government's response to that review, but the pharmaceutical industry has argued there is a need for more urgent action.

"We know patients want more certainty and faster access to cutting edge medicine and treatments," Health Minister Mark Butler said.

"That's why our government is working through the recommendations of the HTA review, so Australians can get faster access to the best medicines and therapies, at a cost that patients and the community can afford."

Ella Somerville Glover, with her partner Sam and son Pippin. (ABC News: Mary Lloyd)

Ms Glover said she thought it was strange that a company would decide to withdraw a drug for "commercial reasons" then announce they would provide it for free.

"I'm not a commercial decision," she said.

"I'm a person. I have a family, I have friends, I have people that love me."

Ms Elson urged drug companies and governments to remember vulnerable people were impacted by their decisions.

"They should realise the people this impacts — and it's not just a board full of suits," she said.

"It's people like myself who have used Zoladex for years to maintain their life or preserve their fertility going through the worst time of their lives."

World.title: Fauci faces contempt finding after pleading Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCoronavirus pandemic Fauci faces contempt finding after pleading Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins Michael Koziol Updated July 30, 2026 — 5:11am ,first published 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Former US chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci faces being held in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about the pandemic’s origins at a heated public hearing, citing his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself. Fauci, an infectious diseases expert who helped steer the US through the pandemic – first under Donald Trump and then under Joe Biden – was summoned to provide evidence about long-held claims that US-funded research in Wuhan led to the virus’ outbreak. Dr Anthony Fauci appears before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the Capitol. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The 85-year-old, who retired in 2022, accused Republican committee chairman Rand Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. He made a brief opening statement and then refused to answer any questions, including about the day of the week or the colour of his tie. “The sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something – anything – that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’,” Fauci said of Paul.



“Therefore, although it pains me to do so ... under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.” Republican lawmakers still attempted to question Fauci over the ensuing three hours, prompting him to plead the Fifth each time. Fox News reported that he invoked the amendment 111 times. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The high-profile hearing came just two days after Paul – Fauci’s long-time congressional nemesis – released more than 1000 pages from the doctor’s personal diary during the pandemic. Among other things, the entries painted a picture of a health bureaucrat who, having become the public face of the pandemic, meticulously tracked his media appearances and how he was being portrayed in various TV, newspaper and magazine profiles.



“The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable,” he wrote after a “very flattering” front-page piece about him in The Washington Post in May 2020. Related Article Coronavirus pandemic Leaked diary reveals US COVID chief’s view on a ‘rambling’ Trump and his own fame “It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world.” Fauci’s diary included appearances on Australia’s 60 Minutes and a discussion with the Doherty Institute’s director Sharon Lewin, who “said that I am a ‘household name’ in Australia”. In late October 2020, as Melbourne emerged from its record-breaking COVID lockdown, Fauci praised the actions of then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews.



“The Australians had zero new infections in the entire city of Melbourne yesterday proving that pure public health measures such a mandatory mask wearing ($1000.00 fine) and avoiding crowds actually works,” Fauci wrote on October 27, 2020. The primary purpose of Paul’s committee hearing, five years after the pandemic subsided, was to interrogate Fauci about US government-funded research at a laboratory in Wuhan, China where some believe COVID-19 originated. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The National Institutes of Health (NIH) for years gave grants to a New York non-profit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to help conduct “gain of function” research with Chinese laboratories studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats.



Gain of function research is the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impacts. It includes general research as well as especially risky experiments. Fauci and the NIH have long maintained that the viruses studied using EcoHealth Alliance funding were genetically distinct from the one that caused COVID-19, including in his private diary entries. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul accused Fauci of semantics. David Schertler, Anthony Fauci’s lawyer, is escorted out of the hearing room by security after being ejected by the Republican chairman. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “When you defended this research you described its benefits in the broadest terms,” he said. “But when Congress demanded accountability, you hid behind the narrowest possible definition. You can’t have it both ways.” At one point, one of Fauci’s lawyers, David Schertler, attempted to speak from the witness table on behalf of his client, leading Paul to ultimately order his removal from the room.



“You’re disputing the proceedings. You are not recognised, sir,” Paul said. “Security, please remove him from the room.” Some people in the gallery applauded, and Schertler was escorted outside by a security guard. Paul promised there would be “repercussions” for Fauci’s failure to answer questions. For years, the libertarian-leaning Republican senator has accused Fauci of lying to Congress over the NIH funding of coronavirus research, and called for him to be indicted. US President Joe Biden with Anthony Fauci and Kizzmekia Corbett at the National Institutes of Health in Maryland. Bloomberg In his opening statement, Fauci pointed out he briefed or testified before Congress “well over 200 times” during his 38 years as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. That included multiple appearances during and after the pandemic, including “several days-long transcribed interviews, answering questions about the very issues that are now the subject of this hearing”.



Before leaving office in 2025, Biden pre-emptively pardoned Fauci for any offences he may have committed in his official roles between January 1, 2014 and January 19, 2025, Biden’s final day. Paul argued the pardon nullified Fauci’s capacity to plead the Fifth. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul specifically asked Fauci whether, during the period of his pardon, he destroyed any federal records, or instructed anyone else to. Fauci also pleaded the Fifth to that question. Anthony Fauci with President Donald Trump in April 2020 as the pandemic took hold. AP Paul said the committee would vote next week on whether to find Fauci in contempt. “He has cited a privilege that is unsupported because of his blanket pardon, and because he waived the privilege by testifying at the start.” The Department of Justice will then decide whether to bring criminal charges through a grand jury. “All I can do is recommend prosecution,” Paul told reporters.



Democrats defended Fauci. Gary Peters, the top Democrat on the committee, said Wednesday’s hearing was a witch-hunt, abuse of congressional power and re-litigation of the past. Related Article Coronavirus pandemic The married scientists torn apart by a COVID bioweapon theory “One-sided investigations designed to validate pre-determined conclusions do not serve the American people,” he said. Republicans rounded on Fauci following Wednesday’s hearing. “[During the pandemic] there was no camera he couldn’t find. No interview he couldn’t give. No American life he wouldn’t micromanage,” said Republican senator Ted Cruz of Texas.



“Today, when the country finally demanded answers, the man who never stopped talking suddenly went silent.” Republican senator Josh Hawley, who tried to get Fauci to answer questions about the colour of his tie or the carpet in front of him, said: “No honest person pleads the Fifth.” Trump posted on Truth Social saying he warned Biden at the time that Fauci “either didn’t have a clue or was dishonest”. Biden “went on to give Fauci vast destructive power”, Trump said. “The rest is history!” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The high-profile man, the extortion case, and the ‘unusual’ step to suppress it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It only took 50 seconds. In the final moments of a public committee hearing, Queensland’s shadow attorney-general asked a question that, ironically, moved the remainder of the session behind closed doors. The symbolic act was the latest twist in a Queensland extortion case that has been shrouded in secrecy since it first emerged in a local courtroom in Far North Queensland, and briefly came to light in the Wild West of social media. The identity of a high-profile man embroiled in the Cairns case, and the fight to unmask him, has sparked concern and curiosity in Queensland’s most influential circles. Intense secrecy surrounds an extortion case being heard in Cairns Magistrates Court. Cloe Read Changes to Queensland law could even follow. Leading criminal lawyer Terry O’Gorman, known for his work in the Fitzgerald Inquiry, believes the saga should prompt the state to seriously consider reforming suppression laws. While the press have been ordered not to report details of the allegations, this has only fuelled interest in the case. The media will on Friday seek to have a non-publication order on the man’s identity overturned. Last Friday, Labor’s Meaghan Scanlon was the latest to ask questions publicly. With LNP Deputy Speaker Jon Krause about to bring a budget estimates session probing police spending to a close, Scanlon made a final intervention.



The Gold Coast-based Labor MP raised a point of order, declaring people “have a right to know the cost of the King’s Counsel to protect the identity of the reported high-profile man”. Scanlon requested the committee shift into a private hearing to ask acting Police Commissioner Brett Pointing and Police Minister Dan Purdie about the bill to taxpayers. Shadow attorney-general Meaghan Scanlon has raised questions about the case in Cairns. Krause accepted. With two minutes left in the session, held in the state’s abolished upper house, he closed the hearing to the public. And that was that. Speaking to media outside the chamber shortly after, Scanlon was asked about the confidential meeting. She noted there were parliamentary restrictions on revealing details of such sessions, and highlighted the government of the day’s absolute control over parliamentary process. “Ultimately, it’s a matter for them,” Scanlon said of the justice committee’s LNP members and chair. It was the second time in as many months the opposition had asked questions in parliament about the bill police have racked up in their fight to uphold the suppression order, and the second time those questions were blocked.



Scanlon and Labor have flagged plans to formally dissent one such ruling by Speaker and Condamine LNP MP Pat Weir, which would likely happen when MPs return to George Street in late August. But the opposition isn’t the first to air concerns over the case; for weeks, it has raised questions about transparency in Queensland’s justice system. Queensland parliament. Matt Dennien Local reporters in Cairns first became aware of the case when prominent defence barrister Brydie Bilic appeared in the court to represent her client, who cannot be named under the current orders. In that proceeding, the name of the high-profile man was also aired, before a suppression order was eventually put over the case. A member of the public in the court who allegedly published the name of the prominent man was also charged. There are limited details the press can report. The man, known only as “MM”, is not facing any charges himself.



O’Gorman, the vice-president of the Queensland Council for Civil Liberties, says there is clearly tension between open courts, open justice, the right of the media to know, and the public interest. He says Queensland’s current suppression laws should be examined. An alternative would be an Open Courts Act, similar to Victoria’s, which was brought in amid concerns suppression orders were being granted too often across courts in the state. Terry O’Gorman. Robertson O'Gorman Solicitors “The law of suppression in Queensland is such that once [this case] is concluded, serious consideration needs to be given to making a referral to the Queensland Law Reform Commission as to whether we should follow Victoria and put all of the Queensland law, in relation to suppression of names in civil and criminal cases, under an act of parliament,” O’Gorman says. He says the suppression order in the Cairns case was an unusual step. “It would be overstating it for me to say it is unprecedented, but it is a pretty unusual step. “Lawyers and journalists interested in the principles of open justice and how courts balance the competing issues of open justice, freedom of the media to report, versus unnecessary destruction of personal reputation, is a centrally important issue in this whole area of suppression of names.”



The media has sought to fight the case on the grounds of open justice. Andrew O’Brien KC, representing several media outlets, including this masthead, told the court last month there was no evidence that lifting the suppression order and identifying the man would in turn identify the complainant. Acting Magistrate Gelma Meoli ultimately ruled to uphold the police order for suppression. She told the court non-publication orders were made in blackmail and extortion cases, and if threats were not suppressed, victims of this type of offending would not come forward with their complaints. The decision has since been taken to the Supreme Court of Cairns for a judicial review, expected to be heard on Friday. Andrew Hemming, an associate law professor at University of Southern Queensland, says there is a high bar for a suppression order. In terms of the media’s judicial review, the question would be whether the magistrate was correct in assuming all three people involved in the case must have their identities suppressed. Hemming says the magistrate has three options: the suppression order stands; it gets lifted, but only for the man; or it gets lifted for the man and the defendant. Kristy Bell, director of Bell Criminal Lawyers, says suppression orders in Queensland are generally rare, given the onus is usually on the applicant to establish why an order should be made.

World.title: Even by Japan’s high standards, this scenic train is exceptional
World.content:
★★★★★ Reviews & adviceTrain journeys Even by Japan’s high standards, this scenic train is exceptional Kristie Kellahan July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The train: Kintetsu Shimakaze, Japan Route Osaka-Namba to Toba (Ise-Shima)

Osaka-Namba to Toba (Ise-Shima) Distance 152 kilometres

152 kilometres Operator Kintetsu

Kintetsu Class Premium express

Premium express Frequency Osaka to Ise-Shima, return, Wednesday to Monday; Kyoto to Ise-Shima, return, Thursday to Tuesday; Nagoya to Ise-Shima, return, Friday to Wednesday. The journey The train’s generous windows have been designed with sightseeing in mind. Osaka-Namba Station to Toba Station, a key jumping-off point for Ise-Shima National Park and Japan’s most sacred shrine, Ise Jingu. I’m onboard the Kintetsu Shimakaze (“Island Wind”) premium sightseeing express train heading to Kashikojima, with a scheduled duration of just under two hours at speeds up to 130mh/h (most of the journey is much slower than the top speed). This popular train is a show pony, not a workhorse, designed for sightseeing with ultra-comfortable, leather reclining seats, observation cars, large windows, an upscale dining car and luxurious private compartments.



Boarding 



This is the most luxurious train seat I’ve ever seen in Japan. It feels more like I’m flying international business class: spacious and opulent in a soft leather that looks either pale green or yellow, depending on the light. There are buttons to move the headrest and footrest, an automatic recline, and a massage function built into the seat back. Every detail has been carefully considered: the fold-down tray table is adjustable, there’s a coat hook and handbag hook, each seat has its own power outlet and a button to control window blinds. There’s fast, free Wi-Fi, plus a Shimakaze Channel that livestreams the driver’s view. Baggage Passengers may bring up to two pieces of luggage free of charge, provided they weigh no more than 30 kilograms each and total dimensions of each don’t exceed 250 centimetres. There are free secure lockers, spacious overhead racks and integrated luggage storage spaces in every carriage. Food + drink Counter seating in the cafe car offers panoramic views.



The two-level cafe car is the heart of the refreshment action, designed to showcase the flavours of the Ise-Shima region. Counter seating offers panoramic views, while comfortable lounges allow for kicking back with a cuppa. Local dishes on the menu include Matsusaka beef curry (a prestigious wagyu brand), Ise lobster miso soup and a Shimakaze bento box featuring seasonal ingredients. As we’re in Japan, there’s also excellent beer, sake and hot tea available. One more thing … Still hungry after a trip to the cafe car? In-seat service will be along shortly. In-seat service is offered from a cart piled high with fresh bento boxes, coffee, cold drinks and souvenirs. The price



Related Article Train journeys The world’s most affordable luxury train journeys (from as little as $14) ¥7730 ($68) for premium or ¥5150 ($45) for a basic fare. Kintetsu is a private railway company, so the Japan Rail (JR) Pass isn’t valid on the Shimakaze sightseeing route. Book premium tickets online and in advance during peak seasons and on weekends. See kintetsu.co.jp The verdict This is a train you should ride at least once to the most sacred shrine region in Japan. My one complaint? I only wish the ride was hours longer. Our rating out of five



★★★★★ The writer travelled as a guest of Mie Prefecture Tourism. See visitmie-japan.travel/en

World.title: A really ‘un-fun club’: How Jennifer Robinson connected Amber Heard and Brittany Higgins
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life A really ‘un-fun club’: How Jennifer Robinson connected Amber Heard and Brittany Higgins Jacqueline Maley July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Jennifer Robinson was a child, she and her sister used to visit their grandma at work. When they were there, they knew they were never to answer the door – there might be a violent man on the other side of it. They knew that the children they played with there were traumatised; their grandmother, Philipa Cracknell, told them so. In the accepting way that children have, they normalised what grandma – a domestic violence survivor herself – did for her job. She worked at Bonnie, a shelter for abused women escaping abusive men, only the second to be established in NSW. “I had a really early experience of understanding the dynamics of domestic violence and how that plays out for families and children,” Robinson says now. “That left a mark on me that I hadn’t appreciated. It wasn’t until my late 30s that I really sat down and asked my grandmother more questions about her life.” Jennifer Robinson turned her legal career fighting for free speech into a crusade for women who are victim-survivors of sexual abuse and assault. Mark Rogers Decades later, Robinson – now a London-based human rights lawyer who had helped defend WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, among other cases – was hanging out with her grandmother on the NSW south coast, on a break from her own work. Her grandmother was depressed and, over a whisky, Robinson asked her why.



“Because, you know, ‘You’re living down the south coast, it’s beautiful, you’re around family, retired, what is wrong with this picture?’” Robinson recounts. “And she was so upset. She said, ‘I just heard the statistics on violence against women on the radio, and it hasn’t gotten better from my time in the refuge.’” That set Robinson thinking. “I was like, ‘I have to find a way to work on violence against women, but what is my way of doing this?’ I’m a free-speech lawyer. What am I going to do?’” And then, Robinson says, “the #MeToo movement happened”. “I was like, ‘OK, I’m a free-speech lawyer. I defend defamation cases. This is what I can do.’” Robinson went on to do it, with great success, most notably in the case of Amber Heard, the actor and ex-wife of actor Johnny Depp. In 2020, Heard gave evidence about the abuse she suffered at the hands of her ex-husband, in the libel suit Depp brought against the UK’s The Sun newspaper, naming him as a “wife beater”.



The court’s decision, that the newspaper’s description of Depp was “substantially true”, and that 12 of the alleged 14 incidents of violence had occurred, should have vindicated her. But in 2022, Depp successfully sued Heard for defamation in a US court, after she wrote an opinion piece for the Washington Post. She didn’t name Depp in the piece but described herself as a survivor of domestic violence. Robinson with Julian Assange after the Wikileaks founder secured his freedom. X.com Heard’s case is the fulcrum of the new Australian film Silenced, adapted from the book How Many More Women?, which Robinson co-wrote with Dr Keina Yoshida. The documentary film, from International Emmy-award winning producers Selina Miles and Blayke Hoffman, is about the weaponisation of defamation law against women who speak out about sexual assault and abuse. It makes the case that the legal system is being used to discredit, intimidate and bankrupt victim-survivors. It focuses on three women to make its point: Heard, Colombian journalist Catalina Ruiz-Navarro, who faced multiple legal suits from Colombian filmmaker Ciro Guerra after she published a #MeToo exposé on him; and finally, Brittany Higgins, who needs no introduction to Australian audiences. In 2021, Higgins did a television interview with journalist Lisa Wilkinson alleging she was raped by fellow political staffer Bruce Lehrmann in 2019.



In the film, Higgins recounts leaving the Parliament House office of their boss, Defence Industry Minister Linda Reynolds, where the assault occurred. “I left, and things were different after that,” she says. “I was different after that.” A 2022 criminal trial was aborted due to juror misconduct, and in 2024 Lehrmann sued Network Ten and Lisa Wilkinson for defamation for airing Higgins’ story. The judgment by the Federal Court’s Justice Michael Lee found, on the balance of probabilities, that Lehrmann had raped Higgins. From left: Robinson, Brittany Higgins and Catalina Ruiz-Navarro in Silenced. Michael Latham Since then, Higgins has herself been sued for defamation, successfully, by her former boss Linda Reynolds. However, that suit does not feature in the film, as the focus is the weaponisation of defamation laws by alleged perpetrators to silence survivors. I meet Robinson and Higgins the morning following the Australian debut of Silenced at the Sydney Film Festival (its international debut was at the Sundance Film Festival in January). Robinson plays delightedly with Higgins’ new baby Freddie, who has accompanied his mother to Sydney from their home in Victoria. After a few minutes, the baby’s father, Higgins’ partner David Sharaz, spirits him away in search of coffee and we settle on sofas to talk about the film.



Both women are wearing blue jeans and the energy between them is easy, with Robinson occasionally taking a protective lead to answer on behalf of Higgins, particularly when it comes to questions on legally contentious topics. “I’m a big believer in the power of storytelling,” Robinson says of the film, on which she is an executive producer. “Speech about violence against women is absolutely in the public interest, when you think about the extent of the problem, how many women in Australia are affected by it. “And as I say, over and over, we can’t begin to tackle it if we can’t talk about it.” Higgins has had a friendship with Robinson ever since the criminal trial of her alleged rapist, Lehrmann, during which Robinson sent her messages of support. It was on the strength of their friendship that Higgins agreed to participate in the film. “It took a while for me to finally go, ‘I’m going to do this’,” Higgins says of her involvement. “I have very natural hesitancy towards a media lens.” But, Higgins adds with a laugh, “she’s a very hard person to say no to”.



The film depicts the heavy psychological toll the litigation takes on all the women, not least because the media spotlight is accompanied by torrents of internet abuse. In the case of Amber Heard, the abuse spilled over into real life. The film shows her arriving at London’s Royal Courts of Justice as Depp’s fans yell misogynistic hatred at her. Related Article Lunch with The international lawyer who specialises in breaking the silence “Honestly, it was horrific,” says Robinson. “I’ve never seen anything like it, and you know, I worked on Julian Assange’s trial. I felt under threat from the most powerful government in the world … but I’ve never been attacked online as I was when I was representing Amber Heard.” Higgins, who has also weathered much internet abuse, not to mention intense and sometimes malicious media scrutiny, says that the treatment “does fundamentally change you in a way that it’s difficult to articulate meaningfully. You definitely become hardened, and you definitely learn to be guarded.” In one poignant scene in the film, Heard and Higgins meet and embrace. “We are in a really, un-fun club,” Heard quips.



Robinson also cops online abuse (according to one charmer, she has a “punchable face, like Amber”). She splits her time between her practice in London, and her home on the NSW south coast. She surfs to unwind, and is in therapy. Robinson says she is concerned by “a real backsliding in women’s rights globally”. I ask Robinson and Higgins what they think of the contemporary backlash against feminism, from the rise of the manosphere, to the elevation of tradwife culture, as well as the pushback against reproductive rights in the United States and other countries. “I mean, to an extent, there’s almost a compliment in there, that we did gain meaningful ground, so much so that it galvanised an opposing force to reclaim territory,” says Higgins. But, she adds, the rise of what she dubs the “online metasphere of misogyny content” has spread into other areas of life.



“That language has become normalised and metabolised, even by politicians,” Higgins says. “The veil has dropped ... people are out and open and saying these things. It’s scary … because I know it will have a trickle-down effect on the next woman who decides to come forward.” Related Article Sunday Life Frances Rings just did something no other Australian has. She leads this year’s Trailblazers Robinson says she is concerned by “a real backsliding in women’s rights globally”. “When there’s a lot of misogyny in the online space and in public discussion … that has a knock-on effect for violence against women. Those two things are connected in very direct ways.” But both women are optimistic about the advances already made, and Robinson says that “I actually don’t think that we can walk back the progress that was made with #MeToo”.



Higgins points to affirmative consent laws, anti-stealthing laws (which criminalise removing or not using a condom without your sexual partner’s consent) and better courtroom protections for alleged victims of sexual assault (reforms she has advocated for) as proof of progress. “As my grandma said, it’s one step forward, two steps back, but then we progress again,” says Robinson. Robinson’s grandmother, who features in the film, is a common thread throughout it. “What I love about my grandmother’s story is she reminds us how recent the gains were,” Robinson says. “She was lucky to have a bank account. When she left my grandfather, she couldn’t get credit to buy bunk beds for my mum and my aunt because she needed her husband’s signature.” Perhaps the greatest act of defiance is survival. Cracknell, now 89 years old, was at the film’s Sydney premiere, glowing with pride and particularly eager to meet Higgins. The two had a long chat, Higgins tells me. Silenced screens at the Melbourne International Film Festival from August 6-23 and in cinemas nationally from September 3. World.title: Visiting wineries is a waste of time. I already know what I like
World.content:
Reviews & adviceFoodie travel Opinion Visiting wineries is a waste of time. I already know what I like Brian Johnston Travel writer July 30, 2026 — 5:00am

July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Some time ago, in the mists of time, probably during the 1990s, cellar doors became a thing. Three decades on and we’re still visiting them. They’ve become a staple of escorted tours and weekend getaways. Let me make a confession. Cellar doors aren’t enjoyable, and I suspect I’m not alone in that view. But it’s the dislike that dare not speak its name, because cellar doors tick trendy traveller boxes: cultured, food-minded, local, experiential, social-media friendly. Illustration: Jamie Brown But I don’t know what the enduring travel fashion for visiting grape farms is all about. Why not pig farms, or pickle farms? I only need to hear about the wine-making process once. And I only have to see a wine cellar once: rows of old barrels (French oak!) festooned with cobwebs in a gloomy dungeon.



Or OK, maybe twice, since others are warehouses with big stainless-steel vats. But I guarantee that the words, “That was a beautiful industrial vat” will never be part of your post-travel dinner conversation. 



About 50 years ago in Australia, the term cellar door could be taken literally. Wine bottles were stored in cool cellars and sold to customers who quickly went on their way. By the 1990s however the emergence of hobbyist winemakers had seen cellar doors become buildings in which passersby tasted wine. They were great for the owners, who benefited from the large margins on each bottle of wine sold. One of the enduring misapprehensions of cellar doors is that you get a bargain. And although many cellar doors are rustic cliches, many have become agro-tourism businesses run by managers who’ve never picked a grape in their lives. Cellar doors then began offering restaurants, shops, museums and concerts. They were no longer simply about buying wine, rather about consuming wine on the spot and being upsold an “experience”. And that’s when cellar doors began to fill up with tour-coach groups, drunken friends, wedding parties, oenophile mansplainers, Instagram poseurs and families with rambunctious kids.



Not many visitors want to buy wine, or to learn much about the skill that goes into winemaking. And fair enough. Most of us already know what types of wine we like. Related Article Western Australia This Aussie wine region is outstanding, even if you don’t drink It doesn’t matter whether the bottle costs $10 or $200, whether you can detect hints of strawberry or old leather, or whether the grapes were picked at midnight under a full moon. You either like it, or you don’t. What’s more, you know you’re never going to pair your wine again with buffalo-milk cheese, or dark chocolate and sea salt. You’re never again going to realise it tastes less acidic after you’ve eaten a macadamia nut than it did before. You want something you can drink after work, or with your daily dinner. Something you can reliably find at your local bottle shop. I say skip the cellar door, and just enjoy the wine-country scenery.

World.title: The type of buyer that just dropped out of the property market
World.content:
PropertyNewsResidential property The type of buyer that just dropped out of the property market Alice Uribe July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The number of first home buyers looking to take out a home loan has fallen in a year even as property prices soften in some parts of the country and investors exit the market. First home buyer demand nationally rose at the end of 2025 and in early 2026, before dropping back in April, data from credit data company Equifax shows. By last month, mortgage demand from new home buyers was down almost 20 per cent compared with the same time in 2025. Higher interest rates, concerns over buying in a falling market, property-related budget reforms and a lack of supply have led to reduced demand from first home hopefuls, experts say. Confidence has also dipped among this cohort, with some now holding back as they wait for property prices to reach a floor. According to Equifax, demand for mortgages from first home buyers jumped by 13.7 per cent in October compared with the year prior. This was bettered only by a 17.1 per cent spike year-on-year in December.



Equifax chief solutions officer Kevin James said its data tracks the number of loan inquiries made where an applicant has never had a mortgage, to determine demand. More first home buyers, he said, looked to enter the market in the second half of 2025 in part due to the October expansion of the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme. “We saw the first home buyers come in … and we saw some real positive stories come out of that,” he said. First home buyer mortgage demand jumped after the federal government expanded the 5 per cent deposit scheme. James Brickwood But by April this year, Equifax data showed demand for first home loans down 2.9 per cent on the same time in 2025. In May, demand was 13.4 per cent lower, and there was a 17.2 per cent year-on-year drop in June. Three rate hikes over 2026 and serviceability challenges had prompted first home buyers to hang back, James said, but now many were also taking a wait-and-see approach, expecting prices to soften as investor demand slows.



“I think people are just waiting to see what’s going to actually happen with interest rates and with pricing,” he said. Cost-of-living pressures, rate hikes and weak consumer sentiment were helping to constrain activity generally, but Dr Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief residential economist, said first home buyers were also facing deposit hurdles and borrowing limits, with some now more cautious. “That caution is driven by the fact that prices overall are falling …they don’t want to buy on a Friday to find out their home is worth less than on a Monday,” she said. Sydney and Melbourne fell more than 3 per cent last quarter. “It means that they’re perhaps feeling apprehensive about buying in a falling market because they obviously don’t want to get into negative equity. But then it also drives this other thought process that, ‘if I wait a bit longer, I might be able to get greater value for money’.”



Domain was expecting minor price falls nationally, with deeper falls in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra, while banks were tipping further falls of about 5 to 10 per cent nationally. Related Article Property prices What the median house price buys around Australia now Jack Elliott, national first home buyer specialist at Alcove Mortgages, highlighted low confidence and a reduction in buying capacity due to higher interest rates. Still, some first-timers were making preparations for the upcoming spring selling season, with inquiries ticking up. “Naturally, winter is always a little bit slower. You’ve got fewer listings, fewer buyers, with fewer properties to purchase,” he said, adding clients reported less competition from investors now. Indeed, investors started to exit the property market after the federal budget in May introduced negative-gearing and capital-gains tax concessions reforms.



According to preliminary Equifax data, there was a 9.8 per cent reduction in demand year-on-year in May from investors, or those with two or more mortgages. By June, there was a 12.7 per cent drop compared with the same time the previous year. “I think people are actually seeing some of the investor market softening,” James said. There is less demand from property investors for mortgages. James Brockwood Enosh Tampoe, a mortgage and finance advisor at Smartmove, agreed there were fewer investors in the market now. But there were also fewer listings as some investors held on to their properties due to grandfathering of negative-gearing arrangements. “If you’re a first home buyer who’s actively looking, you can potentially get one for a good deal there, which a few of my clients have been able to do. But then, in saying that as well, they have obviously a lot less to pick from, given their supply has dropped significantly.”



Related Article Property prices Meet the home owners who don’t mind if their home falls in value KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said while first home buyers were sitting on the sidelines, so were investors. “When you’ve seen the investor activity drop off historically, you see house-price-values growth cool, which is an opportunity for first-time buyers to get into the market,” he said. “But I think, just given levels of uncertainty at the moment, probably … the next six months, everyone’s going to be sort of sitting on their hands, waiting to see what happens with prices, interest rates, and the broader economy.”

World.title: Melbourne Fashion Festival rebrands amid fresh strategic direction
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleFashionMelbourne Fashion Festival Melbourne Fashion Festival rebrands amid fresh strategic direction Courtney Thompson July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The perennial fashion debate pitting Melbourne against Sydney may soon be obsolete as Melbourne Fashion Festival today announces its rebranding to Australian Fashion Festival. The change is part of a suite of updates that seek to deepen the organisation’s commitment to being a consumer-led program, strengthen designer relationships and reinforce their nationwide celebration of Australian fashion. Models Bela Palcio and Trang Nguyen wearing outfits by Australian designers Alemais and Bianca Spender, respectively. Eddie Jim “We need to have a national name because the designers aren’t only exclusive to Victoria,” says Launa Inman, chair of the Australian Fashion Festival board, who explains the festival’s usual two-week program will be expanded to include events all year round. “The fashion industry is changing – consumers now engage with fashion through live events or retail experiences, social media, cultural moments, even destination travel,” she says. “The name change really supported a broader strategy to lift designer engagement, grow our audiences, and then also strengthen our commercial partnerships.”



Though before you rid your wardrobe of black, Inman is quick to note the festival will remain anchored to the Garden City. “It’s still very much going to be based in Melbourne,” she says. “We are not losing sight of our Victorian designers.” Related Article Opinion

Culture wars Which city is better, Sydney or Melbourne? I’m in a unique position to decide Damien Woolnough Fashion editor It’s a move supported by the Australian Fashion Council, which oversees Australian Fashion Week, the separate and more industry-focused event that takes place in Sydney every May. “It’s a good change because Australian designers don’t operate within state boundaries,” says Marianne Perkovic, chair of the Australian Fashion Council. “If we really want to compete and give our designers the best chance to showcase their great talents, we have to start talking nationally, and internationally, about Australian fashion.” The news comes three months after Caroline Ralphsmith resigned as chief executive of the organisation amid a tough period financially.



According to the last financial report, the event filed a loss of $711,390 in 2025, with revenue falling to $4.57 million from $5.75 million in the 2024 financial year. The financial results for the 2026 festival will be released later this year, though festival attendance was up 47 per cent year-on-year. “Our financial wellbeing is very important because without us being financially stable, it’s very difficult to be creative,” Inman says, which also goes to explain why they didn’t replace Ralph with a new chief executive. Rather than installing a new chief executive, they have split the role, hiring Prue Mahar from REA Group and Victorian Racing Group as executive director and Damien Woolnough-Reid (former fashion editor of this masthead) as creative director. “It’s a strategic investment in the leadership, making sure we’ve got absolutely the right team around us to strengthen the momentum for the festival’s future,” says Inman. The approach is welcomed by designer Bianca Spender, who is excited about the festival building upon its offering for consumers to engage with designers and their clothes.



“The festival has a really wonderful atmosphere that is very unique,” Spender says. “There’s a lot of noise out there and we’re living in a virtual world in the way that we absorb clothes. Actually feeling it, seeing how the fabric moves, really engaging with it is so important now more than ever.” Inman agrees: “It’s all about offering those memorable experiences that will help the Australian designers connect emotionally with anyone who loves style.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Fauci faces contempt finding after pleading Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCoronavirus pandemic Fauci faces contempt finding after pleading Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins Michael Koziol Updated July 30, 2026 — 5:11am ,first published 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Former US chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci faces being held in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about the pandemic’s origins at a heated public hearing, citing his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself. Fauci, an infectious diseases expert who helped steer the US through the pandemic – first under Donald Trump and then under Joe Biden – was summoned to provide evidence about long-held claims that US-funded research in Wuhan led to the virus’ outbreak. Dr Anthony Fauci appears before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the Capitol. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The 85-year-old, who retired in 2022, accused Republican committee chairman Rand Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. He made a brief opening statement and then refused to answer any questions, including about the day of the week or the colour of his tie. “The sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something – anything – that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’,” Fauci said of Paul.



“Therefore, although it pains me to do so ... under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.” Republican lawmakers still attempted to question Fauci over the ensuing three hours, prompting him to plead the Fifth each time. Fox News reported that he invoked the amendment 111 times. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The high-profile hearing came just two days after Paul – Fauci’s long-time congressional nemesis – released more than 1000 pages from the doctor’s personal diary during the pandemic. Among other things, the entries painted a picture of a health bureaucrat who, having become the public face of the pandemic, meticulously tracked his media appearances and how he was being portrayed in various TV, newspaper and magazine profiles.



“The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable,” he wrote after a “very flattering” front-page piece about him in The Washington Post in May 2020. Related Article Coronavirus pandemic Leaked diary reveals US COVID chief’s view on a ‘rambling’ Trump and his own fame “It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world.” Fauci’s diary included appearances on Australia’s 60 Minutes and a discussion with the Doherty Institute’s director Sharon Lewin, who “said that I am a ‘household name’ in Australia”. In late October 2020, as Melbourne emerged from its record-breaking COVID lockdown, Fauci praised the actions of then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews.



“The Australians had zero new infections in the entire city of Melbourne yesterday proving that pure public health measures such a mandatory mask wearing ($1000.00 fine) and avoiding crowds actually works,” Fauci wrote on October 27, 2020. The primary purpose of Paul’s committee hearing, five years after the pandemic subsided, was to interrogate Fauci about US government-funded research at a laboratory in Wuhan, China where some believe COVID-19 originated. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert The National Institutes of Health (NIH) for years gave grants to a New York non-profit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to help conduct “gain of function” research with Chinese laboratories studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats.



Gain of function research is the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impacts. It includes general research as well as especially risky experiments. Fauci and the NIH have long maintained that the viruses studied using EcoHealth Alliance funding were genetically distinct from the one that caused COVID-19, including in his private diary entries. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul accused Fauci of semantics. David Schertler, Anthony Fauci’s lawyer, is escorted out of the hearing room by security after being ejected by the Republican chairman. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “When you defended this research you described its benefits in the broadest terms,” he said. “But when Congress demanded accountability, you hid behind the narrowest possible definition. You can’t have it both ways.” At one point, one of Fauci’s lawyers, David Schertler, attempted to speak from the witness table on behalf of his client, leading Paul to ultimately order his removal from the room.



“You’re disputing the proceedings. You are not recognised, sir,” Paul said. “Security, please remove him from the room.” Some people in the gallery applauded, and Schertler was escorted outside by a security guard. Paul promised there would be “repercussions” for Fauci’s failure to answer questions. For years, the libertarian-leaning Republican senator has accused Fauci of lying to Congress over the NIH funding of coronavirus research, and called for him to be indicted. US President Joe Biden with Anthony Fauci and Kizzmekia Corbett at the National Institutes of Health in Maryland. Bloomberg In his opening statement, Fauci pointed out he briefed or testified before Congress “well over 200 times” during his 38 years as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. That included multiple appearances during and after the pandemic, including “several days-long transcribed interviews, answering questions about the very issues that are now the subject of this hearing”.



Before leaving office in 2025, Biden pre-emptively pardoned Fauci for any offences he may have committed in his official roles between January 1, 2014 and January 19, 2025, Biden’s final day. Paul argued the pardon nullified Fauci’s capacity to plead the Fifth. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul specifically asked Fauci whether, during the period of his pardon, he destroyed any federal records, or instructed anyone else to. Fauci also pleaded the Fifth to that question. Anthony Fauci with President Donald Trump in April 2020 as the pandemic took hold. AP Paul said the committee would vote next week on whether to find Fauci in contempt. “He has cited a privilege that is unsupported because of his blanket pardon, and because he waived the privilege by testifying at the start.” The Department of Justice will then decide whether to bring criminal charges through a grand jury. “All I can do is recommend prosecution,” Paul told reporters.



Democrats defended Fauci. Gary Peters, the top Democrat on the committee, said Wednesday’s hearing was a witch-hunt, abuse of congressional power and re-litigation of the past. Related Article Coronavirus pandemic The married scientists torn apart by a COVID bioweapon theory “One-sided investigations designed to validate pre-determined conclusions do not serve the American people,” he said. Republicans rounded on Fauci following Wednesday’s hearing. “[During the pandemic] there was no camera he couldn’t find. No interview he couldn’t give. No American life he wouldn’t micromanage,” said Republican senator Ted Cruz of Texas.



“Today, when the country finally demanded answers, the man who never stopped talking suddenly went silent.” Republican senator Josh Hawley, who tried to get Fauci to answer questions about the colour of his tie or the carpet in front of him, said: “No honest person pleads the Fifth.” Trump posted on Truth Social saying he warned Biden at the time that Fauci “either didn’t have a clue or was dishonest”. Biden “went on to give Fauci vast destructive power”, Trump said. “The rest is history!” With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
