World.title: The high-profile man, the extortion case, and the ‘unusual’ step to suppress it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It only took 50 seconds. In the final moments of a public committee hearing, Queensland’s shadow attorney-general asked a question that, ironically, moved the remainder of the session behind closed doors. The symbolic act was the latest twist in a Queensland extortion case that has been shrouded in secrecy since it first emerged in a local courtroom in Far North Queensland, and briefly came to light in the Wild West of social media. The identity of a high-profile man embroiled in the Cairns case, and the fight to unmask him, has sparked concern and curiosity in Queensland’s most influential circles. Intense secrecy surrounds an extortion case being heard in Cairns Magistrates Court. Cloe Read Changes to Queensland law could even follow. Leading criminal lawyer Terry O’Gorman, known for his work in the Fitzgerald Inquiry, believes the saga should prompt the state to seriously consider reforming suppression laws. While the press have been ordered not to report details of the allegations, this has only fuelled interest in the case. The media will on Friday seek to have a non-publication order on the man’s identity overturned. Last Friday, Labor’s Meaghan Scanlon was the latest to ask questions publicly. With LNP Deputy Speaker Jon Krause about to bring a budget estimates session probing police spending to a close, Scanlon made a final intervention.



The Gold Coast-based Labor MP raised a point of order, declaring people “have a right to know the cost of the King’s Counsel to protect the identity of the reported high-profile man”. Scanlon requested the committee shift into a private hearing to ask acting Police Commissioner Brett Pointing and Police Minister Dan Purdie about the bill to taxpayers. Shadow attorney-general Meaghan Scanlon has raised questions about the case in Cairns. Krause accepted. With two minutes left in the session, held in the state’s abolished upper house, he closed the hearing to the public. And that was that. Speaking to media outside the chamber shortly after, Scanlon was asked about the confidential meeting. She noted there were parliamentary restrictions on revealing details of such sessions, and highlighted the government of the day’s absolute control over parliamentary process. “Ultimately, it’s a matter for them,” Scanlon said of the justice committee’s LNP members and chair. It was the second time in as many months the opposition had asked questions in parliament about the bill police have racked up in their fight to uphold the suppression order, and the second time those questions were blocked.



Scanlon and Labor have flagged plans to formally dissent one such ruling by Speaker and Condamine LNP MP Pat Weir, which would likely happen when MPs return to George Street in late August. But the opposition isn’t the first to air concerns over the case; for weeks, it has raised questions about transparency in Queensland’s justice system. Queensland parliament. Matt Dennien Local reporters in Cairns first became aware of the case when prominent defence barrister Brydie Bilic appeared in the court to represent her client, who cannot be named under the current orders. In that proceeding, the name of the high-profile man was also aired, before a suppression order was eventually put over the case. A member of the public in the court who allegedly published the name of the prominent man was also charged. There are limited details the press can report. The man, known only as “MM”, is not facing any charges himself.



O’Gorman, the vice-president of the Queensland Council for Civil Liberties, says there is clearly tension between open courts, open justice, the right of the media to know, and the public interest. He says Queensland’s current suppression laws should be examined. An alternative would be an Open Courts Act, similar to Victoria’s, which was brought in amid concerns suppression orders were being granted too often across courts in the state. Terry O’Gorman. Robertson O'Gorman Solicitors “The law of suppression in Queensland is such that once [this case] is concluded, serious consideration needs to be given to making a referral to the Queensland Law Reform Commission as to whether we should follow Victoria and put all of the Queensland law, in relation to suppression of names in civil and criminal cases, under an act of parliament,” O’Gorman says. He says the suppression order in the Cairns case was an unusual step. “It would be overstating it for me to say it is unprecedented, but it is a pretty unusual step. “Lawyers and journalists interested in the principles of open justice and how courts balance the competing issues of open justice, freedom of the media to report, versus unnecessary destruction of personal reputation, is a centrally important issue in this whole area of suppression of names.”



The media has sought to fight the case on the grounds of open justice. Andrew O’Brien KC, representing several media outlets, including this masthead, told the court last month there was no evidence that lifting the suppression order and identifying the man would in turn identify the complainant. Acting Magistrate Gelma Meoli ultimately ruled to uphold the police order for suppression. She told the court non-publication orders were made in blackmail and extortion cases, and if threats were not suppressed, victims of this type of offending would not come forward with their complaints. The decision has since been taken to the Supreme Court of Cairns for a judicial review, expected to be heard on Friday. Andrew Hemming, an associate law professor at University of Southern Queensland, says there is a high bar for a suppression order. In terms of the media’s judicial review, the question would be whether the magistrate was correct in assuming all three people involved in the case must have their identities suppressed. Hemming says the magistrate has three options: the suppression order stands; it gets lifted, but only for the man; or it gets lifted for the man and the defendant. Kristy Bell, director of Bell Criminal Lawyers, says suppression orders in Queensland are generally rare, given the onus is usually on the applicant to establish why an order should be made.

World.title: Even by Japan’s high standards, this scenic train is exceptional
World.content:
★★★★★ Reviews & adviceTrain journeys Even by Japan’s high standards, this scenic train is exceptional Kristie Kellahan July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The train: Kintetsu Shimakaze, Japan Route Osaka-Namba to Toba (Ise-Shima)

Osaka-Namba to Toba (Ise-Shima) Distance 152 kilometres

152 kilometres Operator Kintetsu

Kintetsu Class Premium express

Premium express Frequency Osaka to Ise-Shima, return, Wednesday to Monday; Kyoto to Ise-Shima, return, Thursday to Tuesday; Nagoya to Ise-Shima, return, Friday to Wednesday. The journey The train’s generous windows have been designed with sightseeing in mind. Osaka-Namba Station to Toba Station, a key jumping-off point for Ise-Shima National Park and Japan’s most sacred shrine, Ise Jingu. I’m onboard the Kintetsu Shimakaze (“Island Wind”) premium sightseeing express train heading to Kashikojima, with a scheduled duration of just under two hours at speeds up to 130mh/h (most of the journey is much slower than the top speed). This popular train is a show pony, not a workhorse, designed for sightseeing with ultra-comfortable, leather reclining seats, observation cars, large windows, an upscale dining car and luxurious private compartments.



Boarding 



This is the most luxurious train seat I’ve ever seen in Japan. It feels more like I’m flying international business class: spacious and opulent in a soft leather that looks either pale green or yellow, depending on the light. There are buttons to move the headrest and footrest, an automatic recline, and a massage function built into the seat back. Every detail has been carefully considered: the fold-down tray table is adjustable, there’s a coat hook and handbag hook, each seat has its own power outlet and a button to control window blinds. There’s fast, free Wi-Fi, plus a Shimakaze Channel that livestreams the driver’s view. Baggage Passengers may bring up to two pieces of luggage free of charge, provided they weigh no more than 30 kilograms each and total dimensions of each don’t exceed 250 centimetres. There are free secure lockers, spacious overhead racks and integrated luggage storage spaces in every carriage. Food + drink Counter seating in the cafe car offers panoramic views.



The two-level cafe car is the heart of the refreshment action, designed to showcase the flavours of the Ise-Shima region. Counter seating offers panoramic views, while comfortable lounges allow for kicking back with a cuppa. Local dishes on the menu include Matsusaka beef curry (a prestigious wagyu brand), Ise lobster miso soup and a Shimakaze bento box featuring seasonal ingredients. As we’re in Japan, there’s also excellent beer, sake and hot tea available. One more thing … Still hungry after a trip to the cafe car? In-seat service will be along shortly. In-seat service is offered from a cart piled high with fresh bento boxes, coffee, cold drinks and souvenirs. The price



Related Article Train journeys The world’s most affordable luxury train journeys (from as little as $14) ¥7730 ($68) for premium or ¥5150 ($45) for a basic fare. Kintetsu is a private railway company, so the Japan Rail (JR) Pass isn’t valid on the Shimakaze sightseeing route. Book premium tickets online and in advance during peak seasons and on weekends. See kintetsu.co.jp The verdict This is a train you should ride at least once to the most sacred shrine region in Japan. My one complaint? I only wish the ride was hours longer. Our rating out of five



★★★★★ The writer travelled as a guest of Mie Prefecture Tourism. See visitmie-japan.travel/en

World.title: A really ‘un-fun club’: How Jennifer Robinson connected Amber Heard and Brittany Higgins
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life A really ‘un-fun club’: How Jennifer Robinson connected Amber Heard and Brittany Higgins Jacqueline Maley July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Jennifer Robinson was a child, she and her sister used to visit their grandma at work. When they were there, they knew they were never to answer the door – there might be a violent man on the other side of it. They knew that the children they played with there were traumatised; their grandmother, Philipa Cracknell, told them so. In the accepting way that children have, they normalised what grandma – a domestic violence survivor herself – did for her job. She worked at Bonnie, a shelter for abused women escaping abusive men, only the second to be established in NSW. “I had a really early experience of understanding the dynamics of domestic violence and how that plays out for families and children,” Robinson says now. “That left a mark on me that I hadn’t appreciated. It wasn’t until my late 30s that I really sat down and asked my grandmother more questions about her life.” Jennifer Robinson turned her legal career fighting for free speech into a crusade for women who are victim-survivors of sexual abuse and assault. Mark Rogers Decades later, Robinson – now a London-based human rights lawyer who had helped defend WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, among other cases – was hanging out with her grandmother on the NSW south coast, on a break from her own work. Her grandmother was depressed and, over a whisky, Robinson asked her why.



“Because, you know, ‘You’re living down the south coast, it’s beautiful, you’re around family, retired, what is wrong with this picture?’” Robinson recounts. “And she was so upset. She said, ‘I just heard the statistics on violence against women on the radio, and it hasn’t gotten better from my time in the refuge.’” That set Robinson thinking. “I was like, ‘I have to find a way to work on violence against women, but what is my way of doing this?’ I’m a free-speech lawyer. What am I going to do?’” And then, Robinson says, “the #MeToo movement happened”. “I was like, ‘OK, I’m a free-speech lawyer. I defend defamation cases. This is what I can do.’” Robinson went on to do it, with great success, most notably in the case of Amber Heard, the actor and ex-wife of actor Johnny Depp. In 2020, Heard gave evidence about the abuse she suffered at the hands of her ex-husband, in the libel suit Depp brought against the UK’s The Sun newspaper, naming him as a “wife beater”.



The court’s decision, that the newspaper’s description of Depp was “substantially true”, and that 12 of the alleged 14 incidents of violence had occurred, should have vindicated her. But in 2022, Depp successfully sued Heard for defamation in a US court, after she wrote an opinion piece for the Washington Post. She didn’t name Depp in the piece but described herself as a survivor of domestic violence. Robinson with Julian Assange after the Wikileaks founder secured his freedom. X.com Heard’s case is the fulcrum of the new Australian film Silenced, adapted from the book How Many More Women?, which Robinson co-wrote with Dr Keina Yoshida. The documentary film, from International Emmy-award winning producers Selina Miles and Blayke Hoffman, is about the weaponisation of defamation law against women who speak out about sexual assault and abuse. It makes the case that the legal system is being used to discredit, intimidate and bankrupt victim-survivors. It focuses on three women to make its point: Heard, Colombian journalist Catalina Ruiz-Navarro, who faced multiple legal suits from Colombian filmmaker Ciro Guerra after she published a #MeToo exposé on him; and finally, Brittany Higgins, who needs no introduction to Australian audiences. In 2021, Higgins did a television interview with journalist Lisa Wilkinson alleging she was raped by fellow political staffer Bruce Lehrmann in 2019.



In the film, Higgins recounts leaving the Parliament House office of their boss, Defence Industry Minister Linda Reynolds, where the assault occurred. “I left, and things were different after that,” she says. “I was different after that.” A 2022 criminal trial was aborted due to juror misconduct, and in 2024 Lehrmann sued Network Ten and Lisa Wilkinson for defamation for airing Higgins’ story. The judgment by the Federal Court’s Justice Michael Lee found, on the balance of probabilities, that Lehrmann had raped Higgins. From left: Robinson, Brittany Higgins and Catalina Ruiz-Navarro in Silenced. Michael Latham Since then, Higgins has herself been sued for defamation, successfully, by her former boss Linda Reynolds. However, that suit does not feature in the film, as the focus is the weaponisation of defamation laws by alleged perpetrators to silence survivors. I meet Robinson and Higgins the morning following the Australian debut of Silenced at the Sydney Film Festival (its international debut was at the Sundance Film Festival in January). Robinson plays delightedly with Higgins’ new baby Freddie, who has accompanied his mother to Sydney from their home in Victoria. After a few minutes, the baby’s father, Higgins’ partner David Sharaz, spirits him away in search of coffee and we settle on sofas to talk about the film.



Both women are wearing blue jeans and the energy between them is easy, with Robinson occasionally taking a protective lead to answer on behalf of Higgins, particularly when it comes to questions on legally contentious topics. “I’m a big believer in the power of storytelling,” Robinson says of the film, on which she is an executive producer. “Speech about violence against women is absolutely in the public interest, when you think about the extent of the problem, how many women in Australia are affected by it. “And as I say, over and over, we can’t begin to tackle it if we can’t talk about it.” Higgins has had a friendship with Robinson ever since the criminal trial of her alleged rapist, Lehrmann, during which Robinson sent her messages of support. It was on the strength of their friendship that Higgins agreed to participate in the film. “It took a while for me to finally go, ‘I’m going to do this’,” Higgins says of her involvement. “I have very natural hesitancy towards a media lens.” But, Higgins adds with a laugh, “she’s a very hard person to say no to”.



The film depicts the heavy psychological toll the litigation takes on all the women, not least because the media spotlight is accompanied by torrents of internet abuse. In the case of Amber Heard, the abuse spilled over into real life. The film shows her arriving at London’s Royal Courts of Justice as Depp’s fans yell misogynistic hatred at her. Related Article Lunch with The international lawyer who specialises in breaking the silence “Honestly, it was horrific,” says Robinson. “I’ve never seen anything like it, and you know, I worked on Julian Assange’s trial. I felt under threat from the most powerful government in the world … but I’ve never been attacked online as I was when I was representing Amber Heard.” Higgins, who has also weathered much internet abuse, not to mention intense and sometimes malicious media scrutiny, says that the treatment “does fundamentally change you in a way that it’s difficult to articulate meaningfully. You definitely become hardened, and you definitely learn to be guarded.” In one poignant scene in the film, Heard and Higgins meet and embrace. “We are in a really, un-fun club,” Heard quips.



Robinson also cops online abuse (according to one charmer, she has a “punchable face, like Amber”). She splits her time between her practice in London, and her home on the NSW south coast. She surfs to unwind, and is in therapy. Robinson says she is concerned by “a real backsliding in women’s rights globally”. I ask Robinson and Higgins what they think of the contemporary backlash against feminism, from the rise of the manosphere, to the elevation of tradwife culture, as well as the pushback against reproductive rights in the United States and other countries. “I mean, to an extent, there’s almost a compliment in there, that we did gain meaningful ground, so much so that it galvanised an opposing force to reclaim territory,” says Higgins. But, she adds, the rise of what she dubs the “online metasphere of misogyny content” has spread into other areas of life.



“That language has become normalised and metabolised, even by politicians,” Higgins says. “The veil has dropped ... people are out and open and saying these things. It’s scary … because I know it will have a trickle-down effect on the next woman who decides to come forward.” Related Article Sunday Life Frances Rings just did something no other Australian has. She leads this year’s Trailblazers Robinson says she is concerned by “a real backsliding in women’s rights globally”. “When there’s a lot of misogyny in the online space and in public discussion … that has a knock-on effect for violence against women. Those two things are connected in very direct ways.” But both women are optimistic about the advances already made, and Robinson says that “I actually don’t think that we can walk back the progress that was made with #MeToo”.



Higgins points to affirmative consent laws, anti-stealthing laws (which criminalise removing or not using a condom without your sexual partner’s consent) and better courtroom protections for alleged victims of sexual assault (reforms she has advocated for) as proof of progress. “As my grandma said, it’s one step forward, two steps back, but then we progress again,” says Robinson. Robinson’s grandmother, who features in the film, is a common thread throughout it. “What I love about my grandmother’s story is she reminds us how recent the gains were,” Robinson says. “She was lucky to have a bank account. When she left my grandfather, she couldn’t get credit to buy bunk beds for my mum and my aunt because she needed her husband’s signature.” Perhaps the greatest act of defiance is survival. Cracknell, now 89 years old, was at the film’s Sydney premiere, glowing with pride and particularly eager to meet Higgins. The two had a long chat, Higgins tells me. Silenced screens at the Melbourne International Film Festival from August 6-23 and in cinemas nationally from September 3. World.title: Visiting wineries is a waste of time. I already know what I like
World.content:
Reviews & adviceFoodie travel Opinion Visiting wineries is a waste of time. I already know what I like Brian Johnston Travel writer July 30, 2026 — 5:00am

July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Some time ago, in the mists of time, probably during the 1990s, cellar doors became a thing. Three decades on and we’re still visiting them. They’ve become a staple of escorted tours and weekend getaways. Let me make a confession. Cellar doors aren’t enjoyable, and I suspect I’m not alone in that view. But it’s the dislike that dare not speak its name, because cellar doors tick trendy traveller boxes: cultured, food-minded, local, experiential, social-media friendly. Illustration: Jamie Brown But I don’t know what the enduring travel fashion for visiting grape farms is all about. Why not pig farms, or pickle farms? I only need to hear about the wine-making process once. And I only have to see a wine cellar once: rows of old barrels (French oak!) festooned with cobwebs in a gloomy dungeon.



Or OK, maybe twice, since others are warehouses with big stainless-steel vats. But I guarantee that the words, “That was a beautiful industrial vat” will never be part of your post-travel dinner conversation. 



About 50 years ago in Australia, the term cellar door could be taken literally. Wine bottles were stored in cool cellars and sold to customers who quickly went on their way. By the 1990s however the emergence of hobbyist winemakers had seen cellar doors become buildings in which passersby tasted wine. They were great for the owners, who benefited from the large margins on each bottle of wine sold. One of the enduring misapprehensions of cellar doors is that you get a bargain. And although many cellar doors are rustic cliches, many have become agro-tourism businesses run by managers who’ve never picked a grape in their lives. Cellar doors then began offering restaurants, shops, museums and concerts. They were no longer simply about buying wine, rather about consuming wine on the spot and being upsold an “experience”. And that’s when cellar doors began to fill up with tour-coach groups, drunken friends, wedding parties, oenophile mansplainers, Instagram poseurs and families with rambunctious kids.



Not many visitors want to buy wine, or to learn much about the skill that goes into winemaking. And fair enough. Most of us already know what types of wine we like. Related Article Western Australia This Aussie wine region is outstanding, even if you don’t drink It doesn’t matter whether the bottle costs $10 or $200, whether you can detect hints of strawberry or old leather, or whether the grapes were picked at midnight under a full moon. You either like it, or you don’t. What’s more, you know you’re never going to pair your wine again with buffalo-milk cheese, or dark chocolate and sea salt. You’re never again going to realise it tastes less acidic after you’ve eaten a macadamia nut than it did before. You want something you can drink after work, or with your daily dinner. Something you can reliably find at your local bottle shop. I say skip the cellar door, and just enjoy the wine-country scenery.

Opinion Brian Johnston seemed destined to become a travel writer: he is an Irishman born in Nigeria and raised in Switzerland, who has lived in Britain and China and now calls Australia home.

World.title: The type of buyer that just dropped out of the property market
World.content:
PropertyNewsResidential property The type of buyer that just dropped out of the property market Alice Uribe July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The number of first home buyers looking to take out a home loan has fallen in a year even as property prices soften in some parts of the country and investors exit the market. First home buyer demand nationally rose at the end of 2025 and in early 2026, before dropping back in April, data from credit data company Equifax shows. By last month, mortgage demand from new home buyers was down almost 20 per cent compared with the same time in 2025. Higher interest rates, concerns over buying in a falling market, property-related budget reforms and a lack of supply have led to reduced demand from first home hopefuls, experts say. Confidence has also dipped among this cohort, with some now holding back as they wait for property prices to reach a floor. According to Equifax, demand for mortgages from first home buyers jumped by 13.7 per cent in October compared with the year prior. This was bettered only by a 17.1 per cent spike year-on-year in December.



Equifax chief solutions officer Kevin James said its data tracks the number of loan inquiries made where an applicant has never had a mortgage, to determine demand. More first home buyers, he said, looked to enter the market in the second half of 2025 in part due to the October expansion of the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme. “We saw the first home buyers come in … and we saw some real positive stories come out of that,” he said. First home buyer mortgage demand jumped after the federal government expanded the 5 per cent deposit scheme. James Brickwood But by April this year, Equifax data showed demand for first home loans down 2.9 per cent on the same time in 2025. In May, demand was 13.4 per cent lower, and there was a 17.2 per cent year-on-year drop in June. Three rate hikes over 2026 and serviceability challenges had prompted first home buyers to hang back, James said, but now many were also taking a wait-and-see approach, expecting prices to soften as investor demand slows.



“I think people are just waiting to see what’s going to actually happen with interest rates and with pricing,” he said. Cost-of-living pressures, rate hikes and weak consumer sentiment were helping to constrain activity generally, but Dr Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief residential economist, said first home buyers were also facing deposit hurdles and borrowing limits, with some now more cautious. “That caution is driven by the fact that prices overall are falling …they don’t want to buy on a Friday to find out their home is worth less than on a Monday,” she said. Sydney and Melbourne fell more than 3 per cent last quarter. “It means that they’re perhaps feeling apprehensive about buying in a falling market because they obviously don’t want to get into negative equity. But then it also drives this other thought process that, ‘if I wait a bit longer, I might be able to get greater value for money’.”



Domain was expecting minor price falls nationally, with deeper falls in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra, while banks were tipping further falls of about 5 to 10 per cent nationally. Related Article Property prices What the median house price buys around Australia now Jack Elliott, national first home buyer specialist at Alcove Mortgages, highlighted low confidence and a reduction in buying capacity due to higher interest rates. Still, some first-timers were making preparations for the upcoming spring selling season, with inquiries ticking up. “Naturally, winter is always a little bit slower. You’ve got fewer listings, fewer buyers, with fewer properties to purchase,” he said, adding clients reported less competition from investors now. Indeed, investors started to exit the property market after the federal budget in May introduced negative-gearing and capital-gains tax concessions reforms.



According to preliminary Equifax data, there was a 9.8 per cent reduction in demand year-on-year in May from investors, or those with two or more mortgages. By June, there was a 12.7 per cent drop compared with the same time the previous year. “I think people are actually seeing some of the investor market softening,” James said. There is less demand from property investors for mortgages. James Brockwood Enosh Tampoe, a mortgage and finance advisor at Smartmove, agreed there were fewer investors in the market now. But there were also fewer listings as some investors held on to their properties due to grandfathering of negative-gearing arrangements. “If you’re a first home buyer who’s actively looking, you can potentially get one for a good deal there, which a few of my clients have been able to do. But then, in saying that as well, they have obviously a lot less to pick from, given their supply has dropped significantly.”



Related Article Property prices Meet the home owners who don’t mind if their home falls in value KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said while first home buyers were sitting on the sidelines, so were investors. “When you’ve seen the investor activity drop off historically, you see house-price-values growth cool, which is an opportunity for first-time buyers to get into the market,” he said. “But I think, just given levels of uncertainty at the moment, probably … the next six months, everyone’s going to be sort of sitting on their hands, waiting to see what happens with prices, interest rates, and the broader economy.”

World.title: Melbourne Fashion Festival rebrands amid fresh strategic direction
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleFashionMelbourne Fashion Festival Melbourne Fashion Festival rebrands amid fresh strategic direction Courtney Thompson July 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The perennial fashion debate pitting Melbourne against Sydney may soon be obsolete as Melbourne Fashion Festival today announces its rebranding to Australian Fashion Festival. The change is part of a suite of updates that seek to deepen the organisation’s commitment to being a consumer-led program, strengthen designer relationships and reinforce their nationwide celebration of Australian fashion. Models Bela Palcio and Trang Nguyen wearing outfits by Australian designers Alemais and Bianca Spender, respectively. Eddie Jim “We need to have a national name because the designers aren’t only exclusive to Victoria,” says Launa Inman, chair of the Australian Fashion Festival board, who explains the festival’s usual two-week program will be expanded to include events all year round. “The fashion industry is changing – consumers now engage with fashion through live events or retail experiences, social media, cultural moments, even destination travel,” she says. “The name change really supported a broader strategy to lift designer engagement, grow our audiences, and then also strengthen our commercial partnerships.”



Though before you rid your wardrobe of black, Inman is quick to note the festival will remain anchored to the Garden City. “It’s still very much going to be based in Melbourne,” she says. “We are not losing sight of our Victorian designers.” Related Article Opinion

Culture wars Which city is better, Sydney or Melbourne? I’m in a unique position to decide Damien Woolnough Fashion editor It’s a move supported by the Australian Fashion Council, which oversees Australian Fashion Week, the separate and more industry-focused event that takes place in Sydney every May. “It’s a good change because Australian designers don’t operate within state boundaries,” says Marianne Perkovic, chair of the Australian Fashion Council. “If we really want to compete and give our designers the best chance to showcase their great talents, we have to start talking nationally, and internationally, about Australian fashion.” The news comes three months after Caroline Ralphsmith resigned as chief executive of the organisation amid a tough period financially.



According to the last financial report, the event filed a loss of $711,390 in 2025, with revenue falling to $4.57 million from $5.75 million in the 2024 financial year. The financial results for the 2026 festival will be released later this year, though festival attendance was up 47 per cent year-on-year. “Our financial wellbeing is very important because without us being financially stable, it’s very difficult to be creative,” Inman says, which also goes to explain why they didn’t replace Ralph with a new chief executive. Rather than installing a new chief executive, they have split the role, hiring Prue Mahar from REA Group and Victorian Racing Group as executive director and Damien Woolnough-Reid (former fashion editor of this masthead) as creative director. “It’s a strategic investment in the leadership, making sure we’ve got absolutely the right team around us to strengthen the momentum for the festival’s future,” says Inman. The approach is welcomed by designer Bianca Spender, who is excited about the festival building upon its offering for consumers to engage with designers and their clothes.



“The festival has a really wonderful atmosphere that is very unique,” Spender says. “There’s a lot of noise out there and we’re living in a virtual world in the way that we absorb clothes. Actually feeling it, seeing how the fabric moves, really engaging with it is so important now more than ever.” Inman agrees: “It’s all about offering those memorable experiences that will help the Australian designers connect emotionally with anyone who loves style.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Wellington not alone in struggling to get public transport up and running, Dutch expert says
World.content:
Why cities struggle to make public transport work Morning Report Download MP3 3m

It's not just Wellington - cities around the world struggle to change their transport infrastructure, an expert reveals.

Public Transport Association Australia New Zealand (PTAANZ) flew in a Dutch expert to speak about the challenges to delivering better mobility networks - including walking cycling and public transport - in cities.

Professor in urban mobility futures at the University of Amsterdam Marco te Brömmelstroet told RNZ he came to have a conversation about tackling "the paralysis many cities around the world are facing".

"So Wellington is facing [challenges]. It's a uniquely beautiful place, but it's not unique in facing this problem of transforming urban mobility systems," he said.

Wellington City councillors last month voted to ditch the $139 million Golden Mile project.

The upgrade of the Golden Mile, which stretches from Lambton Quay to Courtenay Place, sought to remove cars from the latter during the day, widen footpaths, create a cycle lane, and improve lighting.

Te Brömmelstroet's studies showed most city dwellers did not oppose change, but that a vocal minority skewed perceptions of public support for projects.

Professor in urban mobility futures at the University of Amsterdam Marco te Brömmelstroet. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said he did not know how to overcome this problem: "If I would have the answer to that, I would be rich by now."

However, he said, the current car-dependent system could not be sustained: it required enormous amounts of money, space and maintenance, despite only being a few decades old.

He explained that the foundations of this system - concrete, steel, asphalt - were now too expensive to maintain and re-create it.

"So we need more choices so that people can also develop and have a good life without being dependent on the car," he said.

He added that the current system saddled individuals with more costs than that of a large public transport infrastructure project.

The Golden Mile project sought to remove cars from Courtenay Place during the day, widen footpaths, and create a cycle lane. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He cited the expenses of owning cars and refuelling as examples. On top of that, there were non-financial costs displaced onto other members of society: road deaths, air and noise pollution, or isolation.

"So actually, you could say that we cannot afford to not change that system in the future."

Te Brömmelstroet said public transport was connected to many societal issues; it could fight isolation and foster connection and independence, especially for the elderly and children.

"Children have lost their right to roam through the city, to go to friends, to have autonomous trips through the city, which is crucial for the development of their brains and the development of their basically social being."

Wellington Railway Station. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He identified one challenge in changing societal thinking as the loss of identity for some locals who had been born into a system of car dependency.

This mindset was evident in one passerby on Lambton Quay who told RNZ he enjoyed driving and wanted people to adapt to driving cars more.

"I'd say most people just see it as going from A to B, whereas I more enjoy the journey. That's why I've got an old school car," he said.

However, PTAANZ chief executive Lauren Streifer said there was more to be gained in investing in public transport.

"We've seen across the world that when you invest significant amounts of money in public and active transport, it has exponential results, whether it's health outcomes, societal outcomes, economic benefit - $3 billion from rail alone in New Zealand every year," she said.

"We know that investing in this creates long-term returns for society."

PTAANZ chief executive Lauren Streifer RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The PTAANZ team took conference attendees on a tour of the long-awaited Te Ara Tupua cycleway.

The $348m walking and cycling path between Ngauranga and Petone opened in May.

It was celebrated at the conference as a success story of Wellingtonian infrastructure - especially as a vital resilience project, having already weathered storms since opening.

"It's so exciting for our sector, but it's actually more exciting for the community who finally get to use it and get to see all the opportunities that open up when you can actually access the network," said Streifer.

But many other projects had struggled to get to the finish line.

The Te Ara Tupua walking and cycling path. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Councillor Nicola Young said the Golden Mile project failed because of spiraling costs and changing scopes.

"It started out as a light rail project which would provide value uplift to all the properties adjacent to the light rail route, which is why it was going to Island Bay.

"And then that was killed off when they realised we couldn't afford it and some doubts about its value.

"And then it became part of Let's Get Wellington Moving and then that died. Now we've got a situation where the city has no money and businesses in the city ... are really struggling."

Councillor Nicola Young. RNZ / Sharon Brettkelly

She said the "botched" project had made Wellingtonians wary of change after so much money had gone "down the drain".

Around $12m had already been spent on the Golden Mile when the plug was pulled.

Young called for restraint, for targeted, affordable projects, especially as residents were struggling with costs of living.

"We don't have to have everything gold plated. We don't need to have bike racks like the one on the Terrace, which was $560,000, for example, or was the [$2.4] million lavatory block in Taranaki Street.

"You know, we need to do things simply and well until we can afford more elaborate things,"

And pedestrians walking down Lambton Quay agreed with her.

One said: "People want to see some of the basics done, so get it right, get it sorted, make it easy to come into the city and then people won't worry about parking."

World.title: Scaled-back Scott Base redevelopment plans signed off by Cabinet
World.content:
Redevelopment of Scott Base to get underway Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Plans to redevelop Scott Base have been signed off by Cabinet, after being scaled back to get the project under budget.

The project was previously paused and reset because the Antarctica New Zealand board said it could not be delivered within its budget.

Board chair Leon Grice said the organisation had come up with a more affordable plan, which included refurbishing the Hillary Field Centre instead of replacing it.

"So by getting more life out of a building that didn't need to come down, and by building in a more traditional way, we were able to get it under budget."

Scott Base. Antarctia NZ / Al Chapman

Grice said redeveloping Scott Base was crucial to continuing New Zealand's legacy in the region.

"We've had continuous presence there since 1957. So this project continues that legacy, and continues to support our science programme which is crucial to understanding the planet."

The redevelopment would increase the total size of the base by about 1500 square metres.

That included a new Base Services Building, refurbishment of the Hillary Field Centre, and replacement of ageing water and power infrastructure.

Building in Antarctica was incredibly difficult, due to logistics and the weather, Grice said.

"You can build from October to February. So you have to have all of the building materials supplied the February before your October start."

"You can't make any mistakes in terms of what you're building, because there's no hardware store to pop down to and pick up an extra bag of bolts."

Science in Antarctica was more important now than ever to help understand climate change, Grice said.

"Last year, we did all the logistics and support for a multinational science team that did a 500 metres ice claw drill... to get 20 million years of atmospheric record... so that will be an incredibly rich resource that will be studied for many many years."

World.title: Nauru officially changes name to Naoero 'after thoughtful deliberation', bypassing referendum
World.content:
Nauru has officially changed its name to 'Naoero', the Micronesian Island nation's governments announced in a statement on Wednesday night.

The Nauruan parliament had passed a constitutional amendment in May to rename the country 'Naoero' after the proposal was initially tabled by President David Adeang in January.

Adeang said at the time that while the name 'Nauru' had been recognised internationally since the island's independence, the proposed change sought to "more faithfully honour our nation's heritage, our language, and our identity".

However, a national referendum was expected to follow to complete the constitutional procedures.

Nauru is the world's smallest independent republic, with a population of approximately 12,000 and a land area of 21 square kilometres.

The government said in May that the name change would be reflected across national official records and symbols, and official identity regionally and internationally, including at the United Nations.

"The Republic of Naoero is the new official designation for what was previously known as Nauru. The abbreviated form will be Naoero, with the code updated to NRO, and the people will be referred to as dei-Naoero," the government statement said.

It added that Adeang delivered his opening message to parliament on 20 July and addressed the decision to return the country to its traditional name, Naoero, "following extensive discussions".

"The decision not to pursue a referendum was reached after thoughtful deliberation that Naoero is not a new name seeking acceptance by the people.

"It is already the identity of the people, is on the national coat of arms, and spoken in the community; and importantly is allowed by the Constitution.

"While a referendum is intended to determine the will of the people, the name Naoero has never been lost, but rather waiting to be fully embraced."

According to the Nauru government, a Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026, proposing to rename Nauru to Naoero was tabled pon 29 January. It was followed by a layover period of 90 days and the unanimous vote by the members of parliament in favour of the change.

Speaker Marcus Stephen then certified the amendment on 13 May to enact the name change.

"International organisations and countries have formally been notified of the change and have begun making the transition," the government statement said.

"Naoero is the beginning of renewed national pride, and a new chapter founded on unity, responsibility, patriotism, better health, education, and sustainable development.

"The future of Naoero will be built by learning from the mistakes of the past and using their experience to make wiser decisions for the generations to come."

World.title: Glasgow Commonwealth Games: Gold for Samoa's super Stowers
World.content:
Samoa has a gold medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games after weightlifter Seine Stowers won the women's 77kg category overnight.

She lifted a Games record 107kg in the snatch, and 130kg in the clean-and-jerk, for a Games record total of 237.

The silver medal went to England's Isabella Brown, who lifted a total of 229 kg, and bronze went to Wales' Laura Hughes, with a total lift of 224kg.

It is Samoa's second medal of the Glasgow Games, with a silver, also in weightliting, to John Tafi earlier in the week.

Another Samoan weightlifter, Emmanuel Shalom Palota Ulimasao, came sixth in the men's 94kg category, and Sefulu Seuao was competing in the women's 86kg on Thursday morning. After the snatch, she was in seventh place with a lift of 96kg.

In other results overnight, a number of Pacific island athletes had a season's best performance in the track and field.

Fiji's Heleina Valetta Young ran an equal season's best of 24.45 seconds in the women's 200m heats but did not qualify - 23.88 was the slowest qualification time.

Tuvalu's Vaioleta Luka also ran a season's best in the event, but she was disqualified so the time is not officially recorded.

Papua New Guinea's Isila Apkup ran a time of 25.88 for sixth in her heat.

In the men's mile, there were season's best times run by Fiji's Yeshnil Karan (4:12:28) and PNG's Jiuteis Robinson (4:19:14) but they were not quick enough to progress.

Two PNG runners featured in the men's 400m hurdles heats, Daniel Baul and William Camilus Peka. They both ran season's bests of 52.83 and 54.16 seconds respectively, but they did not progress.

Nauru's Jonathan-Deiwea Detageouwa and Tonga's Penisimani Taeiloa qualified for the final of the men's shotput, to be held Friday morning.

Niue's Caleb Misipeka threw a personal best of 11.10 metres but did not make the cut.

Tonga's Ata Maama Tu'utafaiva and Samoa's Nu'u Tuilefano were featuring in the women's shotput on Thursday morning.

In the boxing ring, Fiji's Jasmine Daunakamakama beat Sri Lanka's Keshani Hansika in the women's 57kg quarterfinals. Daunakamakama is now guaranteed a medal as there is no bronze medal fight in boxing - once a boxer is beaten, they cannot fight again, so the losing semifinalists both get bronze.

In the men's 90+kg, Samoa's Michael Seko lost his quarterfinal to India's Narender Narender.

There were no wins for Pacific lawn bowlers overnight, but the action was continuing Thursday morning.

World.title: Why KiwiSaver members are $10b richer - and which fund returned 98% in a year
World.content:
KiwiSaver members ended the June quarter a combined $10 billion richer, thanks to their contributions and market returns.

And one fund returned nearly 100 percent over 12 months.

Morningstar's latest KiwiSaver survey shows returns ranged from an average 3.3 percent in the quarter for conservative fund to 11.9 percent for the aggressive category.

Morningstar said markets had benefited as investors started to look through the geopolitical tensions that dominated the start of the year. International equities had delivered solid positive returns in New Zealand dollar terms.

"New Zealand equities also recovered, although they continued to lag global peers amid subdued domestic economic conditions and relatively weak earnings expectations."

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Morningstar said many funds that suffered falls in the first months of the year had since recovered.

"For KiwiSaver investors, the June quarter was a reminder of how quickly market sentiment can shift once uncertainty begins to recede. Diversified portfolios that experienced heightened volatility in the March quarter generally participated well in the recovery as risk assets rallied and energy markets normalised."

Morningstar said the quarter also showed that while events offshore could trigger sharp market moves, their long-term impact was determined by whether they materially altered economic growth or the profitability of listed companies.

Morningstar said the top performer in the quarter was Koura's clean energy fund, which delivered a 31.8 percent return.

Koura founder Rupert Carlyon said clean energy funds were being boosted by AI and high oil prices. There was significant demand for energy, he said.

The lowest performance was from Koura's bitcoin scheme, which fell 13 percent.

Over a year, Kernel's global clean energy fund was the standout, up 98.4 percent, while Koura's bitcoin fund was down 41.9 percent.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson. Supplied / Kernel

Kernel founder Dean Anderson agreed there had been a surge in energy demand. "Part of that is obviously driven by AI and data centre growth... they are hungry for energy."

He said fears about energy security were also driving interest in renewable energy sources.

"Governments are looking at ways they can expedite energy security through all levers and renewables are one of them."

He said near-100 percent returns were not normal and should not be expected. "But that flows on to the broader conversation, what we are seeing in markets generally is that very wide dispersion. Some sectors are faring incredibly well where others have been very much lagging. Whether those same sectors continue to have the momentum going forward is the question mark."

Among conservative funds, Morningstar said ASB performed best over a year, up 7.9 percent, and three years, up 7.7 percent.

Of moderate funds, MAS was best over a year, up 10.7 percent, and ASB was best over three, up 9.4 percent a year.

Among balanced funds, Fisher Funds was ranked first over a year, up 16.1 percent, and Kernel's balanced fund was up 12.7 percent a year, the best over three years.

AMP was the top performer over one year among growth funds, up 21.5 percent, and three years, up 14.2 percent a year.

Among aggressive funds, Koura was top over one year with 26.5 percent and Kernel was ranked first over three years at 17.1 percent a year.
